治詩經 字天祐行二年四十四七月初六日生
曾祖貴 祖翺 父昱〔知縣〕 母單氏
永感下 兄恩 弟息 娶高氏
順天府鄉試第一百十九名 會試第一百七十五名
punctuated:
王汝楫〔貫山東濟南府德州，民籍，國子生，治書經，字利民，行二，年三十八，十月初一日生〕。曾祖樔〔教授〕，祖中〔教諭〕，父寧，前母顧氏，母曹氏。慈侍下，兄汝翼〔知縣〕、汝爲、汝明、汝礪，弟汝欽、汝輔、汝舟、汝咨、汝揆、汝器、汝相，娶楊氏。山東鄉試第四十二名，會試第九十四名。

張志選〔貫福建泉州府晉江縣，民籍，府學增廣生，治易經，字以學，行二，年三十三，十二月二十三日生〕。曾祖寬〔教授〕，祖秉德，父良保〔典史〕，母薛氏。重慶下，兄志魁，弟志純、志騰、志顯、志實、志尹，娶黃氏。福建鄉試第六十五名，會試第六十三名。

杜朝聘〔貫山東兗州府東平州東阿縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字莘夫，行六，年四十一，二月二十六日生〕。曾祖麟，祖昂〔贈通判〕，父萱〔知府〕，母張氏。具慶下，兄朝卿，弟朝言、朝雍，娶劉氏。山東鄉試第四十八名，會試第二百九十五名。

馮惠〔貫直隸河間府滄州鹽山縣，竈籍，國子生，治詩經，字天祐，行二，年四十四，七月初六日生〕。曾祖貴，祖翱，父昱〔知縣〕，母單氏。永感下，兄恩，弟悳，娶高氏。順天府鄉試第一百十九名，會試第一百七十五名。
translation_en:
Wang Ruji, registered in Dezhou, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Limin, he ranked second in his family, and he was aged thirty-eight, born on the first day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Chao, a Prefectural School Professor; his grandfather was Zhong, a County School Instructor; his father was Ning; his father's former wife was Lady Gu, and his mother was Lady Cao. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Ruyi, a District Magistrate, Ruwei, Ruming, and Ruli; his younger brothers were Ruqin, Rufu, Ruzhou, Ruzi, Rukui, Ruqi, and Ruxiang. He married Lady Yang and placed forty-second in the Shandong Provincial Examination and ninety-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Zhixuan, registered in Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was an additional student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Yixue, he ranked second in his family, and he was aged thirty-three, born on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Kuan, a Prefectural School Professor; his grandfather was Bingde; his father was Liangbao, a County Registrar; and his mother was Lady Xue. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brother was Zhikui, and his younger brothers were Zhichun, Zhiteng, Zhixian, Zhishi, and Zhiyin. He married Lady Huang and placed sixty-fifth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and sixty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Du Chaopin, registered in Dong'e County, Dongping Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Songs; his courtesy name was Shenfu, he ranked sixth in his family, and he was aged forty-one, born on the twenty-sixth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Lin; his grandfather was Ang, posthumously granted the title of Assistant Prefect; his father was Xuan, a Prefect; and his mother was Lady Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Chaoqing, and his younger brothers were Chaoyan and Chaoyong. He married Lady Liu and placed forty-eighth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and two hundred ninety-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Feng Hui, registered in Yanshan County, Cangzhou, Hejian Prefecture, Zhili, belonged to a salt-producing household and was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Songs; his courtesy name was Tianyou, he ranked second in his family, and he was aged forty-four, born on the sixth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Gui; his grandfather was Ao; his father was Yu, a District Magistrate; and his mother was Lady Shan. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was En, and his younger brother was De. He married Lady Gao and placed one hundred nineteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and one hundred seventy-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Qiao You, courtesy name Dezheng, was registered in a military household in Luoyang County, Henan Prefecture, Henan. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-seven, born on the twenty-fourth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Silao, his grandfather Hong, his father Xian, and his mother née Li; his mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brother was Zuo. He married a woman née Xu and was subsequently betrothed to a woman née Liu. He placed third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 208th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Rao Sicong, courtesy name Ziwen, was registered in a civilian household in Xingan County, Linjiang Prefecture, Jiangxi. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked fifth among his brothers and was aged twenty-four, born on the eighteenth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shunheng, his grandfather Dengyong, his father Guanzhi, and his mother née Xu; his parents and grandparents were living. His elder brothers were Tian’en, Tianxi, Tianxian, Shizhen, and Siyan, and his younger brothers Siming, Sizeng, and Simeng. He married a woman née Yao. He placed seventy-fourth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 263rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Xuan, courtesy name Zhongxi, was registered in a military household in Qingyuan Guard, Guangxi, and was a native of Huating County in the directly administered metropolitan region. An Instructor at the Taicang Subprefectural School specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the ninth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lin, his grandfather Qing, his father Chong, and his mother née Yan; both parents were living. His elder brothers were Rong and Can, and his younger brother Sui. He married a woman née Qin. He placed twenty-first in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and seventieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Yingkui, courtesy name Zhixiang, was registered in a civilian household in Taihe County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-five, born on the fourth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shaoyi, his grandfather Zhongyong, his father Changrong, and his mother née Hu; both parents were living. His younger brother was Yingbi. He married a woman née Jin. He placed fortieth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 159th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Gao Jian, courtesy name Gongjing, was registered in a civilian household in Mianzhou, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty [?; the transcription has 午 in place of the expected 年], and born on the fourth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Ziqing; his grandfather, Benzheng; and his father, Teng, who was granted the title of Secretary in the Nanjing Ministry of Justice. His mother, née Li, was posthumously granted the title of Lady of Peace (anren); his stepmother, née Wang, was granted the same title. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Di, a Prefect; Jie, a tribute scholar (gongshi); and Ce. He married a woman née Gong. He ranked fourth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 260th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Tang Shiying, courtesy name Zicai, was registered in a military household of Pingyi Guard, Yunnan, and was a native of Luxi County, Huguang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-one, and born on the twelfth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Yi; his grandfather, Hong, held an honorary official title bestowed for longevity; and his father, Jing, held an honorary official title bestowed for public benefaction. His mother was née Wu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Shixian, and he married a woman née Zhang. He ranked eighth in the Yunnan–Guizhou Provincial Examination and forty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Ziwen, courtesy name Zaizhong, was registered in a civilian household in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was fourth in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the twenty-fourth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Jing; his grandfather, Heng (𢘆); and his father, Jian, an Assistant Prefect. His mother was née Huang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Ziyuan, Ziheng, and Zike; his younger brothers were Ziyan, Ziliang, Zili, and Zifang. He married a woman née Wang. He ranked twenty-first in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 107th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Sui, courtesy name Liangbo, was registered in a civilian household in Jiangling County, Jingzhou Prefecture, Huguang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged forty, and born on the twenty-seventh day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Shen; his grandfather, Jing, held an honorary official title bestowed for public benefaction; and his father, Yuan (㟶), was an Assistant Instructor. His mother was née Liu, and his stepmother was née Chen. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yu and Da. He married a woman née Shen and subsequently a woman née Xu. He ranked fifteenth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 311th in the Metropolitan Examination.

路珠〔貫河南衛輝府新鄉縣民籍，國子生，治易經，字子明，行二，年三十三，十二月二十八日生〕。曾祖坦，祖通，父睿，母曹氏。具慶下，兄寶，娶張氏。河南鄉試第三十三名，會試第一百五十七名。

趙國良〔貫陝西西安府同州軍籍，國子生，治書經，字邦遂，行三，年三十七，正月二十四日生〕。曾祖玉，祖琰〔贈監察御史〕，父繼爵〔按察司副使〕，母劉氏〔贈孺人〕，繼母劉氏〔贈孺人〕、張氏〔封孺人〕。慈侍下，兄國卿〔南京鴻臚寺序班〕、國相〔驛丞〕，弟國臣、國光、國獻、國明，娶王氏，繼娶雷氏。陝西鄉試第十六名，會試第二百六十二名。
translation_en:
Huang Guangsheng, registered in a civilian household in Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was an additional student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Mingju. Third in birth order, he was twenty-four years old and was born on the fifth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhen; his grandfather, Sheng, was a Registrar; and his father, Shou, was an Instructor. His mother was née Chen. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Guangyuan and Guangqing; his younger brothers were Guanghe, Guangji, and Guangzu. His wife was née Liu 留. He placed twenty-first in the Fujian Provincial Examination and eighty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Yi, registered in a civilian household in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Shicheng. Second in birth order, he was forty-four years old and was born on the second day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Weichu. His grandfather, Jingyang, was posthumously granted the title of Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue. His father, Tan, was a Prefect, posthumously granted the title of Grand Master for Constitutional Service. His mother, née Lin, was granted the title of Lady of Peace; his stepmother, née Tao, was granted the title of Lady of Respect. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His elder brother, Lun, was a Case Reviewer; his younger brothers were Shou, a Vice Magistrate, Zuan, and Ji, a Bureau Director in the Ministry of Revenue. His wife was née Lin. He placed ninth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 254th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lu Zhu, registered in a civilian household in Xinxiang County, Weihui Prefecture, Henan, was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ziming. Second in birth order, he was thirty-three years old and was born on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Tan; his grandfather was Tong; his father was Rui; and his mother was née Cao. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Bao, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed thirty-third in the Henan Provincial Examination and 157th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Guoliang, registered in a military household in Tongzhou, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Bangsui. Third in birth order, he was thirty-seven years old and was born on the twenty-fourth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yu. His grandfather, Yan, was posthumously granted the title of Investigating Censor. His father, Jijue, was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner. His mother, née Liu, and his stepmother, also née Liu, were each posthumously granted the title of Lady; another stepmother, née Zhang, was granted the title of Lady. His father was deceased, and he attended his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Guoqing, an Usher in the Court of State Ceremonial at Nanjing, and Guoxiang, a Station Master. His younger brothers were Guochen, Guoguang, Guoxian, and Guoming. His wife was née Wang; he subsequently married a woman née Lei. He placed sixteenth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 262nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

王祚〔貫大寧保定右衞，官籍，國子生，治詩經，字永錫，行一，年三十五，二月二十八日生〕。曾祖海〔百戶〕，祖鑑〔副千戶〕，父守憲〔訓導〕，母丁氏。具慶下，弟禧、禖、禎，娶李氏。順天府鄉試第一百三十三名，會試第二百七十二名。

translation_en:
Rong Kai, courtesy name Shunju, was registered in Daxing County, Shuntian Prefecture, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged forty, and born on the fifteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Bingzhong; his grandfather, Can; and his father, Jun. His father’s former wife was née Zhang, and his mother was née Du. His father was deceased and his mother living. He married a woman née Tian. He ranked ninety-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 165th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Qi, courtesy name Weiwang, was registered in Renqiu County, Hejian Prefecture, in the directly administered region, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was fourth in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Tinggui; his grandfather, Ming; and his father, Hao. His father’s former wife was née Wang, and his mother was née Li. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Tan, a deliberative official [?]; Zeng; and Yu, a Station Master. He married a woman née Shi and subsequently a woman née He. He ranked eightieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 130th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zuo, courtesy name Yongxi, was registered in the Baoding Right Guard of Daning, in an officer household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-five, and born on the twenty-eighth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Hai, a Company Commander; his grandfather was Jian, a Vice Battalion Commander; and his father was Shouxian, an Assistant Instructor. His mother was née Ding. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xi, Mei, and Zhen. He married a woman née Li. He ranked 133rd in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 272nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Li Shen, courtesy name Chaoyi, was registered in Xiangfu County, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, in a civilian household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was second in birth order, aged forty, and born on the eighth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Rang; his grandfather, Jin; and his father, Xiong, an Instructor. His mother was née Lei. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Jin, and his younger brothers were Shou, Hong, Wan, and Ying. He married a woman née Wu and subsequently a woman née Wang. He ranked eighteenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 112th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Gao Zhuo, courtesy name Shiyuan, was registered in Luanzhou, Yongping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. A student of the departmental school specializing in the Classic of Poetry, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-six, and born on the nineteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather Bing was a Police Chief; his grandfather Cong was a District Magistrate, posthumously awarded the prestige title Wenlin lang; his father Qian was a Prefect; and his mother, née Wu, was granted the title Lady (ruren). His mother alone survived. His elder brother was Shang, and his younger brothers were Lin and Guan [?]. He married a woman née Hao. He ranked thirty-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 244th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Jiaxiu, courtesy name Wenying, was registered with Haining Guard, Zhejiang, in a military household. A student of the Haiyan County school specializing in the Classic of Documents, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-eight, and born on the first day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather Zhu was honorifically appointed Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites and awarded the prestige title Zhengshi lang; his grandfather Ning was a Prefect; his father was Qihong; and his mother was née Cai. Both parents were deceased. His younger brothers were Yingqi and Yinglong. He married a woman née Wang. He ranked thirteenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 200th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Yiguan, courtesy name Lude, was registered in Fuqing County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, in a civilian household. An attached student of the county school specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-five, and born on the eleventh day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lu; his grandfather was Kuan; his father was Cheng; his mother was née Lin; and his stepmother was née Zhou. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yijing, Yizhong, Yixin, and Yifeng. He married a woman née Wu and subsequently a woman née Lin. He ranked fifty-second in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 259th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Qian, courtesy name Zigong, was registered in Fushun County, Xuzhou Prefecture, Sichuan, in a civilian household. A student of the county school specializing in the Classic of Documents, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fucai; his grandfather was Yongxiang; his father was Shangji; and his mother was née Yang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Wanyu. He married a woman née Che. He ranked thirty-sixth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and fifty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

汪宗元〔貫湖廣武昌府崇陽縣軍籍，縣學增廣生，治詩經，字子允，行一，年二十七，二月二十六日生〕。曾祖璉〔壽官〕，祖藻〔監生，封兵部主事〕，父文明〔知縣〕，母楊氏。重慶下，弟宗凱〔監生〕、宗皐、宗伊、宗召、宗順、宗南、宗光、宗介、宗軾、宗說。娶彭氏。湖廣鄉試第二十三名，會試第一百六名。

translation_en:
Wu Jie, registered in an official household of Shouzhou Guard in Zhili, was a student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zizheng; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-six years old, born on the twentieth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Quan, his grandfather Shu, and his father Lan; his mother was née Wang and his stepmother née Cui. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Kan and Qiao. He married a woman née Xie and subsequently women née Chen and née Zheng. He placed fortieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and three hundred fourteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Zongyuan, registered in a military household of Chongyang County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, was an additional student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Ziyun; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-sixth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lian, who held an honorary official title for longevity; his grandfather was Zao, a student of the Directorate of Education granted the title of Secretary in the Ministry of War; his father was Wenming, a County Magistrate, and his mother was née Yang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Zongkai, a student of the Directorate of Education, Zonggao, Zongyi, Zongzhao, Zongshun, Zongnan, Zongguang, Zongjie, Zongshi, and Zongshuo. He married a woman née Peng. He placed twenty-third in the Huguang Provincial Examination and one hundred sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Yingchen, registered in a civilian household of Kaocheng County, Suizhou, Kaifeng Prefecture, Henan, was a county-school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Gongji; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-three years old, born on the twenty-fifth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yi, his grandfather Quan, and his father Boji; his mother was née Li. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His elder brother was Yingtang, and his younger brothers were Yingjie, Yingshi, and Yingpin. He married a woman née Gao. He placed seventieth in the Henan Provincial Examination and three hundred seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Ying, registered in a military household of Sanyuan County, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi, was a county-school student specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Wenhai; he ranked fifth among his brothers and was thirty-eight years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ke, his grandfather Rang, and his father Run; his mother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Qi, Lan, Yi, and Jian. He married a woman née Du. He placed twentieth in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and two hundred third in the Metropolitan Examination.

高澄〔貫順天府固安縣官籍，國子生，治詩經，字肅卿，行三，年三十四，六月十二日生〕。曾祖全〔百戶〕，祖文〔百戶〕，父大琳，前母胡氏，母陳氏。慈侍下，兄清〔百戶〕、源，弟洪、湧、治、深、浦，娶楊氏。順天府鄉試第十六名，會試第二百五十六名。

translation_en:
Zheng Gong, courtesy name Zi’an, was registered in a civilian household in Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged forty-five, born on the eighth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Qing; his grandfather, Mingde; his father, Wenzuo; and his mother, née Cheng. His mother alone was still living. His elder brother was Liang, and his younger brothers were Xing, Qun, Zhe, Xian, Peng, and Jue. His wife was née Shu. He placed fifty-fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 160th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Gao Cheng, courtesy name Suqing, was registered in an official household in Gu’an County, Shuntian Prefecture. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked third among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the twelfth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather Quan and grandfather Wen were both company commanders. His father was Dalin; his father’s former wife was née Hu, and his mother was née Chen. His mother alone was still living. His elder brothers were Qing, a company commander, and Yuan; his younger brothers were Hong, Yong, Zhi, Shen, and Pu. His wife was née Yang. He placed sixteenth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 256th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Xilong, courtesy name Ruyan, was registered in an official household of the Weihui Front Guard Battalion under the Huaiqing Guard in Henan; his ancestral home was Lingling County, Huguang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked second among his brothers and was aged forty, born on the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather Shu and grandfather Ying were both company commanders, each posthumously awarded the title of Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His father Zan held an honorary office for longevity; his father’s former wife was née Chen, his mother was née Li, and his stepmother was née Shen. His mother alone was still living. His elder brothers were Xiyan, an honorary official recognized for public beneficence; Xizhou, a Director of Food Services; Ximeng, an honorary official recognized for public beneficence; Xizeng; Xiwen, an Usher; and Xikui. His younger brothers were Xiqi, Xifu, Xilu, a Metropolitan Examination graduate (gongshi), Xidong, Xiru, Xiyin, and Xigao, a company commander. His wife was née Chang. He placed fourteenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 201st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Xiang, courtesy name Junbi, was registered in a civilian household in Wujiang County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A county government school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-eight, born on the fifth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Li; his grandfather, Min; his father, Zhang; and his mother, née Hu. Both parents were still living. His wife was née Zhang. He placed eleventh in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 202nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Bai Jun 白濬, registered in Lingui County, Guilin Prefecture, Guangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a prefectural school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zishen; he ranked first in his family and was twenty-nine, born on the second day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Li, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his grandfather was Min, an Usher; his father was Huan, a Steward of Provisions; and his mother was née Tao. His father alone was still living. His elder brothers were Jie, Shen (an Imperial University student), Xiu (an Assistant Prefect), Su, Zhun (a District Magistrate), Han, Si (a School Instructor), Shou (a Commissioner of a Transport Station), Lian, and Lan; his younger brothers were Qing, Hong, Ji, and Mei. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed twentieth in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and 310th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Pan 徐泮, registered in Gushi County, Guang Zhou, Runing Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Chongjiao; he ranked seventh in his family and was twenty-eight, born on the fifteenth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Huang, his grandfather was Shi, and his father was Dao. His father's previous wives were née Hu and née Xu; his mother was née Hu. His mother alone was still living. His elder brothers were Yuan, Ji, Pei, Ji, and Tang; his younger brothers were Han and Zhu. He married a woman née Gao. He placed sixty-sixth in the Henan Provincial Examination and eighteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cao Cha 曹察, registered in Wuxi County, Changzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a military household and was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Mingqing; he ranked third in his family and was thirty, born on the thirteenth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Wenhui; his grandfather was Zhihe, an honorary official recognized for righteousness; his father was Fu, a prestige official of the eighth rank; and his mother was née Zou. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yin (a tribute scholar) and Chong; his younger brother was Yu. He married a woman née Hua. He placed seventy-fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 156th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Xianke 楊獻可, registered in Qingcheng County, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, belonged to a military household and was a county school student specializing in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Zixiang; he ranked second in his family and was twenty-seven, born on the fourth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Xiu, his grandfather was Hui, and his father was Lun, an Imperial University student. His mother, née Cui, had received official recognition as a chaste widow. Both parents are recorded as living [?]. His elder brother was Xianzhang; his younger brothers were Xiance, Xiantu, Xianmou, Xianzhi, and Xianshu. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed thirteenth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 275th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Long Dashi 龍大湜 was registered in Chongyang County, Wuchang Prefecture, Huguang, in a military household. He was a student of the Directorate of Education and specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Maoyang; he ranked eighth among his brothers and was aged forty-two, born on the twenty-sixth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhiguang, who held an honorary title for longevity; his grandfather was Xuan; and his father was Boning, a District Magistrate. His father's former wife was née Hu, and his mother was née Bao. Both parents were deceased. He married a woman née Zheng. He placed twenty-fourth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 189th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Huang Jinrong 黃謹容 was registered in Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, in an artisan household. He was a Confucian scholar and specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Wangzhi; he ranked second among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the tenth day of the third lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yongda; his grandfather was Cong; his father was Zhao; and his mother was née Zeng. His mother alone survived. His elder brother was Jinlu. He married a woman née Ou. He placed twenty-sixth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and fifty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Cunyi 徐存義 was registered in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. He was an auxiliary student of the county Confucian school and specialized in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Zhifu; he ranked sixth among his brothers and was aged twenty-three, born on the twenty-second day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wensheng; his grandfather was Kai; his father was Yin; and his mother was née Zheng. His parents and grandparents were living. His elder brothers were Cunde, Cunhui, and Cun'en; his younger brothers were Cundao, Cunxin, and Nian [?]. He married a woman née Huang. He placed thirty-second in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and ninety-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Zhu 陳洙 was registered in Shangyu County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. He was an auxiliary student of the county Confucian school and specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Daoyuan; he ranked third among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the first day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Kejing; his grandfather was Mo; his father was Zan; and his mother was née Pan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Lian and Luo; his younger brothers were Si and Yi. He married a woman née Wang. He placed sixtieth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and forty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Xing 王杏, courtesy name Shiwen, was registered in Fenghua County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. An supplementary student of the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He ranked first among his brothers and was aged thirty-four, born on the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary second month. His great-grandfather was Can, his grandfather Shou, and his father Xun; his mother was née Sun. His mother was living and his father deceased. His younger brother was Jia, and his wife was née Wu. He placed sixty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 315th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Shixian 沈師賢, courtesy name Dexiu, was registered in Deqing County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. A student of the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He ranked second among his brothers and was aged twenty-nine, born on the eighth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Huang, his grandfather Fu, and his father Guan; his mother was née Wu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Shisheng, and his younger brother Shiru. His wife was née Zhou; he subsequently married a woman née Chen. He placed twenty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 245th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕惟治天下
之道其端不可槩舉
特以大者論之在乎
知人安民二者而已
夫知人則哲必能官
===
而任之安民則惠必
使匹夫匹婦各得其
所雖然堯舜尚於此
猶難夫豈後世所能
及也朕本藩服仰承

translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “I consider that the principles of governing all under Heaven cannot be exhaustively enumerated. To speak only of the greatest, they consist simply in these two things: discerning men’s worth and bringing peace to the people. Discerning men’s worth constitutes wisdom: one must be able to appoint them to office and entrust them with responsibilities. Bringing peace to the people constitutes benevolence: one must ensure that every ordinary man and woman finds a proper place. Yet even Yao and Shun found these tasks difficult; how could later generations match them? I was originally a prince of a regional fief and reverently received …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
天命入奉
祖宗大統朝夕戰兢不
遑寧處何自即位以
来災變頻仍旱潦相
繼歲復一歲無處無
===
之生民流亡朕甚恐
懼此非朕官非人以
虐民歟或賢與不肖
進退倒置歟或勸懲
之典而失其宜歟抑

punctuated: 天命，入奉祖宗大統，朝夕戰兢，不遑寧處。何自即位以来，災變頻仍，旱潦相繼，歲復一歲，無處無之？生民流亡，朕甚恐懼。此非朕官非人以虐民歟？或賢與不肖進退倒置歟？或勸懲之典而失其宜歟？抑
translation_en: …Heaven’s mandate and assumed the great succession of my ancestors. Morning and evening I tremble with apprehension, with no leisure to rest at ease. Why, since my accession, have calamities and ominous disturbances occurred so frequently, droughts and floods following one another, year after year, with no place spared? The people are displaced and wandering; I am deeply fearful. Is this not because I have appointed unsuitable men to office, thereby subjecting the people to oppression? Or have the worthy and the unworthy been advanced and dismissed in the reverse of their proper order? Or have the established measures for encouragement and punishment been applied inappropriately? Or…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
為我選任者而失公
平之道歟夫天聽自
我民聽天視自我民
視非民不聊生而
天垂深戒者如此何歟
===
至于內有盜賊之擾
外有戎狄之患此亦
以為民之害者民為
邦本而使飢寒困苦
流離死亡至于如此
alt_text:
為我選任者而失公
平之道歟夫天聽自
我民聽天視自我民
視非民不聊生而
天埀深戒者如此何歟
===
至於內有盜賊之擾
外有戎狄之患此亦
以爲民之害者民爲
邦本而使飢寒困苦
流離死亡至於如此
punctuated:
為我選任者而失公平之道歟？夫天聽自我民聽，天視自我民視，非民不聊生而天垂深戒者如此，何歟？

至于內有盜賊之擾，外有戎狄之患，此亦以為民之害者。民為邦本，而使飢寒困苦，流離死亡，至于如此，
translation_en:
…have those who select and appoint officials on my behalf departed from the way of fairness and impartiality? Heaven hears through what our people hear; Heaven sees through what our people see. If it were not because the people could no longer sustain their livelihoods, why would Heaven send down such grave warnings?

As for disturbances by bandits within and threats from the Rong and Di beyond our borders, these too bring harm to the people. The people are the foundation of the state, yet they have been left to suffer hunger and cold, hardship and distress, displacement and death, to such an extent…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
邦欲安而得乎朕雖
存保邦安民之念求
其所以實無一得朕
欲俾災沴潜消民生
安堵盜賊息邊方靖
===
財充而食足不知如
之何可以臻此特進
尔多士于廷尔多士
明於王道有日矣且
目覩時艱豈無真識

punctuated: 邦欲安而得乎？朕雖存保邦安民之念，求其所以，實無一得。朕欲俾災沴潜消，民生安堵，盜賊息，邊方靖，財充而食足，不知如之何可以臻此？特進尔多士于廷。尔多士明於王道有日矣，且目覩時艱，豈無真識
translation_en: …can the state attain the peace it seeks? Though I cherish the intention of preserving the state and securing the people’s peace, I have gained no understanding of the means to accomplish this. I wish to bring about the quiet disappearance of calamities and baleful influences, to let the people live in security, to put an end to banditry, to pacify the frontiers, and to ensure abundant financial resources and sufficient food. I do not know how these ends may be attained. I have therefore specially summoned you scholars to court. You scholars have long understood the Way of the True King, and you have witnessed the hardships of the times with your own eyes. Can you have no true understanding…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
的見以匡我者當悉
心吐露推衍所以于
篇朕當勉為親覽焉
勿諂勿憚勿泛勿畧
庶副朕意
===
嘉靖八年三月十五日
alt_text:
的見以匡我者當悉
心吐露推衍所以予
簫朕當勉爲親覽焉
勿諂勿悍勿泛勿略
庶副朕意
===
嘉靖八年三月十五日
punctuated:
的見以匡我者？當悉心吐露，推衍所以于篇。朕當勉為親覽焉。勿諂，勿憚，勿泛，勿畧，庶副朕意。

嘉靖八年三月十五日。
translation_en:
…sound insights with which to assist me? You should reveal your thoughts wholeheartedly and expound the reasons in your essays. I shall endeavor to read them personally. Do not flatter, do not be afraid, do not be vague, and do not be cursory, so that you may fulfill my wishes.

The fifteenth day of the third month of the eighth year of Jiajing (1529).

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
御批學正有見言讜而意必忠宜擢之首者
臣羅洪先
臣對臣聞帝王之致治也有覆天下之仁而以
不費為施有周天下之智而以不勞為用施之
溥而後順時鼓舞之權行用不勞而後憲天聰
明之實盡盡聰明者存乎誠誠無疑矣妙鼓舞
者存乎變變無方矣無方而顯作用於旁行仁
之發也以天下之才盡天下之故得天下之故
神天下之化夫何費之有無疑而別賢否於不
===
遺智之運也以天下之公為一己之度廓一己
之度定天下之情夫何勞之有是故誠以基智
智以廣仁仁以盡化化以格天天順而時化和
而理仁廣而通智睿而辨非夫先天而天不違
後天而奉天時者其孰能與於此故仁而不得
其要必疎陋而文勝智而不本於誠必穿鑿而
術煩文勝之弊泛而寡效術煩之弊雜而不明
天下之事廢者多矣是故帝王存之為理要之
原舉之為易簡之善不以察為明不以私為惠
盖其所執者要而所尚者審故也是以天地可

Your servant, Luo Hongxian.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in bringing about good government, emperors and kings possess benevolence that embraces all under Heaven, yet bestow it without expenditure; they possess wisdom that encompasses all under Heaven, yet employ it without toil. Only when their beneficence is widespread can they exercise the adaptive power to inspire and animate people in accordance with the seasons; only when their exercise of wisdom entails no toil can they fully realize the perceptiveness that takes Heaven as its model. Fully realizing perceptiveness rests upon sincerity, and sincerity admits no doubt. Marvelously inspiring and animating people rests upon change, and change has no fixed pattern. Having no fixed pattern, yet manifesting its efficacy in every direction, is the unfolding of benevolence. By employing the talents of all under Heaven, they comprehend all the affairs of the world; by grasping those affairs, they make the world's transformation wondrous. What expenditure could this entail? Admitting no doubt, yet distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy without overlooking anyone, is the operation of wisdom. They take the impartiality of all under Heaven as their own measure; by broadening their own measure, they bring order to the circumstances of all under Heaven. What toil could this entail?

Thus sincerity provides the foundation for wisdom; wisdom extends benevolence; benevolence brings transformation to its fullness; and transformation reaches Heaven. Heaven is favorable and timely; transformation is harmonious and orderly; benevolence is expansive and all-pervading; wisdom is penetrating and discriminating. Who could attain this except one who, acting before Heaven, encounters no opposition from Heaven and, acting after Heaven, accords with Heaven's seasons? Thus benevolence that fails to grasp what is essential must become shallow and crude, with outward forms predominating; wisdom that is not rooted in sincerity must become forced and contrived, with an excess of techniques. The defect of predominant outward forms is diffuseness with little effect; the defect of excessive techniques is complexity without clarity. Many of the world's affairs are consequently neglected.

Therefore emperors and kings preserve this as the source of the essentials of order and put it into practice as the excellence of ease and simplicity. title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
位萬物可育氣化太和災沴不作其上下一貫
之理顯微無間之機乎是故仁智合德之謂聖
志氣交感之謂通天人同歸之謂治是說之不
明也亦久矣古人之言曰上有好言之君則下
必有盡言之臣又曰益智廣德莫善於問乘事
演道莫善於對臣愚恭遇
陛下精明納言得其時矣觀時勢之故究恊濟之本
極理亂之說廣德業之規臣非其人也而竊有
志焉敢不敬述其畧以對惟天生民不能無欲
欲之不制亂之成也茍非至德大道不行故夫
===
德合天者謂之皇德合地者謂之帝兼乎三才
足以合倫盡制者謂之天子故亶聰明為元后
而佑下民也作之君師子夏問孔子以民之父
母孔子曰四方有敗必先知之一人而安四方
者君也是故天者立君之命也君者立民之命
也裁成之道輔相之宜所自成也典禮之衷命
討之權必有歸也安民非君之責乎勢一而後
定於義職分而後詳于仁是故惟王建國體國
經野設官分職以立民極也樹后王君公承以
大夫師長以奉天道也此則共濟之義大公之

punctuated:
位，萬物可育，氣化太和，災沴不作，其上下一貫之理、顯微無間之機乎？是故仁智合德之謂聖，志氣交感之謂通，天人同歸之謂治。是說之不明也，亦久矣。古人之言曰：「上有好言之君，則下必有盡言之臣。」又曰：「益智廣德，莫善於問；乘事演道，莫善於對。」臣愚恭遇陛下精明納言，得其時矣。觀時勢之故，究恊濟之本，極理亂之說，廣德業之規，臣非其人也，而竊有志焉。敢不敬述其畧以對？

惟天生民，不能無欲。欲之不制，亂之成也。茍非至德，大道不行。故夫德合天者謂之皇，德合地者謂之帝，兼乎三才，足以合倫盡制者謂之天子。故亶聰明，為元后，而佑下民也；作之君師。子夏問孔子以民之父母，孔子曰：「四方有敗，必先知之。」一人而安四方者，君也。是故天者，立君之命也；君者，立民之命也。裁成之道，輔相之宜，所自成也；典禮之衷，命討之權，必有歸也。安民非君之責乎？勢一而後定於義，職分而後詳于仁。是故惟王建國，體國經野，設官分職，以立民極也；樹后王君公，承以大夫師長，以奉天道也。此則共濟之義，大公之
translation_en:
…be properly situated, and the myriad things can be nurtured; the transforming vital forces attain supreme harmony, and calamities and baleful influences do not arise. Is this not the principle that runs continuously through above and below, the workings that admit no separation between the manifest and the hidden? Thus, the union of benevolence and wisdom in virtue is called sagehood; the mutual responsiveness of intention and vital force is called communion; and Heaven and humanity reaching the same end is called good government. This teaching has long remained obscure. An ancient saying declares: “When above there is a ruler who welcomes counsel, below there will surely be ministers who speak fully.” Another says: “To increase wisdom and broaden virtue, nothing is better than asking; to expound the Way through affairs, nothing is better than answering.” Foolish though I am, I have respectfully encountered Your Majesty, discerning and receptive to counsel: I have found the opportune time. To examine the causes underlying present circumstances, investigate the foundations of cooperative endeavor, explore fully the explanations of order and disorder, and broaden the plans for virtuous achievement—I am not equal to these tasks, yet privately aspire to them. How could I fail respectfully to set forth their outlines in reply?

Heaven gives birth to the people, and they cannot be without desires. When desires are not restrained, disorder takes shape. Without consummate virtue, the great Way cannot prevail. Thus, one whose virtue accords with Heaven is called an august sovereign; one whose virtue accords with Earth is called an emperor; and one who embraces the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—and can harmonize human relationships and fully establish institutions is called the Son of Heaven. Hence one who is truly perceptive and discerning becomes the great sovereign and protects the people below; he is made their ruler and teacher. Zixia asked Confucius about being the father and mother of the people. Confucius said: “When there is trouble anywhere in the four quarters, he must know of it first.” The one person who brings peace to the four quarters is the ruler. Thus Heaven establishes the ruler’s mandate, and the ruler establishes the people’s livelihood. Through him are accomplished the way of regulating and completing the work of Heaven and Earth and the appropriate means of assisting it; the proper measure of canonical rites and the authority to command and punish must have a locus. Is bringing peace to the people not the ruler’s responsibility? Only when authority is unified can it be firmly grounded in righteousness; only when duties are apportioned can benevolence be applied in full detail. Thus the king establishes the capital, lays out its divisions and demarcates the countryside, sets up offices and assigns duties, thereby establishing the highest standard for the people. Sovereigns, kings, rulers, and dukes are established, supported by grand masters and heads of officials, to uphold the Way of Heaven. This, then, is the principle of working together toward a common end, and of complete impartiality…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
制也官人非君之助乎然地遠則德未易徧情
異則化未易行求萬姓之咸休難得也聽言則
易於匿情責實則乖於廣容求九德之咸事難
得也然臣嘗求之矣四凶之惡未著也堯不逆
探其奸元凱之善未著也堯不責備其用是道
也其知人之要乎黎民敏德在臣下之克艱帝
力不知由官師之翕受是道也其安民之要乎
然而當時病其難後世忘其守豈非誠偽之別
而治忽亦因之歟仰惟
陛下即位以來孜孜求理敬慎夙夜不遑寧處求直
===
言以廣聽納除冗役以止蠹害謹鬻爵以簡任
使嚴章法以辨優劣其於知人可謂謹矣免雜
租以重民命發餘幣以蘇時艱減貢獻以節浮
費明冤獄以示平反其於撫民可謂密矣是宜
海內興富足之歌天下樂有年之頌朝著極相
讓之休郡邑向承德之美而休徵畢集嘉氣聿
暢矣夫何近年災故迭見旱魃為凶千里相繼
淫潦損苗逾時不止白虹示警坤象載震星變
上現霾氣四昏夫天人之應自古不誣氣數之
說匪經之訓故曰聖王在上日月不薄食雷發

制也。官人非君之助乎？然地遠則德未易徧，情異則化未易行，求萬姓之咸休難得也。聽言則易於匿情，責實則乖於廣容，求九德之咸事難得也。然臣嘗求之矣：四凶之惡未著也，堯不逆探其奸；元凱之善未著也，堯不責備其用。是道也，其知人之要乎？黎民敏德，在臣下之克艱；帝力不知，由官師之翕受。是道也，其安民之要乎？然而當時病其難，後世忘其守，豈非誠偽之別，而治忽亦因之歟？

translation_en:
…an institution serving the common good. Are officials not the ruler’s helpers? Yet where places are distant, his virtue cannot readily reach everywhere; where people’s dispositions differ, his transforming influence cannot readily take effect. It is difficult to secure well-being for all the people. If one listens to words, true intentions are easily concealed; if one demands actual achievement, one falls short of broad-minded tolerance. It is difficult to bring into service all those who possess the nine virtues. Yet your servant has sought the essentials of this. Before the wickedness of the Four Malefactors became manifest, Yao did not anticipate and probe their treachery; before the goodness of the Eight Yuan and Eight Kai became manifest, Yao did not demand perfection in their service. Is this not the essential way to understand men? That the common people should strive toward virtue depends on ministers’ ability to undertake difficult tasks; that the emperor’s contribution should go unnoticed depends on the officials’ united acceptance of their responsibilities. Is this not the essential way to bring peace to the people? Yet people in that age found this difficult, and later generations forgot to uphold it. Is this not the distinction between sincerity and insincerity, upon which good government and disorder also depend?
With reverence I consider how, since Your Majesty ascended the throne, you have diligently sought good government, remaining reverent and cautious morning and night, with no leisure to rest at ease. You have sought frank speech to broaden what you hear and accept, abolished superfluous service obligations to end abuses, exercised caution in selling ranks so as to select those entrusted with service, and rigorously enforced regulations to distinguish the capable from the inferior. In understanding men, you may indeed be called careful. You have remitted miscellaneous taxes out of regard for the people’s lives, disbursed surplus treasury funds to relieve present hardship, reduced tribute offerings to curb needless expenditure, and investigated unjust imprisonment to secure the reversal of wrongful judgments. In caring for the people, you may indeed be called thorough. Surely, then, songs of prosperity and sufficiency ought to arise within the seas, and all under Heaven ought joyfully to praise abundant harvests. The ranks at court ought to display the fullest beauty of mutual deference, and prefectures and counties ought to incline toward the excellence of receiving your virtuous influence. Auspicious signs ought all to gather, and beneficent influences to flow freely.
Why, then, have disasters appeared one after another in recent years? The drought demon wreaks havoc across successive stretches of a thousand li; excessive flooding damages the crops and continues beyond its season without ceasing. White rainbows give warning, and the earth trembles again; anomalous stars appear above, and dust haze darkens all four quarters. The correspondence between Heaven and humanity has never proved false since antiquity; explanations based on cycles of cosmic forces and predestined fate are not the teaching of the Classics. Thus it is said: “When a sage king rules above, the sun and moon suffer no eclipses, and thunder sounds…”

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
不震雨雹不為災一氣之流行故也今也仰窺
晷度俯攷璣衡豈惟
陛下慮之在臣亦且疑之矣然延詢博訪備察逺聞
民之困也倉箱無卒嵗之儲田里無口分之業
耕穫未已而稱貸復行亦有牧不以時如蘇軾
之所慮者矣播種巳施而券契亦行亦有欲亟
其死如陸贄之所憂者矣南則病於税產之虚
北則病於夫役之擾至於災異之地猶失撫字
之方栗烈不免於懸鶉桑野誰飼夫蒙袂是以
流離載道轉相嗷嗷攘劫為生益為糜敗邊塵
===
屡起積骸在野夫天心之仁靡不欲其相安以
生而民之司牧乃視其轉死而不救知人之道
可不重省乎哉
陛下既深思而歷言其弊矣臣也復何所言惟
聖問有曰官非其人以虐民臣不敢謂無是也盖古
之仕也祿不計其厚薄職不計其大小惟以盡
分為賢不以年數為限今也上無責成之心下
有苟安之計善政未必行能聲未必著是安得
不以利為利也
陛下有以處之乎

punctuated:
不震，雨雹不為災，一氣之流行故也。今也仰窺晷度，俯攷璣衡，豈惟陛下慮之，在臣亦且疑之矣。然延詢博訪，備察逺聞，民之困也，倉箱無卒嵗之儲，田里無口分之業。耕穫未已，而稱貸復行，亦有牧不以時，如蘇軾之所慮者矣；播種巳施，而券契亦行，亦有欲亟其死，如陸贄之所憂者矣。南則病於税產之虚，北則病於夫役之擾。至於災異之地，猶失撫字之方。栗烈不免於懸鶉，桑野誰飼夫蒙袂？是以流離載道，轉相嗷嗷，攘劫為生，益為糜敗。邊塵屡起，積骸在野。夫天心之仁，靡不欲其相安以生，而民之司牧乃視其轉死而不救，知人之道可不重省乎哉？
陛下既深思而歷言其弊矣，臣也復何所言？惟聖問有曰：「官非其人，以虐民。」臣不敢謂無是也。盖古之仕也，祿不計其厚薄，職不計其大小，惟以盡分為賢，不以年數為限。今也上無責成之心，下有苟安之計，善政未必行，能聲未必著，是安得不以利為利也？陛下有以處之乎？
translation_en:
…does not shake the earth, and rain and hail cause no calamity: this is because the single vital force flows freely. Yet now, looking up to observe the sun’s measured course and down to examine the astronomical instruments, how could Your Majesty alone be troubled? Your servant too is perplexed. Through extensive inquiries and consultations, thorough investigation and reports from afar, I have learned of the people’s distress. Their granaries and bins hold no reserves sufficient to last the year, and in the countryside they lack the land allotted per person to sustain them. Before tilling and harvesting are finished, borrowing begins again: there are indeed cases of tending the people at improper times [?], such as Su Shi feared. Once seed has been sown, loan contracts are already put into effect: there are indeed those who seem intent on hastening the people’s death, as Lu Zhi feared. In the south, people suffer from taxes assessed on property that exists only on paper; in the north, from the disruption caused by compulsory labor. Even in places afflicted by calamities and portents, officials still fail to provide proper care. In the bitter cold, people cannot escape wearing rags like dangling quails; in the mulberry fields, who feeds the starving man who covers his face with his sleeve? Thus displaced people fill the roads, crying out to one another. They resort to robbery to survive, and the devastation grows ever worse. The dust of warfare repeatedly rises on the frontier, and corpses lie heaped in the fields. Heaven, in its benevolence, desires that all should live together in peace; yet those charged with shepherding the people watch them die in their wanderings without coming to their aid. Can the means of judging men’s fitness for office go without earnest reconsideration?
Your Majesty has already reflected deeply and set out these abuses in detail. What more can your servant say? Yet your sagely question states: “Offices are held by unsuitable men, who oppress the people.” Your servant dares not claim that this is untrue. In antiquity, those who served in office did not reckon whether their salaries were generous or meager, or their offices high or low. They regarded only the full discharge of their duties as worthy, without setting a limit by years of service. Today, those above have no intention of demanding results, while those below scheme merely to remain comfortably secure. Good administration is not necessarily put into practice, nor is a reputation for ability necessarily established. How, then, can they fail to regard personal profit as their gain? Does Your Majesty have a means of dealing with this?

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
聖問有曰賢與不肖進退倒置臣不敢謂無是也盖
古之仕也進以實德不以空言故靜言如兜不
得長奸有能如鯀猶謂方命今也任其論說無
以考其素行取其才藝不復校其道術是安得
不以不肖為賢也
陛下有以辨之乎以勸懲言之古之課績也日有日
成月有月要歲有歲會故不紊也今給由之制
足以擬之否乎是賞罰無可稽矣以選任言之
古之舉用也官長舉其屬親怨無所避故以情
也今資格之限亦有避嫌者乎是公平有所礙
===
矣四患不除則庶理不得庶理不得則群賢不
登群賢不登則處置失宜而百姓無賴是故潢
池多弄兵之警緣邊無固守之防以此立國則
國運不泰以此制民則民紀弗寧是故天聽自
我民聽天視自我民視信乎感應之道察乎幾
瑊之萌是安得不來
宵旰之憂而切多士之問也然臣以為知致弊之
由則必有救弊之方病化理之鬱則必有更化
之道毋亦於知人者而加之意乎臣亦不敢為
近世苟且之見習熟之說以負

聖問有曰：「賢與不肖，進退倒置。」臣不敢謂無是也。盖古之仕也，進以實德，不以空言，故靜言如兜，不得長奸；有能如鯀，猶謂方命。今也任其論說，無以考其素行；取其才藝，不復校其道術，是安得不以不肖為賢也？陛下有以辨之乎？
以勸懲言之，古之課績也，日有日成，月有月要，歲有歲會，故不紊也。今給由之制，足以擬之否乎？是賞罰無可稽矣。以選任言之，古之舉用也，官長舉其屬，親怨無所避，故以情也。今資格之限，亦有避嫌者乎？是公平有所礙矣。
四患不除，則庶理不得；庶理不得，則群賢不登；群賢不登，則處置失宜，而百姓無賴。是故潢池多弄兵之警，緣邊無固守之防。以此立國，則國運不泰；以此制民，則民紀弗寧。是故「天聽自我民聽，天視自我民視」，信乎感應之道，察乎幾瑊之萌，是安得不來宵旰之憂，而切多士之問也？
然臣以為，知致弊之由，則必有救弊之方；病化理之鬱，則必有更化之道。毋亦於知人者而加之意乎？臣亦不敢為近世苟且之見、習熟之說，以負
translation_en:
Your sagely question states: “In the advancement and dismissal of the worthy and the unworthy, the proper order is reversed.” Your servant dares not say that this does not occur. In antiquity, men in office advanced through genuine virtue, not empty words. Thus, one whose fine words belied his conduct, like Dou, was not allowed to foster wickedness; even one with abilities like Gun was still judged disobedient to commands. Today, men are entrusted with office on the strength of their arguments, without any means of examining their habitual conduct; they are chosen for their talents and accomplishments, without further scrutiny of their moral principles and methods. How, then, can the unworthy fail to be taken for the worthy? Does Your Majesty have a means of distinguishing them?
As for encouragement and punishment, in ancient assessments of performance there were daily records of accomplishments, monthly summaries, and annual accounts; hence there was no disorder. Is the present system of issuing certificates of service sufficient to match this? Rewards and punishments thus lack a basis for verification. As for selection and appointment, in antiquity heads of offices recommended their subordinates, avoiding neither relatives nor enemies, and thus acted according to the actual circumstances. Under the present restrictions based on qualifications and seniority, are there also those who avoid recommendations for fear of suspicion? Impartiality is thereby obstructed.
Unless these four afflictions are removed, the many affairs of government cannot be properly ordered. Unless those affairs are properly ordered, worthy men cannot rise to office. Unless worthy men rise to office, measures will be inappropriate, and the common people will have nothing to rely upon. Thus there are frequent alarms of people taking up arms beside the pools, while along the frontiers there are no defenses capable of holding firm. To sustain the state in this fashion leaves its fortunes troubled; to govern the people in this fashion leaves order among them unsettled. Hence: “Heaven hears through what our people hear; Heaven sees through what our people see.” Trusting in the principle of stimulus and response, and discerning the first stirrings of incipient developments [?], how could Your Majesty fail to be beset by anxieties that keep you occupied before dawn and late into the day, and urgently question the assembled scholars?
Yet your servant believes that, if the causes of these abuses are known, there must be a means of remedying them; if the obstruction of moral transformation and good government is a source of distress, there must be a way to renew that transformation. Might greater attention therefore be given to discerning men’s character? Your servant likewise dares not put forward the expedient views and well-worn arguments of recent times, thereby betraying …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之誠意請揆其本而論之夫天聰明聖時憲古
之訓也然天之聰明不可度也有德則降祥有
惡則降殃大以成大小以成小各因其宜而未
嘗有為也各適其用而未嘗有心也山澤之廣
大汙疾之納藏而未嘗靡容也觀於天道可知
君人之度矣舜之大智也在隱惡而揚善禹之
大智也在於行所無事是故虛心以應之則得
失自别下己以待之則狡偽獻誠聖貴改過不
言絕德必察其從中才豈免必摘其短尚何自
新不與其往不必徧物是故水平則妍媸必見
===
也衡平則輕重自倫也必以形迹觀人則不可
以盡人必以法制繩人則不可以服人而況在
人之心實為至神上之好惡靡不審上之情偽
靡不知示之以誠猶恐其渝示之以詐弊將安
極己未信而欲人之信己不可得也人之弗信
而欲惟意之從亦不可得矣可不戒哉雖然此
其本也槩舉其端則教育不可不端也選舉不
可不慎也考課不可不精也欲端教育在於正
道術之習嚴考校之則欲正其習則
訓所謂一以記誦為能卒無實用者可戒也欲舉

punctuated:
陛下之誠意。請揆其本而論之。夫「天聰明，聖時憲」，古之訓也。然天之聰明不可度也，有德則降祥，有惡則降殃，大以成大，小以成小，各因其宜而未嘗有為也，各適其用而未嘗有心也。山澤之廣大，汙疾之納藏，而未嘗靡容也。觀於天道，可知君人之度矣。舜之大智也，在隱惡而揚善；禹之大智也，在於行所無事。是故虛心以應之，則得失自别；下己以待之，則狡偽獻誠。聖貴改過，不言絕德，必察其從。中才豈免？必摘其短，尚何自新？不與其往，不必徧物。是故水平則妍媸必見也，衡平則輕重自倫也。必以形迹觀人，則不可以盡人；必以法制繩人，則不可以服人。而況在人之心，實為至神，上之好惡靡不審，上之情偽靡不知。示之以誠，猶恐其渝；示之以詐，弊將安極？己未信而欲人之信己，不可得也；人之弗信而欲惟意之從，亦不可得矣。可不戒哉！
雖然，此其本也。槩舉其端，則教育不可不端也，選舉不可不慎也，考課不可不精也。欲端教育，在於正道術之習，嚴考校之則。欲正其習，則訓所謂「一以記誦為能，卒無實用」者，可戒也。欲舉
translation_en:
…Your Majesty’s sincerity. Allow me to consider the root of the matter and discuss it. “Heaven is discerning; the sage takes it as his model”: this is an ancient teaching. Yet Heaven’s discernment cannot be fathomed. Where there is virtue, it sends down blessings; where there is evil, it sends down calamities. It enables the great to achieve greatness and the small to achieve what is small, accommodating each according to its proper circumstances without deliberate action, and fitting each to its use without conscious intent. Like the vastness of mountains and marshes, which receive and harbor filth and corruption, it leaves nothing unaccommodated. By observing the Way of Heaven, one may understand the breadth of mind required of a ruler. Shun’s great wisdom lay in concealing faults and proclaiming goodness; Yu’s great wisdom lay in acting without contrivance. Thus, if one responds with an open mind, merits and faults distinguish themselves; if one treats others humbly, even the crafty and deceitful offer sincerity. The sage values the correction of faults: he does not declare someone wholly devoid of virtue, but must examine what that person follows [?]. How can people of middling ability avoid faults? If one insists on exposing their shortcomings, what opportunity remains for them to renew themselves? One does not endorse their past conduct, nor need one scrutinize everything exhaustively [?]. Thus, when water is level, beauty and ugliness are necessarily revealed; when a balance is even, lightness and heaviness fall naturally into order. If one insists on judging people by outward conduct alone, one cannot understand them fully; if one insists on measuring them by laws and regulations, one cannot win their submission. Moreover, the human mind is supremely perceptive: there is nothing about a superior’s likes and dislikes that it does not discern, and nothing about his sincerity or pretense that it does not know. Even when one shows people sincerity, one still fears they may waver; if one shows them deceit, where will the resulting abuses end? To desire others’ trust before one has oneself proved trustworthy is impossible. To desire that people follow one’s wishes when they do not trust one is likewise impossible. Can one fail to take warning?
Nevertheless, this is the root of the matter. To outline its principal aspects: education must be properly directed, selection for office must be undertaken carefully, and assessments of officials’ performance must be exacting. To put education in order requires correcting the practices through which the Way and its arts are studied, and strictly enforcing standards of examination. To correct those practices, one should heed the warning in the Instructions against “taking memorization and recitation alone as ability, with ultimately no practical usefulness.” As for wishing to select…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
其師則
祖訓所謂必求端人正士以為模範者可行也敦本
而尚質先德而後藝如是而教有不成乎欲慎
選舉在謹資格之弊崇德行之科謹資格也則
當鑒裴光庭混淆之失崇德行也則當考程顥
薦達之議而又止奔競之風重廉恥之節如是
而選有不當乎欲精考課在久賢能之任明賞
罰之權久任則杜恕所謂以親民長吏轉為郡
守有績則進爵加秩者可法也明權則傅嘏所
謂君志定國體崇而後可責其成者可取也如
===
是而課有不精乎然而數者之要非秉聰明之
德不能行憲天之說無亦所當留意者乎既得
知人之說則安民者舉而措之耳然道有升降
政由俗革法不變則道不融制不更則化不顯
無以時久則窮事煩則弊守其故則滯而不通
反其原斯順而可達是故新民之耳目不可無
作倦之道一心志之趨向不可無檢制之法正
月之布象和法以歲變者也刑罰世輕世重以
世變者也時未至而不守常則至於扞格時已
至而不用權則至於膠固故觀其機會反其理

punctuated: 其師，則《祖訓》所謂「必求端人正士以為模範」者可行也。敦本而尚質，先德而後藝，如是而教有不成乎？欲慎選舉，在謹資格之弊，崇德行之科。謹資格也，則當鑒裴光庭混淆之失；崇德行也，則當考程顥薦達之議。而又止奔競之風，重廉恥之節，如是而選有不當乎？欲精考課，在久賢能之任，明賞罰之權。久任，則杜恕所謂「以親民長吏轉為郡守，有績則進爵加秩」者可法也；明權，則傅嘏所謂「君志定，國體崇，而後可責其成」者可取也。如是而課有不精乎？然而數者之要，非秉聰明之德不能行。憲天之說，無亦所當留意者乎？既得知人之說，則安民者舉而措之耳。然道有升降，政由俗革，法不變則道不融，制不更則化不顯。無以時久則窮，事煩則弊，守其故則滯而不通，反其原斯順而可達。是故新民之耳目，不可無作倦之道；一心志之趨向，不可無檢制之法。正月之布象和法，以歲變者也；刑罰世輕世重，以世變者也。時未至而不守常，則至於扞格；時已至而不用權，則至於膠固。故觀其機會，反其理
translation_en: …their teachers, then the injunction in the Ancestral Instructions that one “must seek upright and honorable men to serve as models” should be put into practice. Strengthen the foundations and esteem substance; put virtue before accomplishments. With teaching conducted thus, could it fail to succeed? To exercise care in selecting officials, one must guard against the abuses of formal qualifications and give prominence to selection on the basis of virtuous conduct. In guarding against abuses of qualifications, one should take warning from Pei Guangting’s error of confounding distinctions; in honoring virtuous conduct, one should examine Cheng Hao’s proposals for recommending men for office. Furthermore, curb the tendency to scramble for advancement and give weight to integrity and a sense of shame. With selection conducted thus, could appointments be unsuitable? To make performance evaluations exact, retain worthy and capable men in their posts for longer terms and clarify the authority to reward and punish. For long tenure, one may follow Du Shu’s proposal to “promote senior magistrates who govern the people directly to commandery governors, and, if they achieve results, advance their noble rank and increase their official grade.” For clarifying authority, one may adopt Fu Gu’s statement: “Only after the ruler’s purpose is settled and the dignity of the state upheld can men be held accountable for their accomplishments.” With evaluations conducted thus, could they fail to be exact? Yet the essential point in these several measures is that they cannot be carried out without the virtue of clear perception. Should not the teaching of taking Heaven as one’s model also receive attention? Once the principles of discerning men’s character have been grasped, securing the people’s peace is simply a matter of putting them into practice. Yet the Way rises and declines, and government changes with customs. Unless laws change, the Way cannot operate freely; unless institutions are renewed, transforming influence cannot become manifest. With the passage of time, means become exhausted, and with the multiplication of affairs, abuses arise [?]. Clinging to old practices brings stagnation and obstruction; returning to their underlying principles makes things proceed smoothly and reach their ends. Thus, to refresh what the people hear and see, there must be a means of rousing the weary [?]; to unify the direction of their intentions, there must be methods of restraint and regulation. The promulgation of the xianghe laws in the first month [?] represents change according to the year; making punishments lighter in one age and heavier in another represents change according to the age. If one fails to uphold established practices before the time for change has arrived, incompatibility results; if one fails to exercise discretion once that time has arrived, rigidity results. Therefore, observe the opportunities presented by circumstances and return to their underlying principles…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
要以此為當官之法固足以盡其才能以此為
責效之規尤易於底績矣雖然此其本也槩舉
其端則東南有可耕之人而無其地西北有可
耕之地而無其法曠土隙田之未耕晁錯之所
憂也鑿源灌渠之有法召信臣之所行也因旱
得雨而
皇祖猶憂其傷苗乃免田租今則雖有善政視為彌
文多矣無亦以實意行之乎陝西告饑請粟而
皇祖陪其賚予且令速發今則雖有急請稽違歲月
久矣無亦以便宜處之乎田無定分富貧不均
畧為防制可也稅有巧計虛實莫究加以清量
可也禁侈靡之風而民自足黃霸之惠政也豫
儲蓄之備而歲不饑朱熹之良規也然而數者
之要非達變易之宜不能行順時之說無亦所
當致省者乎順時以行則賢才無掣肘之虞任
人以公則閭閻有切實之效遂飽煖安逸之欲
而無饑寒盜賊何從生乎盖不但如龔遂之治

要，以此為當官之法，固足以盡其才能；以此為責效之規，尤易於底績矣。雖然，此其本也。槩舉其端，則東南有可耕之人而無其地，西北有可耕之地而無其法。曠土隙田之未耕，晁錯之所憂也；鑿源灌渠之有法，召信臣之所行也。

因旱得雨，而皇祖猶憂其傷苗，乃免田租。今則雖有善政，視為彌文多矣，無亦以實意行之乎？陝西告饑請粟，而皇祖陪其賚予，且令速發。今則雖有急請，稽違歲月久矣，無亦以便宜處之乎？田無定分，富貧不均，畧為防制可也；稅有巧計，虛實莫究，加以清量可也。禁侈靡之風而民自足，黃霸之惠政也；豫儲蓄之備而歲不饑，朱熹之良規也。然而數者之要，非達變易之宜不能行。順時之說，無亦所當致省者乎？

順時以行，則賢才無掣肘之虞；任人以公，則閭閻有切實之效。遂飽煖安逸之欲而無饑寒，盜賊何從生乎？盖不但如龔遂之治渤海也。得撫綏攻戰之備而無敗衂，夷狄何由至乎？盖不但如趙充國之在湟中也。生之有道，用之有節，積之有備，取之有制，財用足而衣食
translation_en:
…essential principles. Taking this as the method for discharging official duties will assuredly enable officials to exercise their abilities fully; taking it as the standard for demanding results will make achievements still easier to attain. Nevertheless, these are the fundamentals. To outline particular matters: in the southeast there are people able to cultivate but no land for them, while in the northwest there is land fit for cultivation but no suitable methods. Uncultivated wasteland and unused plots were what concerned Chao Cuo; methods for opening water sources and constructing irrigation channels were what Shao Xinchen put into practice.

When rain came after a drought, the imperial ancestor remained concerned that the seedlings had been damaged and therefore remitted the land tax. Nowadays, even when good policies exist, they are all too often treated as mere formalities. Should they not be carried out with sincere intent? When Shaanxi reported famine and requested grain, the imperial ancestor increased his grants [?] and ordered their prompt dispatch. Nowadays, even urgent requests encounter delays lasting months and years. Should they not be handled as circumstances require? Landholdings have no fixed allotments, and wealth and poverty are unevenly distributed: some preventive regulation would be appropriate. Taxation involves ingenious evasions, and actual holdings cannot be distinguished from false declarations: thorough surveying would be appropriate. Suppressing extravagant habits so that the people naturally had enough was Huang Ba’s benevolent policy; preparing reserves beforehand so that the year brought no famine was Zhu Xi’s sound rule. Yet the essential point in these measures is that they cannot be implemented without understanding how to adapt appropriately to change. Should not the principle of acting in accordance with the times receive careful consideration?

If action accords with the times, worthy and capable men need not fear obstruction; if appointments are impartial, the common people will enjoy tangible benefits. When their desire for adequate food, warmth, peace, and ease is fulfilled, and hunger and cold are absent, how could bandits arise? The achievement would surely surpass even Gong Sui’s administration of Bohai. With provision made both for pacification and for military operations, and with no defeats suffered, how could the foreign peoples invade? The achievement would surely surpass even Zhao Chongguo’s work in Huangzhong. If resources are produced by proper methods, used with restraint, accumulated in readiness, and collected according to established limits, funds and supplies will be sufficient, and clothing and food…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
富又不必劉晏之取予而後為善計也又何患
於
天心之不格災患之潜消哉然
聖問於終篇尤有真識的見明於王道之說以誘愚
臣之言而且戒諂畏之弊臣有以知
陛下求治理之切廣謀猷之陳上嘉下樂之至情矣
臣復何所顧忌而不盡哉盖聞
祖訓有曰一民未安猶為未仁一念未誠猶難格天
又曰人情遇祥則有驕心遇災則有懼心而懼心
生者治之基也嗚呼其殆天人之交始終之義
===
安危倚伏之機乎今
陛下遇災而懼因變而警歸過于已加念于民是心
豈有二哉此兢業萬幾者也寅恭和衷者也知
人安民之大原也萬古虛靈不昧之機也今之
災變即潜消也心之敬戒無時可止息也孔子
曰為政在人即知人之可以安民者也取人以
身即知人之本於憲天也修身以道修道以仁
仁也者即今日敬戒之心也是心也是理也天
得之以清地得之以寧人主得之能使天下和
平是故無有內外無有遠近加以意必即非此

安危倚伏之機乎今
陛下遇災而懼因變而警歸過于己加念于民是心
豈有二哉此兢業萬幾者也寅恭和衷者也知
人安民之大原也萬古虛靈不昧之機也今之
災變即潛消也心之敬戒無時可止息也孔子
曰為政在人即知人之可以安民者也取人以

平是故無有內外 自遠近加以意必即非此
punctuated:
富，又不必劉晏之取予而後為善計也。又何患於天心之不格、災患之潜消哉？然聖問於終篇，尤有真識的見、明於王道之說，以誘愚臣之言，而且戒諂畏之弊。臣有以知陛下求治理之切、廣謀猷之陳、上嘉下樂之至情矣。臣復何所顧忌而不盡哉？盖聞祖訓有曰：「一民未安，猶為未仁；一念未誠，猶難格天。」又曰：「人情遇祥則有驕心，遇災則有懼心，而懼心生者，治之基也。」嗚呼！其殆天人之交、始終之義、安危倚伏之機乎！

今陛下遇災而懼，因變而警，歸過于已，加念于民，是心豈有二哉？此兢業萬幾者也，寅恭和衷者也，知人安民之大原也，萬古虛靈不昧之機也。今之災變即潜消也，心之敬戒無時可止息也。孔子曰：「為政在人。」即知人之可以安民者也。「取人以身。」即知人之本於憲天也。「修身以道，修道以仁。」仁也者，即今日敬戒之心也。是心也是理也，天得之以清，地得之以寧，人主得之能使天下和平。是故無有內外，無有遠近，加以意必，即非此
translation_en:
…and clothing and food are abundant; sound financial management need not depend on Liu Yan’s methods of collecting and disbursing revenue. Why, then, need one worry about failing to move Heaven’s heart, or about calamities quietly disappearing [?]? Yet at the close of Your Majesty’s sacred question, you particularly call for true understanding, precise insight, and an explanation illuminating the kingly Way, to draw forth the words of your foolish servant; you also warn against the failings of flattery and fear. From this your servant understands Your Majesty’s earnest desire for good government, your wish for a broad presentation of counsel, and your utmost sincerity in seeking approval above and joy below. What reservations could your servant still have that would prevent him from speaking fully? I have heard that the Ancestral Instructions say: “If even one person has not been brought peace, one is still not fully benevolent; if even one thought is insincere, it remains difficult to move Heaven.” They also say: “It is human nature to become proud upon encountering auspicious signs and fearful upon encountering calamities; the arising of a fearful heart is the foundation of good government.” Ah! Surely here lie the interaction of Heaven and humanity, the meaning of beginnings and endings, and the workings by which security and danger depend upon and conceal one another!

Now Your Majesty feels fear upon encountering calamities and takes warning from anomalies, attributing fault to yourself and giving greater thought to the people. How could this heart be divided? This is the heart that attends conscientiously to the myriad affairs of government, that maintains reverent respect and harmonious purpose. It is the great source of discerning worthy men and bringing peace to the people, the working of the mind’s open, spiritual intelligence, undimmed through all ages. Even if the present calamities and anomalies quietly disappear, the heart’s reverence and vigilance must never cease. Confucius said: “The conduct of government depends upon men.” This means that discerning worthy men can bring peace to the people. “Select men by reference to your own person.” This means that discerning worthy men is rooted in modeling oneself on Heaven. “Cultivate your person through the Way, and cultivate the Way through benevolence.” Benevolence is precisely this heart of reverence and vigilance today. This heart is principle itself. Heaven obtains it and becomes clear; Earth obtains it and becomes tranquil; the ruler obtains it and can bring harmony and peace to all under Heaven. Thus it admits no distinction between inner and outer, distant and near. Add conjecture and insistence, and it is no longer this…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
心加以固我即非此心所謂渾然與物同體者
也其得其失不假外求匪思匪為乃所自得靜
而養之而未始有物實淵深也動而慎之而未
始不定實溥博也故一念之覺即為誠一念之
放即為偽達於此為大智决於此為大勇而飾
外之說不足惑之矣順之而運用也乃為周流
之妙失之而襲取也乃為執一之行而似是之
說不足動之矣以此窮理則中有主而不雜於
二三以此親賢則任必專而不疑於可否以此
為裁制宰物之柄則擬議而不窮以此為事天
===
治民之本則恐懼而不弛此千聖之學也百世
之經也亦愚臣終身學之而未能者也程子言
告君者曰夫鍾怒擊之則武悲擊之則哀係所
感而入也張子之言曰試言乃事君第一義不
可有欺臣之微誠何足為獻然亦不妄舉以陷
於自欺芻蕘之慮有補萬一亦
大聖之所不棄也惟
陛下致審擇而力行之不勝幸甚臣謹對

punctuated: 心；加以固我，即非此心。所謂渾然與物同體者也。其得其失，不假外求；匪思匪為，乃所自得。靜而養之，而未始有物，實淵深也；動而慎之，而未始不定，實溥博也。故一念之覺即為誠，一念之放即為偽。達於此為大智，决於此為大勇，而飾外之說不足惑之矣。順之而運用也，乃為周流之妙；失之而襲取也，乃為執一之行，而似是之說不足動之矣。以此窮理，則中有主而不雜於二三；以此親賢，則任必專而不疑於可否；以此為裁制宰物之柄，則擬議而不窮；以此為事天治民之本，則恐懼而不弛。此千聖之學也，百世之經也，亦愚臣終身學之而未能者也。程子言告君者曰：「夫鍾，怒擊之則武，悲擊之則哀，係所感而入也。」張子之言曰：「試言，乃事君第一義，不可有欺。」臣之微誠，何足為獻？然亦不妄舉以陷於自欺。芻蕘之慮，有補萬一，亦大聖之所不棄也。惟陛下致審擇而力行之，不勝幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…mind; if obstinacy and self-centeredness are added, it is no longer this mind. This is what is meant by being wholly one body with all things. Whether one retains or loses it need not be sought outside oneself; without deliberate thought or contrived action, one apprehends it for oneself. Nurtured in stillness, with no object ever intruding, it is truly profound; guarded in activity, without ever losing its settled state, it is truly broad and all-embracing. Thus, a single awakened thought constitutes sincerity; a single unrestrained thought constitutes falsity. To comprehend this is great wisdom; to act decisively upon it is great courage. Teachings concerned with outward adornment can then no longer mislead one. Following this mind and putting it into practice brings the marvel of its unhindered circulation; losing it and borrowing its outward forms produces conduct that clings rigidly to one thing. Plausible but false teachings can then no longer sway one. By investigating principle through this, one has a master within and is not distracted by divided purposes. By drawing close to the worthy through this, one entrusts them with responsibility wholeheartedly, without wavering over their suitability. By making this the means of judging and governing all things, one can deliberate without exhaustion. By making this the foundation for serving Heaven and governing the people, one remains vigilant and apprehensive without slackening. This is the learning of a thousand sages and the constant standard of a hundred generations. It is also what your ignorant servant has studied throughout his life but has yet to attain.

Master Cheng, speaking of those who counsel their ruler, said: “As for a bell, strike it in anger and its sound is martial; strike it in sorrow and its sound is mournful. What enters depends on what moves it.” Master Zhang said: “Trying out one's words [?] is the foremost principle in serving one's ruler: there must be no deception.” How could your servant's slight sincerity be worthy of offering? Yet I would not recklessly put forward words and thereby fall into self-deception. If the reflections of a grass-cutter or wood-gatherer can be of even the slightest benefit, even the great sage will not discard them. I ask only that Your Majesty examine and select carefully and put these principles vigorously into practice. I would count it an immeasurable blessing. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
御批探本之論
臣程文德
臣對臣聞有敬天之心然後可以語天德有勤
民之政然後可以語王道天者君之父也不知
敬天則心之所存或不能抑畏而無以達乎天
德民者邦之本也不知勤民則政之所推或乖
於輯寧而無以體乎王道然惟天惠民惟辟奉
天知所以敬天則必求所以勤民之道求所以
勤民則又不外於用舍之宜是則用人所以為
===
民也為民所以奉天也此天人合一之理上下
感通之機而人君之心與政孰有大於是者哉
故曰有天德便可語王道又曰有純王之心然
後可以行純王之政盖以是也於是而盡焉唐
虞三代之所以治也於是而未盡或盡矣而未
純漢唐宋之所以不古若也欽惟
皇帝陛下
繼統當天
垂衣聽治
天命所會人心所歸盖自改元下

御批：探本之論。
臣程文德。
臣對：臣聞，有敬天之心，然後可以語天德；有勤民之政，然後可以語王道。天者，君之父也。不知敬天，則心之所存或不能抑畏，而無以達乎天德。民者，邦之本也。不知勤民，則政之所推或乖於輯寧，而無以體乎王道。然惟天惠民，惟辟奉天。知所以敬天，則必求所以勤民之道；求所以勤民，則又不外於用舍之宜。是則用人所以為民也，為民所以奉天也。此天人合一之理、上下感通之機，而人君之心與政，孰有大於是者哉？故曰：「有天德便可語王道。」又曰：「有純王之心，然後可以行純王之政。」盖以是也。於是而盡焉，唐虞三代之所以治也；於是而未盡，或盡矣而未純，漢唐宋之所以不古若也。欽惟皇帝陛下，繼統當天，垂衣聽治，天命所會，人心所歸。盖自改元下
translation_en:
Imperial comment: An argument that probes the root.
Your servant, Cheng Wende.
Your servant replies: I have heard that only with a heart that reveres Heaven can one speak of heavenly virtue, and only with government that diligently cares for the people can one speak of the Kingly Way. Heaven is the ruler’s father. Without knowing how to revere Heaven, one’s inward dispositions may lack restraint and awe, leaving one unable to attain heavenly virtue. The people are the foundation of the state. Without knowing how to care diligently for them, the policies one implements may fail to bring harmony and peace, leaving one unable to embody the Kingly Way. Yet it is Heaven that bestows blessings upon the people, and the sovereign who serves Heaven. To understand how to revere Heaven, one must seek the way to care diligently for the people; and seeking to care diligently for the people depends, in turn, upon properly employing or setting aside men. Thus, employing men is for the sake of the people, and acting for the people is how one serves Heaven. This is the principle of the unity of Heaven and humanity, the means by which those above and below respond to and communicate with one another. In the ruler’s heart and government, what could be greater than this?
Thus it is said, “With heavenly virtue, one may then speak of the Kingly Way.” It is also said, “Only with the heart of a true king can one carry out the government of a true king.” This, indeed, is the reason. Fully realizing this was what brought good government under Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. Failing to realize it fully, or realizing it fully but without purity, was why the Han, Tang, and Song did not equal antiquity.
I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor has succeeded to the imperial line and assumed Heaven’s place [?]. With robes hanging down, you attend to government; upon you the Mandate of Heaven converges, and to you the people’s hearts turn. Indeed, from the beginning of your reign, when you issued …

…when the edict was first issued, everyone within the Four Seas lifted their heads and stood on tiptoe in anticipation of great peace. Now, eight years have passed; the transformation of government and improvement of administration advance anew each day. Your servant, living obscurely among the common people, has repeatedly heard that Your Majesty’s divine sagacity surpasses that of all antiquity, and that the breadth of your designs exceeds that of a hundred kings. You display consummate filial devotion [?] and honor your parents, humble your aspirations and apply yourself to learning, shun music and sensual pleasures, and refrain from accumulating wealth and profit. You invariably offer sacrifices reverently and heed Heaven’s warnings with care: your heavenly virtue is pure. You exert yourself in pursuit of good government and sincerely cherish the people. Imperial relatives cannot presume upon your favor, nor can close attendants violate established discipline. You personally undertake the toil of working from before dawn until late in the day, without enjoying ease or leisure: the Kingly Way has been put into practice. Whenever your servant reflects on this, my hair stands on end, and, deeply moved, I sigh, thinking that anyone who serves such a ruler yet fails him is truly a criminal for all ages. These fervent feelings have remained in my heart, with no means of conveying them. Now I am fortunate enough to participate in answering at the great court—truly an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years. Since your enlightened questions are moreover so earnest and searching, how could your servant dare not exhaust his humble understanding?
Your servant has recited these words of Confucius in the Record of Exemplary Conduct (Biao ji): “In serving a ruler, first offer him one’s words; bow and present oneself, thereby fulfilling one’s trustworthiness” [?]. As for [?] the few words concerning the sudden change of resolve in the fields of Shen, and the three chapters of the Charge to Yue (Yue ming) responding to and extolling the royal command, these were the words Yi Yin and Fu Yue offered beforehand. They spoke first and subsequently fulfilled their pledges, leaving nothing unfulfilled; the government of the Yin sovereigns remains illustrious to this day. Today’s response is indeed your servant’s own prior offering of words. Though your servant dares not claim to equal Yi Yin and Fu Yue, I truly wish to set them as the standard toward which I strive. May Your Majesty graciously listen. Since the Three Dynasties, rulers have also aspired to good government, yet in the end…

之前君必學而後王臣必學而後仕是故上下
交而德業成也後之世君學而臣不學者有之
矣臣學而君不學者有之矣且學與古之人殊
奚惑乎其不治也今

不能致者，非世道之使然也，學之不至也。三代之前，君必學而後王，臣必學而後仕，是故上下交而德業成也。後之世，君學而臣不學者有之矣，臣學而君不學者有之矣，且學與古之人殊，奚惑乎其不治也？今陛下聖學默契，敬一傳心，書之三要有釋，傳之五箴有註，經筵不間於寒暑，講論必究其精微，學已至矣。二三大臣又皆講學明倫，承弼不怠，明良相遇，曠古而僅見矣。然則今日之務，莫大乎立志，莫要於責實焉已矣。

In the time of the Three Dynasties and before, rulers invariably studied before becoming kings, and ministers invariably studied before entering office. Thus those above and below worked in harmony, and virtue and achievement were brought to fruition. Why wonder that they failed to govern well? The three essentials in the Documents have explanations, and the five admonitions handed down in the tradition have annotations. The business of today, therefore, consists above all in establishing firm resolve and insisting on actual results.

天不能自理天下而付其責於君君亦不能獨

君當盡知人之道知人之哲盡則安民之惠行

聰明自我民聰明天明畏自我民明畏言天人
