…the people, appointing rulers for them and appointing teachers for them, that they might assist the Lord on High in cherishing and bringing peace to the four quarters.” Heaven cannot itself administer all under Heaven, so it entrusts this responsibility to the ruler; the ruler likewise cannot govern all under Heaven alone, so he apportions his duties among his ministers. Thus Heaven desires to bring peace to the people, and the ruler must fully practice the way of discerning worthy men. When this discernment is perfected, the beneficence that brings peace to the people takes effect; the responsibilities of ruler and teacher are fulfilled, and Heaven’s heart is comforted. Gao Yao also said: “Heaven’s hearing and sight derive from our people’s hearing and sight; Heaven’s manifestations of awe derive from our people’s manifestations of awe.” This means that Heaven and humanity share one principle, and that the ruler must be reverent. title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
誠未有無故者昔孔子作春秋書災異百二十
有二其曰正月不雨四月不雨見僖公之閔雨
而有志於民也曰自十有二月不雨至于秋七
月者見文公之不閔雨而無志於民也他如書
日食者三十有六地震者五星孛者三大雨雹
者九隕霜不殺草者一雖不書事應而事應具
存皆以明天之不可不敬也董仲舒以為天心
仁愛人君亦善言天者也至胡安國傳春秋又
謂先王克謹天戒則雖有其變而無其應弗克
畏天災咎之来必矣盖天之於君猶父之於子
===
也感格之機顧在我何如耳是故桑穀生朝若
銅駝荆棘之漸也太戊修德而商祚以永雉雊
鼎耳若野鳥入室之兆也武丁思道而殷道中
興感格之機信在我耳古之慢天虐民者莫如
桀弗敬上天降災下民者莫如紂是故有南巢
之放而来牧野之師桀紂之厲階不可循也明
矣然則敬天勤民之道其為治天下之大端也
審矣
今日天變於上民困於下是以盜賊蠭起戎狄内
侵往者山西青陽之寇雲南土舍之變至勞元

誠未有無故者。昔孔子作《春秋》，書災異百二十有二。其曰「正月不雨，四月不雨」，見僖公之閔雨而有志於民也；曰「自十有二月不雨，至于秋七月」者，見文公之不閔雨而無志於民也。他如書日食者三十有六，地震者五，星孛者三，大雨雹者九，隕霜不殺草者一。雖不書事應，而事應具存，皆以明天之不可不敬也。董仲舒以為天心仁愛人君，亦善言天者也。至胡安國傳《春秋》，又謂先王克謹天戒，則雖有其變而無其應；弗克畏天，災咎之来必矣。盖天之於君，猶父之於子也，感格之機，顧在我何如耳。是故桑穀生朝，若銅駝荆棘之漸也，太戊修德而商祚以永；雉雊鼎耳，若野鳥入室之兆也，武丁思道而殷道中興。感格之機，信在我耳。古之慢天虐民者莫如桀，弗敬上天、降災下民者莫如紂。是故有南巢之放，而来牧野之師。桀紂之厲階不可循也，明矣。然則敬天勤民之道，其為治天下之大端也，審矣。
今日天變於上，民困於下，是以盜賊蠭起，戎狄内侵。往者山西青陽之寇、雲南土舍之變，至勞元
translation_en:
…truly never occur without cause. In former times, when Confucius composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, he recorded 122 calamities and anomalies. The entries “In the first month, no rain” and “In the fourth month, no rain” show that Duke Xi was concerned about the drought and attentive to the people. The entry “From the twelfth month there was no rain, down to the seventh month in autumn” shows that Duke Wen was unconcerned about the drought and inattentive to the people. Other entries record thirty-six solar eclipses, five earthquakes, three appearances of comets, nine great hailstorms, and one fall of frost that did not kill the grass. Although the corresponding human events are not recorded, those correspondences are all present. All this makes clear that Heaven must be revered. Dong Zhongshu held that Heaven’s heart cherished the ruler with benevolent love; he too spoke well about Heaven. Later, in his commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, Hu Anguo further stated that when the former kings duly heeded Heaven’s warnings, anomalies might occur without the corresponding disasters; if they failed to stand in awe of Heaven, calamity and misfortune would certainly come. For Heaven’s relationship to the ruler is like a father’s relationship to his son: the means of moving Heaven depend solely on how we ourselves act.
Thus, when mulberry and paper-mulberry trees grew in the royal court, this seemed a first sign of bronze camels standing amid thorns—the desolation of a fallen dynasty. Yet Taiwu cultivated his virtue, and the Shang dynasty’s tenure was prolonged. When a pheasant crowed on the handle of a sacrificial cauldron, this seemed an omen like a wild bird entering a dwelling. Yet Wuding reflected upon the Way, and Yin’s rule flourished anew. The means of moving Heaven truly lie within ourselves. Among the ancients, none treated Heaven with greater contempt or the people with greater cruelty than Jie; none showed less reverence for Heaven above or brought greater calamity upon the people below than Zhou. Hence came the banishment to Nanchao and the army at Muye. It is clear that one must not follow Jie and Zhou along the steps that led to ruin. It is therefore certain that revering Heaven and diligently caring for the people constitute a fundamental principle of governing all under Heaven.
Today, Heaven manifests anomalies above, while the people suffer hardship below. Consequently, bandits rise in swarms, and the Rong and Di invade our territory. Previously, the bandit outbreak at Qingyang in Shanxi [?] and the uprising of native chieftains’ heirs in Yunnan went so far as to trouble the commander-in-chief…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
戎之啓行偏頭關有警寧夏有寇亦貽
聖心之軫念一方有急四方騷動饑寒困苦之際加
之轉徙逃亡斯民之害亦亟矣夫
聖人在上視民如傷一有變異
恐懼修省宜乎感格而民之不聊生者猶若此臣
亦思之而未得其故也比者竊見
陛下憫念川陝荆廣諸方之民水旱饑饉
詔有司大沛蠲恩急行賑貸至其委曲當處者又
曰宜體朕意推而行之誠恐明年青黃不接之時
尤為可慮懇惻哀矜聞者竦動
===
詔下之日都人無不感泣即此亦可以感回天意
矣而何民困之猶未紓也
聖問致疑於用人之道或有未當臣愚亦豈敢謂其
必不然耶夫張官置吏所以為民以一縣言之
一令得其人則蒼生受其福不得其人則蒼生
受其殃推此而上一郡可知也一省又可知也
使為省為郡為縣者皆得其人則民生安而天
下治矣若夫銓選之司又用人之人也銓選得
其人則天下之吏皆得其人如繩之貫物臂之
使指統會無遺矣昔唐玄宗選天下縣令欲先

punctuated:
戎之啓行。偏頭關有警，寧夏有寇，亦貽聖心之軫念。一方有急，四方騷動；饑寒困苦之際，加之轉徙逃亡，斯民之害亦亟矣。夫聖人在上，視民如傷，一有變異，恐懼修省，宜乎感格，而民之不聊生者猶若此，臣亦思之而未得其故也。
比者竊見陛下憫念川陝荆廣諸方之民，水旱饑饉，詔有司大沛蠲恩，急行賑貸。至其委曲當處者，又曰：「宜體朕意，推而行之。誠恐明年青黃不接之時，尤為可慮。」懇惻哀矜，聞者竦動。詔下之日，都人無不感泣。即此亦可以感回天意矣，而何民困之猶未紓也？
聖問致疑於用人之道或有未當，臣愚亦豈敢謂其必不然耶？夫張官置吏，所以為民。以一縣言之，一令得其人，則蒼生受其福；不得其人，則蒼生受其殃。推此而上，一郡可知也，一省又可知也。使為省、為郡、為縣者皆得其人，則民生安而天下治矣。若夫銓選之司，又用人之人也。銓選得其人，則天下之吏皆得其人，如繩之貫物、臂之使指，統會無遺矣。昔唐玄宗選天下縣令，欲先
translation_en:
…the commander-in-chief to set out on campaign. There have been alarms at Piantou Pass and incursions in Ningxia, likewise causing Your Majesty anxious concern. When one region faces an emergency, all quarters are thrown into turmoil. Amid hunger, cold, and hardship, the people must also endure displacement and flight: their suffering is indeed acute. Now, with a sage ruler above them, who tends the people as though they were injured and responds to every anomalous portent with apprehension, self-cultivation, and self-examination, Heaven ought surely to be moved. Yet the people remain unable to sustain their lives. Your servant has pondered this too, but has not discovered the reason.
Recently, I observed that Your Majesty, compassionately mindful of the people of Chuan, Shaan, Jing, Guang, and other regions suffering from floods, droughts, and famine, commanded the responsible officials to grant generous tax remissions and promptly provide relief and loans. Concerning particulars requiring appropriate handling, you further said: “You should embody my intention and extend it in practice. I truly fear that next year, when the old grain is exhausted and the new crop is not yet ripe, there will be still greater cause for concern.” Such heartfelt compassion and pity deeply stirred all who heard these words. On the day the edict was issued, everyone in the capital was moved to tears. This alone should suffice to move Heaven to change its intent. Why, then, has the people’s distress still not been relieved?
Your Majesty’s question raises the possibility that something may be amiss in the employment of officials. How could your ignorant servant dare assert that this certainly cannot be so? Offices are established and officials appointed for the sake of the people. Take a single county: if the right man is appointed Magistrate, the common people enjoy the benefits; if the wrong man is appointed, they suffer the consequences. Extending this upward, the same plainly holds for a prefecture, and likewise for a province. If those administering provinces, prefectures, and counties were all the right men, the people’s livelihood would be secure and all under Heaven well governed. Those responsible for personnel selection, moreover, are the men who appoint other men. If the right men hold responsibility for selection, all official posts throughout the realm will be filled by the right men. Like a cord threading objects together, or an arm directing the fingers, they will coordinate the whole without omission. In former times, when Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang sought to select County Magistrates throughout the realm, he wished first to …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
擇十道觀察使姚崇難之范祖禹譏其非宰相
之體而曰天子在擇一相而任之一相擇十使
而使之十使擇刺史縣令而置之蔑不當矣此
用人之格言
陛下之所當念也若夫知人之道皐陶嘗欲察之於
九德矣曰寬而栗柔而立愿而恭亂而敬擾而
毅直而溫簡而廉剛而塞彊而義舉之雖若迂
闊而欲務知人實不能外是也臣伏讀
聖問又曰朕雖存保邦安民之念求其所以實無一
得兹欲俾災沴潛消民生安堵盜賊息邊方靖
===
財充而食足不知如之何可以臻此臣又有以
仰見
陛下盛德下人虛心訪治必欲民生無不安以無負
上天立
君之意意至篤也誠欲致之則臣前所謂今日之務
莫大乎立志莫要於責實者請為
陛下悉之
陛下斷諸心曰二帝三王之治必可復也大臣亦曰
吾必欲輔吾
君以復二帝三王之治也都俞吁咈同寅協恭如是

punctuated:
擇十道觀察使，姚崇難之。范祖禹譏其非宰相之體，而曰：「天子在擇一相而任之，一相擇十使而使之，十使擇刺史、縣令而置之，蔑不當矣。」此用人之格言，陛下之所當念也。若夫知人之道，皐陶嘗欲察之於九德矣，曰：「寬而栗，柔而立，愿而恭，亂而敬，擾而毅，直而溫，簡而廉，剛而塞，彊而義。」舉之雖若迂闊，而欲務知人，實不能外是也。
臣伏讀聖問，又曰：「朕雖存保邦安民之念，求其所以，實無一得。兹欲俾災沴潛消，民生安堵，盜賊息，邊方靖，財充而食足，不知如之何可以臻此？」臣又有以仰見陛下盛德下人，虛心訪治，必欲民生無不安，以無負上天立君之意，意至篤也。誠欲致之，則臣前所謂今日之務莫大乎立志、莫要於責實者，請為陛下悉之。
陛下斷諸心曰：「二帝三王之治，必可復也。」大臣亦曰：「吾必欲輔吾君，以復二帝三王之治也。」都俞吁咈，同寅協恭，如是
translation_en:
…select Surveillance Commissioners for the ten circuits, but Yao Chong raised objections. Fan Zuyu criticized him for failing to act as a grand councilor should, saying: “The Son of Heaven’s task is to select one grand councilor and entrust him with responsibility; that grand councilor selects ten commissioners and employs them; those ten commissioners select prefects and district magistrates and appoint them. None of these appointments would then be unsuitable.” This is a maxim on employing men that Your Majesty should bear in mind. As for discerning men’s character, Gao Yao sought to examine it through the nine virtues: “Generous yet strict; gentle yet firm; honest yet respectful; capable in administration yet reverent; tractable yet resolute; upright yet warm; straightforward yet principled; unyielding yet substantial; strong yet righteous.” To cite these may seem remote from practical affairs, but anyone intent on discerning men’s character truly cannot go beyond them.
I have reverently read further in Your Majesty’s sagely question: “Although I cherish the intention of preserving the state and bringing peace to the people, in seeking the means to do so I have gained nothing at all. I now wish to cause disasters and malign influences quietly to disappear, the people to dwell in security, banditry to cease, the frontiers to be pacified, and wealth and food to be abundant. I do not know how this can be achieved.” Here again I perceive how Your Majesty, in your abundant virtue, humbles yourself before others and seeks counsel on government with an open mind. You are determined that all the people should live securely, so as not to fail Heaven’s purpose in establishing a ruler. Your intention is most earnest. If you truly wish to achieve this, permit me to explain fully to Your Majesty what I said earlier: among today’s tasks, none is greater than establishing resolve, and none more essential than demanding real results.
Let Your Majesty resolve in your heart: “The government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings can certainly be restored.” Let the great ministers likewise say: “We are determined to assist our ruler in restoring the government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings.” With frank exchanges of assent and dissent, sharing reverence and working together respectfully, in this way…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
而後謂之立志
陛下勵精於上群臣明作於下率作興事覈實課功
勞心撫字者得以考其最也偽增戶口者無所
售其欺也如是而後謂之責實
君臣一德上下同心用一人焉必賢者進而不肖者
無所容行一政焉必慮之審而未善者不妄動
如此則大本立矣至於節目之所在則臣謂今
日之大弊不可不去者又有三焉一曰
詔令不信竊見改元初
詔興利除害斡乾轉坤天下相賀以為自此覩太
===
平矣既而有司奉行者日漸反之十無三四存
者此者蠲
詔之下竊恐悉蠲停徵折徵者皆不得其當奉行
猶前日耳是則
朝廷雖有愛民之心而民不被其澤民何由而安
乎易曰渙汗其大號言詔令之當信而不可反
也今
陛下誠能慎重於謀始丁寧於播告間或使人詢訪
有奉行不至者則重繩之以法勵其餘焉則
詔令無不信矣二曰廉風不振夫守令者民之父

punctuated:
而後謂之立志。陛下勵精於上，群臣明作於下，率作興事，覈實課功。勞心撫字者，得以考其最也；偽增戶口者，無所售其欺也。如是而後謂之責實。君臣一德，上下同心，用一人焉，必賢者進而不肖者無所容；行一政焉，必慮之審而未善者不妄動。如此則大本立矣。至於節目之所在，則臣謂今日之大弊不可不去者，又有三焉。
一曰詔令不信。竊見改元初詔，興利除害，斡乾轉坤，天下相賀，以為自此覩太平矣。既而有司奉行者，日漸反之，十無三四存者。此者蠲詔之下，竊恐悉蠲、停徵、折徵者，皆不得其當，奉行猶前日耳。是則朝廷雖有愛民之心，而民不被其澤，民何由而安乎？易曰：「渙汗其大號。」言詔令之當信而不可反也。今陛下誠能慎重於謀始，丁寧於播告，間或使人詢訪，有奉行不至者，則重繩之以法，勵其餘焉，則詔令無不信矣。
二曰廉風不振。夫守令者，民之父
translation_en:
…only then can this be called establishing resolve. Your Majesty must exert yourself above, while your ministers act with discernment below, leading undertakings and initiating affairs, verifying actual results and assessing achievements. Those who devote their minds to caring for the people can then have their outstanding merit recognized; those who falsely inflate household and population figures will have no means of passing off their deceit. Only then can this be called demanding substantive results. When ruler and ministers share one virtue, and those above and below are of one mind, whenever someone is appointed, the worthy will advance and the unworthy will find no place; whenever a policy is implemented, it will have been carefully considered, and measures that are not yet sound will not be rashly undertaken. In this way the great foundation will be established. As for particular measures, your servant holds that there are also three great abuses today that must be eliminated.
The first is that imperial edicts lack credibility. I humbly observed that the initial edict at the change of reign title promoted benefits and removed harms, turning Heaven and Earth about. All under Heaven congratulated one another, believing that henceforth they would witness great peace. Yet the responsible officials gradually acted contrary to it in carrying it out, until scarcely three or four provisions out of ten remained in force. With the issuance of this remission edict [?], I humbly fear that full remissions, suspensions of collection, and collection in commuted form will all be improperly applied, and that implementation will be just as before. Thus, although the court wishes to cherish the people, the people do not receive its bounty. How, then, can they live in peace? The Book of Changes says: “He disperses his great proclamations as sweat.” This means that imperial edicts must be trustworthy and cannot be taken back. If Your Majesty can now truly deliberate carefully at the outset, give explicit and earnest instructions when promulgating edicts, and occasionally send people to make inquiries, then those who fail to implement them fully should be severely punished according to law, to spur the others on. Imperial edicts will then invariably command trust.
The second is that the spirit of incorruptibility languishes. Prefects and county magistrates are the people's fathers…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
母也守令廉則約己以厚下省費而裕人守令
不廉則浚民膏脂以自奉剥民肌膚以自充民
何由而安乎記曰大臣法小臣廉國之肥也司
銓選者誠能簡擇任用察其果廉者即越次遷
之以風天下而其以貪敗者必刑之至探其本
又在厚其俸禄使仰事俯育之有賴焉則守令
無不廉矣三曰三冗不去蘇轍曰天下之害財
者有三曰冗吏也冗兵也冗費也今天下之吏
之兵之費不可謂不冗矣夫是三者之資皆出
於民民何由而安乎古人有言財者民之心良
===
可念也近聞
陛下慨然有剷除冗官之意令百司查革而費用一
事尤所
注意誠能行之必究不揺於群議執之必堅不泥
於故常而冗兵之清理亦推及焉則三冗無不
去矣大本既立三弊復去則敬天之心不徒為
虚文勤民之政有驗於實用天德純備王道大
成如是而財不充食不足如是而民生不安堵
如是而盗賊不息邊方不靖如是而災沴有不
潜消者則臣斷乎未之間也將見二帝三王之

不廉則浚民膏腊以自奉剥民肌膚以自充民
何由而安乎記曰大臣法小臣廉國之肥也司

之以風天下而其以貪敗者必刑之至擇其本

無不廉矣三曰三冗不去蘇轍曰天下之害財

之兵之費不可謂不冗矣夫是三者之資皆出
於民民何由而安乎古人有言財者民之心良
===

陛下慨然有剗除冗官之意令百司查革而費用一
事尤所
注意誠能行之必究不揺於群議執之必堅不泥
於故常而冗兵之清理亦推及焉則三冗無不

punctuated:
母也。守令廉，則約己以厚下，省費而裕人；守令不廉，則浚民膏脂以自奉，剥民肌膚以自充，民何由而安乎？《記》曰：「大臣法，小臣廉，國之肥也。」司銓選者誠能簡擇任用，察其果廉者，即越次遷之，以風天下；而其以貪敗者，必刑之。至探其本，又在厚其俸禄，使仰事俯育之有賴焉，則守令無不廉矣。
三曰三冗不去。蘇轍曰：「天下之害財者有三：曰冗吏也，冗兵也，冗費也。」今天下之吏、之兵、之費，不可謂不冗矣。夫是三者之資，皆出於民，民何由而安乎？古人有言：「財者，民之心。」良可念也。近聞陛下慨然有剷除冗官之意，令百司查革，而費用一事，尤所注意。誠能行之必究，不揺於群議；執之必堅，不泥於故常，而冗兵之清理亦推及焉，則三冗無不去矣。
大本既立，三弊復去，則敬天之心不徒為虚文，勤民之政有驗於實用，天德純備，王道大成。如是而財不充、食不足，如是而民生不安堵，如是而盗賊不息、邊方不靖，如是而災沴有不潜消者，則臣斷乎未之間也。將見二帝三王之
translation_en:
… mothers of the people. When prefects and magistrates are incorruptible, they restrain themselves to provide generously for those below, reducing expenditure to enrich the people. When they are corrupt, they drain the people's lifeblood to maintain themselves and strip the people's flesh to satisfy themselves. How can the people live in peace? The Book of Rites says: “When great ministers observe the law and lesser ministers are incorruptible, the state flourishes.” If those responsible for personnel selection truly choose appointments carefully, and, upon finding men genuinely incorruptible, promote them ahead of the usual order to set an example throughout the realm, while invariably punishing those disgraced by corruption, this will have its effect. To address the root, moreover, requires increasing their salaries so that they have dependable means to support their parents and raise their children. Then no prefect or magistrate will fail to be incorruptible.
Third, the three forms of redundancy have not been eliminated. Su Zhe said: “Three things injure the wealth of the realm: superfluous officials, superfluous troops, and superfluous expenditure.” Today, the realm's officials, troops, and expenditure certainly cannot be said to be free of excess. The resources for all three come from the people. How can the people live in peace? An ancient saying declares: “Wealth is the people's heart.” This truly deserves consideration. Recently I have heard that Your Majesty has resolutely determined to eliminate superfluous officials and has ordered all offices to investigate and abolish unnecessary posts, with expenditure receiving your particular attention. If you carry this through to completion, unshaken by the many opposing opinions, and hold firmly to it without being bound by established practice, extending the same measures to the elimination of superfluous troops, then all three forms of redundancy will be removed.
Once the great foundation is established and these three abuses are eliminated, reverence for Heaven will no longer be mere empty form, and policies devoted to the people's welfare will demonstrate their practical effectiveness. Heavenly virtue will be pure and complete, and the Kingly Way fully realized. If, under such circumstances, funds were still insufficient and food inadequate; if the people still could not live securely; if banditry still persisted and the frontiers remained unsettled; or if disasters and baleful influences failed to subside imperceptibly—then your servant has certainly never heard of such a thing [?]. We shall then witness that of the Two Emperors and Three Kings …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
治不越是矣
陛下於是復何憂乎抑臣惓惓之私復有獻焉方内
之治亂在
陛下所執天下如大器惟
陛下所置其機則本之心而已矣此心不怠天下雖
未治可得而治也此心或怠天下雖已治終必
至亂也詩曰靡不有初鮮克有終怠心一生未
必不有始而無終矣然心之不怠由於不敢自
足也舜德罔愆矣益兢兢業業故成風動之休
禹德無間矣尤不自滿假故致平成之治我
===
太祖之聖德亦云至矣然嘗
序昭鑒錄有曰才疎德薄不足補過消愆又嘗
序資世通訓有曰菲才薄德宵晝弗敢自寧嗚呼
是心即舜禹之心而萬世
聖子神孫之所當體念者也伏願
陛下遠儀舜禹近法
太祖
篤志力行益勤無怠則敬天勤民之道有終而凡
今日之策臣者可不勞而舉矣臣無任惓惓仰望
之至臣謹對

是心即舜禹之心而萬世
聖子神孫之所當體念者也伏願

太祖
篤志力行益勤無怠則敬天勤民之道有終而凡

之至臣謹對
punctuated: 治不越是矣。陛下於是復何憂乎？抑臣惓惓之私復有獻焉。方内之治亂，在陛下所執；天下如大器，惟陛下所置，其機則本之心而已矣。此心不怠，天下雖未治，可得而治也；此心或怠，天下雖已治，終必至亂也。《詩》曰：「靡不有初，鮮克有終。」怠心一生，未必不有始而無終矣。然心之不怠，由於不敢自足也。舜德罔愆矣，益兢兢業業，故成風動之休；禹德無間矣，尤不自滿假，故致平成之治。我太祖之聖德亦云至矣，然嘗序《昭鑒錄》，有曰：「才疎德薄，不足補過消愆。」又嘗序《資世通訓》，有曰：「菲才薄德，宵晝弗敢自寧。」嗚呼！是心即舜禹之心，而萬世聖子神孫之所當體念者也。伏願陛下遠儀舜禹，近法太祖，篤志力行，益勤無怠，則敬天勤民之道有終，而凡今日之策臣者，可不勞而舉矣。臣無任惓惓仰望之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings would go no further than this. What, then, would Your Majesty have left to worry about? Yet in my earnest devotion I have a further offering to make. Order or disorder within the realm depends on what Your Majesty holds fast to. All under Heaven is like a great vessel: its placement rests with Your Majesty, and the pivotal factor is rooted solely in your heart. If this heart does not grow negligent, the realm can be brought to order even if it is not yet well governed. If this heart should grow negligent, the realm will ultimately fall into disorder even if it is already well governed. The Book of Odes says: “None fail to make a beginning; few can carry it through to the end.” Once negligence arises in the heart, one may well begin but fail to finish. Yet freedom from negligence comes from not daring to be self-satisfied. Shun’s virtue was without fault, yet he became still more vigilant and careful; thus he achieved the glorious transformation of his people, who responded like things stirred by the wind. Yu’s virtue was beyond reproach, yet he was especially unwilling to pride himself on his greatness; thus he achieved a reign in which the land was made level and its ordering completed.

The sagely virtue of our Taizu may likewise be called supreme. Yet in his preface to the Record of the Clear Mirror (Zhaojian lu), he once wrote: “My talent is meager and my virtue slight, insufficient to make amends for my errors and efface my faults.” Again, in his preface to Comprehensive Instructions for Aiding the World (Zishi tongxun), he wrote: “With my meager talent and slight virtue, by night and day I dare not allow myself repose.” Ah! This heart is the very heart of Shun and Yu, and it is what his sagely sons and divine grandsons throughout all generations ought to embody and keep in mind. I humbly pray that Your Majesty take Shun and Yu as distant exemplars and Taizu as your recent model, remain steadfast in purpose and strenuous in practice, and become ever more diligent without negligence. Then the way of revering Heaven and laboring for the people will be carried through to its conclusion, and all the matters on which you have questioned your servant today can be accomplished without toil. Your servant’s earnest hopes and reverent expectations are beyond expression. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
御批能守聖學以為本此乃知要之說
臣楊名
臣對臣聞人君之舉王道也亦惟急其先務而
已矣夫王道雖多端然所當務必有居其先者
人君徒欲舉之而漫不知所致力則行於今者
不能盡合乎古善諸已者未必皆宜於人心動
而道愈遠功勞而事益隳求與王者同治不可
得已吁人君者天之所命以代理而民之所望
以咸熈者也至於道遠而不能舉事隳而不能
===
振則不惟斯民之望之孤而天之命亦鮮克副
矣是故必有務焉以居其先而為所當急茍能
從事於斯守之貞而無所移行之固而不能撓
則一人之圖回足以廣四海之化一日之經營
足以培千萬世之業所謂其事半於古人而其
功倍之者端不外是矣又何王道之不舉而深
以為慮哉欽惟
皇帝陛下堯思欽明舜文濬哲潛龍德以居
藩服承
天命而繼

天命而繼
punctuated:
御批：能守聖學以為本，此乃知要之說。

臣楊名。

臣對：臣聞人君之舉王道也，亦惟急其先務而已矣。夫王道雖多端，然所當務必有居其先者。人君徒欲舉之，而漫不知所致力，則行於今者不能盡合乎古，善諸已者未必皆宜於人，心動而道愈遠，功勞而事益隳，求與王者同治，不可得已。吁！人君者，天之所命以代理，而民之所望以咸熈者也。至於道遠而不能舉，事隳而不能振，則不惟斯民之望之孤，而天之命亦鮮克副矣。是故必有務焉，以居其先而為所當急。茍能從事於斯，守之貞而無所移，行之固而不能撓，則一人之圖回足以廣四海之化，一日之經營足以培千萬世之業。所謂其事半於古人而其功倍之者，端不外是矣。又何王道之不舉，而深以為慮哉？欽惟皇帝陛下，堯思欽明，舜文濬哲，潛龍德以居藩服，承天命而繼
translation_en:
Imperial comment: “He can uphold the learning of the sages as his foundation. These are the words of one who understands what is essential.”

Your servant, Yang Ming.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, in putting the Kingly Way into practice, a ruler need only give urgency to his foremost duties. Although the Kingly Way has many aspects, among the tasks to be undertaken there must be some that come first. If a ruler merely wishes to implement it but has no clear understanding of where to direct his efforts, what he does today cannot fully accord with antiquity, and what is good in himself [?] may not all be suitable for others. His mind grows agitated while the Way becomes ever more distant; he expends his efforts while affairs fall into greater disorder. He cannot thereby attain government equal to that of the sage kings. Alas! The ruler is appointed by Heaven to govern on its behalf, and the people look to him so that all may flourish. If the Way becomes distant and he cannot put it into practice, and affairs fall into disorder and he cannot restore them, he not only disappoints the hopes of these people but can scarcely fulfill Heaven’s mandate.

Thus there must be a task that takes precedence and demands urgency. If he can devote himself to this, hold to it steadfastly without wavering, and carry it out firmly without yielding, then the deliberations of one man will suffice to spread transforming influence throughout the Four Seas, and a single day’s endeavors will suffice to nurture an enterprise lasting thousands upon thousands of generations. What is meant by accomplishing twice as much as the ancients with half their effort lies precisely in this. Why, then, should he be deeply troubled that the Kingly Way might not be put into practice?

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses Yao’s reverent and enlightened thought and Shun’s refinement and profound wisdom. With the virtue of a dragon still hidden, you dwelt in a princely domain; you received Heaven’s mandate and succeeded to …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
大統臨御以来八年于兹修身勵成湯之日新遜志
邁髙宗之時敏其念之所存政之所發實欲追
三代而上之漢唐宋之英君誼辟皆所不屑也
故
中興之休
嘉靖之盛卓乎不可尚已兹進臣等于
廷尤惓惓以王道為問憂勤惕勵之心何其純且
切哉夫天下之士三年一試於有司薦於大宗
伯進於
天子之庭而策試之往者之舉直循故事耳惟
===
陛下深知治本之所先人言之可用乃特降
清穆之容大發
温慰之旨必欲臣等悉心吐露推衍所以于篇於
戲道不遇時雖仲尼亦且徒爾而臣之疎庸遭
際若此寧敢復有忌諱以上負
聖明而下自負其時哉臣竊惟天下者勢而已矣其
土地之遼邈民物之繁衍事務之紛藉皆勢也
天能覆之而不能治之地能載之而不能教之
故即天地之中而特立乎聖人以為治教之君
師所以繼天立極為民作則其任亦大且艱矣

punctuated:
大統。臨御以来，八年于兹，修身勵成湯之日新，遜志邁髙宗之時敏。其念之所存、政之所發，實欲追三代而上之，漢唐宋之英君誼辟，皆所不屑也。故中興之休、嘉靖之盛，卓乎不可尚已。兹進臣等于廷，尤惓惓以王道為問，憂勤惕勵之心，何其純且切哉！
夫天下之士，三年一試於有司，薦於大宗伯，進於天子之庭而策試之。往者之舉，直循故事耳。惟陛下深知治本之所先、人言之可用，乃特降清穆之容，大發温慰之旨，必欲臣等悉心吐露，推衍所以于篇。於戲！道不遇時，雖仲尼亦且徒爾，而臣之疎庸，遭際若此，寧敢復有忌諱，以上負聖明，而下自負其時哉！
臣竊惟天下者，勢而已矣。其土地之遼邈、民物之繁衍、事務之紛藉，皆勢也。天能覆之而不能治之，地能載之而不能教之。故即天地之中，而特立乎聖人，以為治教之君師，所以繼天立極，為民作則，其任亦大且艱矣。
translation_en:
…the imperial succession. Eight years have now passed since Your Majesty assumed the throne. In cultivating yourself, you strive for Cheng Tang’s daily renewal; in humble application of mind, you surpass Gaozong’s constant diligence. What you cherish in your thoughts and put forth in your government truly aims to emulate the Three Dynasties and surpass them. Even the illustrious rulers and righteous sovereigns of the Han, Tang, and Song are beneath your aspirations. Thus the glory of this restoration and the flourishing of the Jiajing reign stand preeminent and unsurpassable. Now you have brought us, your servants, before the court and, with particular earnestness, questioned us about the Kingly Way. How pure and fervent is your concern, diligence, vigilance, and resolve!
The scholars of the realm are examined once every three years by the responsible authorities, recommended to the Minister of Rites, and brought before the Son of Heaven to be tested with policy questions. In former times, this undertaking merely followed established precedent. Your Majesty alone profoundly understands what must take priority at the root of good government and how the words of others may be put to use. You have therefore graciously condescended to appear before us with a serene and dignified countenance and issued words of warm reassurance, desiring above all that we, your servants, disclose our thoughts fully and elaborate their underlying reasons in our essays [?]. Alas! When the Way does not find its proper time, even Zhongni could accomplish nothing. Yet I, your inept and commonplace servant, have encountered an opportunity such as this. How could I dare still to hold back out of fear, thereby failing Your enlightened Majesty above and myself failing the opportunity afforded by these times below?
Your servant humbly considers that the realm consists simply of the configuration of its circumstances. Its far-reaching territory, its teeming people and things, and its tangled affairs all constitute this configuration. Heaven can cover it but cannot govern it; Earth can bear it but cannot instruct it. Thus, between Heaven and Earth, the sage is specially established as sovereign and teacher, to govern and instruct. He thereby carries on Heaven’s work, establishes the supreme standard, and provides rules for the people. His responsibility is indeed great and difficult.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
夫人君以孑然之身成位乎其中與天地參耳
目一聞見也手足一運行也而天下之勢如此
苟無所以先之是日戰於變幻之途事臨乎抵
捂之敵非惟勢之不克一而其身亦已勞矣臣
未見自處其勞而能致人於逸者也故王者之
道必有所以為之要焉君人者不可不加之意
也臣伏讀
聖制有曰朕惟治天下之道其端不可槩舉特以大
者論之在乎知人安民二者而已於戲斯二者
王道也
===
陛下言及之豈徒然哉蓋其嘉樂之心存於中故稱

安民以為舜大聖也皐陶大賢也告戒之際無
他詞說顧諄諄於知人安民之言其故何哉及
觀其九德之任與夫惇典庸禮命德討罪之事
乃知人之難知民之難安雖堯舜同以為病而
後世益甚矣

牾之敵非惟勢之不克一而其身亦已勞矣臣
未見自處其勞而能致人於逸者也故王者之
道必有所以為之要焉君人者不可不加之意

王道也

夫人君以孑然之身成位乎其中，與天地參，耳目一聞見也，手足一運行也，而天下之勢如此。苟無所以先之，是日戰於變幻之途，事臨乎抵捂之敵，非惟勢之不克一，而其身亦已勞矣。臣未見自處其勞而能致人於逸者也。故王者之道必有所以為之要焉，君人者不可不加之意也。
臣伏讀聖制有曰：「朕惟治天下之道，其端不可槩舉，特以大者論之，在乎知人安民二者而已。」於戲！斯二者，王道也。陛下言及之，豈徒然哉？蓋其嘉樂之心存於中，故稱慕之言形於外。臣於此有以知聖意之所嚮矣。
臣嘗感於皐陶之陳謨曰：「在知人，在安民。」以為舜大聖也，皐陶大賢也，告戒之際無他詞說，顧諄諄於知人安民之言，其故何哉？及觀其九德之任，與夫惇典、庸禮、命德、討罪之事，乃知人之難知，民之難安，雖堯舜同以為病，而後世益甚矣。聖制所謂「知人則哲，必能官而任之；安民則惠，必使匹夫匹婦各得其所」者，豈可易易言哉？且
translation_en:
The ruler, with his solitary person, takes his place in the midst of all this, standing alongside Heaven and Earth. His ears and eyes provide but one person's hearing and sight; his hands and feet provide but one person's movements. Yet the circumstances of the realm are so vast and complex. Unless he has some means of anticipating them, he must daily contend with shifting conditions and confront obstructing adversaries [?] in every affair. Not only will he fail to bring these circumstances into unity; he himself will already be exhausted. Your servant has never seen anyone who, while keeping himself in toil, could bring others to repose. Thus the way of a true king must have an essential principle by which to proceed, and one who rules over others cannot fail to give it his attention.
Your servant has reverently read these words in Your Majesty's decree: “I consider that the principles of governing the realm cannot all be enumerated in general terms. To speak only of the greatest, they lie in just two things: knowing men and bringing peace to the people.” Ah! These two constitute the kingly way. Can Your Majesty's mention of them be without purpose? It is because a heart that esteems and delights in them dwells within that words of praise and admiration appear without. From this, your servant can discern the direction of Your Majesty's intentions.
Your servant has often been moved by Gao Yao's exposition of his counsels: “It lies in knowing men; it lies in bringing peace to the people.” I have reflected that Shun was a great sage and Gao Yao a man of great worth. When offering admonition, Gao Yao spoke of nothing else, but earnestly reiterated knowing men and bringing peace to the people. Why was this? Only when I examined his appointments according to the nine virtues, together with the tasks of strengthening the established norms, putting rites into practice, appointing the virtuous, and punishing the guilty, did I understand how difficult it is to know men and how difficult it is to bring peace to the people. Even Yao and Shun alike regarded these as difficult, and in later ages the difficulties became still greater. Your Majesty's decree speaks of “the discernment that comes from knowing men, which must enable one to appoint them to office and entrust them with responsibilities; and the beneficence that brings peace to the people, which must ensure that every ordinary man and woman finds a proper place.” How could these be spoken of lightly? title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
陛下自踐阼之餘勵精圖治人惟求賢事必稽古宜
其在位者皆伊吕之圖在下者遵唐虞之化也
何災變頻仍旱澇相繼東南困於前西北病於
後而地無幸民前年告大饑去年稱大無而歲
無虛日少壮多散於四方老弱同歸於一壑聞
者痛心見者流涕盖我
國朝百六十餘年之所罕有也夫
聖王在上則百祥並臻而今之應非其感豈無其故
與
陛下發自淵衷直歸於用人之失真所謂明見萬里
===
之外心遊八紘之表者也臣請得而備論之天
變之来民心之怨也民心之怨任官之非也任
官之非進退之倒置勸懲之失宜選任無公平
之道也何以曰天變之来民心之怨也盖天聽
自我民聽天視自我民視故民心和則雨暘時
若寒暑順度四時無忒百穀皆登今也號泣之
聲達於四境呻吟之氣蒸於兩間是人心已不
和矣天變不由是而作乎何以曰民心之怨任
官之非也盖國之本在民民之命在官故官得
人則靖共爾位保我黎民生養可遂教化可行

punctuated:
陛下自踐阼之餘，勵精圖治，人惟求賢，事必稽古，宜其在位者皆伊吕之圖，在下者遵唐虞之化也。何災變頻仍，旱澇相繼，東南困於前，西北病於後，而地無幸民；前年告大饑，去年稱大無，而歲無虛日。少壮多散於四方，老弱同歸於一壑，聞者痛心，見者流涕，盖我國朝百六十餘年之所罕有也。夫聖王在上，則百祥並臻，而今之應非其感，豈無其故與？陛下發自淵衷，直歸於用人之失，真所謂明見萬里之外、心遊八紘之表者也。
臣請得而備論之。天變之来，民心之怨也；民心之怨，任官之非也；任官之非，進退之倒置、勸懲之失宜、選任無公平之道也。何以曰天變之来，民心之怨也？盖天聽自我民聽，天視自我民視。故民心和，則雨暘時若，寒暑順度，四時無忒，百穀皆登。今也號泣之聲達於四境，呻吟之氣蒸於兩間，是人心已不和矣。天變不由是而作乎？何以曰民心之怨，任官之非也？盖國之本在民，民之命在官。故官得人，則靖共爾位，保我黎民，生養可遂，教化可行。
translation_en:
…Since Your Majesty ascended the throne, you have devoted yourself earnestly to good government, seeking only worthy men for service and consulting antiquity in every undertaking. Those holding office ought therefore all to be men in the image of Yi and Lü [?], and those below ought to follow the civilizing influence of Tang Yao and Yu Shun. Why, then, have calamities and anomalies occurred so frequently, with droughts and floods following one another? The southeast suffered first, and the northwest afterward, leaving no region whose people escaped misfortune. The year before last brought reports of great famine; last year was described as a year of utter dearth, with not a day of respite throughout the year. Many of the young and strong have scattered in all directions, while the old and weak share a single burial gully. Those who hear of it are heartsick; those who see it shed tears. Such suffering has rarely occurred in the more than 160 years of our dynasty. When a sage king reigns, auspicious signs should arrive together in abundance. Yet the responses now appearing do not accord with what should have evoked them. Can this be without a cause? Speaking from the depths of your heart, Your Majesty has attributed it directly to failures in employing men. Truly, this is what is meant by seeing clearly beyond ten thousand li and letting the mind range beyond the eight extremities of the world.
Permit your servant to discuss this fully. Heavenly anomalies arise from the people's resentment. The people's resentment arises from the appointment of unsuitable officials. Unsuitable appointments arise from the inversion of promotion and dismissal, the improper use of encouragement and punishment, and the absence of fairness and impartiality in selection and appointment. Why do I say that heavenly anomalies arise from the people's resentment? Because Heaven hears through what our people hear, and Heaven sees through what our people see. Thus, when the people's hearts are harmonious, rain and sunshine come at the proper times, cold and heat follow their prescribed measure, the four seasons do not deviate, and all grains ripen. Now, however, the sound of wailing reaches the four borders, and the breath of groaning rises between Heaven and Earth. The people's hearts are already without harmony. Would heavenly anomalies not arise from this? Why do I say that the people's resentment arises from the appointment of unsuitable officials? Because the people are the foundation of the state, and their lives depend upon its officials. Thus, when the right men hold office, they reverently discharge the duties of their posts and protect our common people; the people's livelihood and sustenance can be secured, and moral instruction can be put into practice.…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
今也食君祿者惟急私室視民瘼者不切已身
是任官巳非人矣民心不由是而怨乎何以曰
任官非人進退倒置勸懲失宜選任無公平之
道也蓋進退審則賢者樂為用不肖者無倖進
之途矣勸懲當則善者必蒙賞不善者甘顯戮
之法矣選任果公且平則所獲皆真才而政効
著矣一或毀譽信於人喜怒任於已三者之施
有不得其中俾憸夫細人得厠其間則其為害
豈淺淺哉夫數者之政
陛下析而言之欲各求其故臣愚乃合而為一正以
===
其各有所當先務也臣願
陛下昭離明之照奮乾剛之斷知天變之消和人心
其先務也凡所以撙節民財愛養民力者無所
不用其極宮室可卑也衣服可惡也飲食可菲
也惟恐戾人心之所欲以傷國本也知人心之
和官得人其先務也凡所以敷求哲人明揚側
陋者無所不用其謹左右可問也諸大夫可詳
也國人可察也惟恐拂公論之所在以貽民害
也知任官之先務在進退勸懲選任也虛心以
采人言直道以行已法人皆以為賢吾察之果

臣願陛下昭離明之照，奮乾剛之斷。知天變之消，和人心其先務也，凡所以撙節民財、愛養民力者，無所不用其極。宮室可卑也，衣服可惡也，飲食可菲也，惟恐戾人心之所欲，以傷國本也。知人心之和，官得人其先務也，凡所以敷求哲人、明揚側陋者，無所不用其謹。左右可問也，諸大夫可詳也，國人可察也，惟恐拂公論之所在，以貽民害也。知任官之先務在進退、勸懲、選任也，虛心以采人言，直道以行已法。人皆以為賢，吾察之果
translation_en:
Today, however, those who receive the ruler’s stipend concern themselves only with their own households; those charged with attending to the people’s suffering do not feel it as touching themselves. Thus unsuitable men have already been appointed to office. How could the people’s resentment fail to arise from this? Why do I say that unsuitable appointments arise from the inversion of promotion and dismissal, inappropriate rewards and punishments, and the absence of impartiality and fairness in selection and appointment? When promotion and dismissal are carefully judged, worthy men gladly enter service, while the unworthy have no avenue for advancement by mere good fortune. When rewards and punishments are appropriate, the good are certain to receive rewards, while the bad accept the law’s public punishment. When selection and appointment are truly impartial and fair, all those recruited possess genuine ability, and the results of government become manifest. But if one trusts others’ slanders and praises, or gives free rein to one’s own pleasure and anger, these three practices may fail to strike the proper balance, allowing crafty and petty men to insinuate themselves among the officials. Could the harm they cause then be slight? Your Majesty has discussed these several matters of government separately, seeking the cause of each. Your foolish servant has instead joined them into one, precisely because each has something that must receive attention first.
I wish Your Majesty to shine forth with the illuminating clarity of Li and exercise the resolute strength of Qian. Recognize that, to dispel Heaven’s anomalies, the first task is to bring harmony to the people’s hearts. Spare no effort in conserving the people’s wealth and nurturing their strength. Palaces may be modest, clothing coarse, and food plain: fear only that you might oppose what the people desire and thereby injure the foundation of the state. Recognize that, to bring harmony to the people’s hearts, the first task is to obtain suitable men for office. Exercise the utmost care in seeking wise men far and wide and bringing to prominence those of humble station who remain obscure. Your attendants may be questioned, the views of the great officers examined in detail, and those of the people of the realm scrutinized: fear only that you might disregard public judgment and thereby bring harm upon the people. Recognize that the first tasks in appointing officials lie in promotion and dismissal, rewards and punishments, and selection and appointment. Keep an open mind in receiving others’ words, and follow the upright Way in putting your own standards into practice [?]. If everyone considers a man worthy, and upon examining him I find that he truly…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
賢也則進之而不貳人皆以為不肖吾察之果
不肖也則退之而不疑苟人本賢矣以一事未
協於心而不進本不肖矣以一言偶中其欲而
不退皆非臣之所敢知也以至勸懲之加必審
其善惡之實如曰廉吏也以某事知之知之果
真然後勸如曰貪吏也以某事知之知之果真
然後懲使毋至於失宜可也選任之法必責之
有司選者必協乎人望任者必合乎輿情使毋
失公平之道可也夫如是則先務急而王道舉
矣譬之柁以運舟括以發弩功用神速無難致
者在
陛下加之意而已臣讀
聖制之末又曰朕欲俾災沴潛消民生安堵盜賊息
邊方靖財充而食足不知如之何可以臻此特進
爾多士于廷爾多士明於王道有日矣且目覩時
艱豈無真識的見以匡我者當悉心吐露推衍所
以于篇朕當勉為親覽焉勿諂勿憚勿泛勿畧庶
副朕意於戲理惟可以一貫治不在乎多言臣前
所謂急先務者已見其槩矣請因
明問之丁寧者而申言之災沴之作天將藉之以

賢也，則進之而不貳；人皆以為不肖，吾察之果不肖也，則退之而不疑。苟人本賢矣，以一事未協於心而不進；本不肖矣，以一言偶中其欲而不退，皆非臣之所敢知也。以至勸懲之加，必審其善惡之實。如曰廉吏也，以某事知之，知之果真，然後勸；如曰貪吏也，以某事知之，知之果真，然後懲，使毋至於失宜可也。選任之法，必責之有司。選者必協乎人望，任者必合乎輿情，使毋失公平之道可也。夫如是，則先務急而王道舉矣。譬之柁以運舟，括以發弩，功用神速，無難致者，在陛下加之意而已。
臣讀聖制之末，又曰：「朕欲俾災沴潛消，民生安堵，盜賊息，邊方靖，財充而食足，不知如之何可以臻此。特進爾多士于廷，爾多士明於王道有日矣，且目覩時艱，豈無真識的見以匡我者？當悉心吐露，推衍所以于篇，朕當勉為親覽焉。勿諂，勿憚，勿泛，勿畧，庶副朕意。」於戲！理惟可以一貫，治不在乎多言。臣前所謂急先務者，已見其槩矣。請因明問之丁寧者而申言之。災沴之作，天將藉之以
translation_en:
…worthy, then promote him without wavering. If everyone considers a man unworthy, and upon examining him I find that he is indeed unworthy, then dismiss him without hesitation. If a man is fundamentally worthy, yet is denied advancement because one action fails to accord with the ruler’s wishes; or if he is fundamentally unworthy, yet is not dismissed because one remark happens to suit the ruler’s desires—neither practice is something your servant would presume to countenance. In administering encouragement and punishment, one must likewise carefully ascertain the facts of good and evil conduct. If someone is called an incorrupt official, determine what particular deed establishes this; only after verifying its truth should he be rewarded. If someone is called a corrupt official, determine what particular deed establishes this; only after verifying its truth should he be punished. What matters is to ensure that neither measure is inappropriate. Responsibility for the procedures of selection and appointment must be placed upon the competent authorities. Those selected must accord with public expectations, and those appointed must accord with public sentiment, so that the principle of fairness and impartiality is preserved. If this is done, the foremost tasks will receive urgent attention, and the Kingly Way will be put into practice. Like a rudder steering a boat or a release mechanism [?] discharging a crossbow, their effects will be wondrously swift, and nothing will be difficult to achieve. It rests only with Your Majesty to give this your attention.
Your servant reads further at the end of the imperial decree: “I wish to cause calamities and baleful influences to fade away unseen, the people to live securely, banditry to cease, the frontiers to become tranquil, and wealth and food to be abundant. I do not know how this can be achieved. I have therefore specially summoned you assembled scholars to court. You have understood the Kingly Way for some time and have personally witnessed the difficulties of the age. Surely you possess genuine understanding and sound insights with which to guide me aright? You should express yourselves with complete candor and expound in your essays the means by which these ends may be attained. I shall endeavor to examine them personally. Do not flatter, do not be afraid, do not be vague, and do not be cursory, so that you may fulfill my intentions.” Ah! Principles can be unified by a single thread; good government does not depend upon many words. The broad outline of what your servant earlier called giving urgency to the foremost tasks has already been set out. Allow me to elaborate in response to the earnest admonitions in your enlightened question. When calamities and baleful influences arise, Heaven intends to use them to…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
警人君仁愛之意也馴至於民生擾攘盜賊繁
熾夷狄侵凌財食匱乏以成莫大之憂固理勢
之必至也抑欲其消之安之息之靖之亦必有
先務焉非財充而食足不可蓋惟財不充食不
足然後邊方不靖盜賊不息民生不安災沴不
消然是二者又皆有其故焉是故財之不充冗
費害之也而所以為冗費者不止一事土木之
興也兵旅之用也禱醮之需也三者不去則財
不充臣願
陛下斟酌時宜不惑人議斷然止之而不為則財不
===
期充而自充矣食之不足冗食縻之也而所以
為冗食者不止一端額外之官吏也宮中之宦
妾也老羸之軍匠也三者不簡則食不足臣願
陛下裁定常數毋拘故事奮然省之而不吝則食不
期足而自足矣財充食足則邊方靖盜賊息民
生可安而人心和矣人心和於下天心和於上
災沴不消有是理乎雖然臣之所已言者皆
聖制之所及者也至其區區忠愛之私尚有一言以
塵瀆
聖聽惟

punctuated:
警人君，仁愛之意也。馴至於民生擾攘、盜賊繁熾、夷狄侵凌、財食匱乏，以成莫大之憂，固理勢之必至也。抑欲其消之、安之、息之、靖之，亦必有先務焉，非財充而食足不可。蓋惟財不充、食不足，然後邊方不靖、盜賊不息、民生不安、災沴不消。然是二者又皆有其故焉。是故財之不充，冗費害之也。而所以為冗費者，不止一事：土木之興也，兵旅之用也，禱醮之需也。三者不去，則財不充。臣願陛下斟酌時宜，不惑人議，斷然止之而不為，則財不期充而自充矣。食之不足，冗食縻之也。而所以為冗食者，不止一端：額外之官吏也，宮中之宦妾也，老羸之軍匠也。三者不簡，則食不足。臣願陛下裁定常數，毋拘故事，奮然省之而不吝，則食不期足而自足矣。財充食足，則邊方靖、盜賊息，民生可安而人心和矣。人心和於下，天心和於上，災沴不消，有是理乎？

雖然，臣之所已言者，皆聖制之所及者也。至其區區忠愛之私，尚有一言以塵瀆聖聽，惟
translation_en:
…to admonish the ruler: this expresses Heaven’s benevolent concern. That matters gradually reach the point where the people’s lives are thrown into turmoil, bandits proliferate, foreign peoples encroach, and funds and provisions run short, producing the gravest anxiety, is indeed the inevitable course of events. Yet to dispel these calamities, settle the people, quell the bandits, and pacify the frontiers, there must likewise be a task that takes precedence: funds must be ample and provisions sufficient. For it is only when funds are inadequate and provisions insufficient that the frontiers remain unsettled, banditry persists, the people cannot live in peace, and calamities do not abate. These two shortages, however, each have their causes.

Funds are inadequate because excessive expenditure depletes them. Such expenditure takes more than one form: construction projects, military expenses, and the demands of prayers and Daoist offering rites. Unless these three are eliminated, funds will remain inadequate. Your servant hopes that Your Majesty will weigh what is appropriate to the times, remain unswayed by others’ opinions, and resolutely halt these activities and cease undertaking them. Then funds will become ample of themselves, without any deliberate effort to make them so.

Provisions are insufficient because superfluous mouths consume them. These too take more than one form: officials and clerks beyond the authorized quotas, eunuchs and concubines within the palace, and aged and infirm soldiers and artisans. Unless these three groups are reduced, provisions will remain insufficient. Your servant hopes that Your Majesty will establish fixed quotas, refuse to be bound by precedent, and vigorously reduce their numbers without reluctance. Then provisions will become sufficient of themselves, without any deliberate effort to make them so. With ample funds and sufficient provisions, the frontiers will be pacified, banditry will cease, the people’s lives can be secure, and their hearts will be harmonious. When people’s hearts are harmonious below and Heaven’s heart is harmonious above, could calamities possibly fail to abate?

Nevertheless, all that your servant has said concerns matters addressed in the imperial decree. Out of my humble personal devotion and love, I still have one further word with which to trouble Your Majesty’s sacred hearing. I only ask that…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
陛下察其衷矜其愚不錄其罪俾臣得畢其說斯臣
之命也臣嘗聞宋儒蔡沉有言曰帝王之治本
於道帝王之道本於心及稽諸經史凡堯舜禹
湯文武之盛所以卓乎不可及而漢唐宋之治
所以不古若者皆此心之純駁以為之差乃知
人之一心其量不盈一掬其體不踰方寸能充
則四海有頼不充則一身莫保所謂其端甚微
其効甚大差之毫釐謬以千里其機正在於此
况人主之心又與人殊有聲色貨利之慾則易
以淫有崇高富貴之勢則易以驕有讒諂面諛
===
之徒則易以誘有神仙怪誕之說則易以惑波
蕩紛華震撼撞擊者固不止此而四者其甚也
一或省察不周持守不力偶投抵間隙而入焉
則心為之病而萬不能救矣又何以言治然則
人主之心其所當謹也不章章乎哉夫心之所
係雖云至重而功用之推廣其大者不過有六
曰修身曰敬天曰法祖曰愛民曰體臣曰講學
心純則六者皆得其極不純則六者皆失其理
臣觀
陛下燕居有服動止有法所以修身者嚴矣

punctuated:
陛下察其衷，矜其愚，不錄其罪，俾臣得畢其說，斯臣之命也。臣嘗聞宋儒蔡沉有言曰：「帝王之治本於道，帝王之道本於心。」及稽諸經史，凡堯舜禹湯文武之盛，所以卓乎不可及，而漢唐宋之治所以不古若者，皆此心之純駁以為之差。乃知人之一心，其量不盈一掬，其體不踰方寸，能充則四海有頼，不充則一身莫保。所謂其端甚微，其効甚大，差之毫釐，謬以千里，其機正在於此。况人主之心又與人殊，有聲色貨利之慾則易以淫，有崇高富貴之勢則易以驕，有讒諂面諛之徒則易以誘，有神仙怪誕之說則易以惑。波蕩紛華，震撼撞擊者，固不止此，而四者其甚也。一或省察不周，持守不力，偶投抵間隙而入焉，則心為之病，而萬不能救矣，又何以言治？然則人主之心，其所當謹也，不章章乎哉？夫心之所係雖云至重，而功用之推廣，其大者不過有六：曰修身，曰敬天，曰法祖，曰愛民，曰體臣，曰講學。心純則六者皆得其極，不純則六者皆失其理。
臣觀陛下燕居有服，動止有法，所以修身者嚴矣。
translation_en:
…may Your Majesty discern my true intent, pity my foolishness, refrain from holding me guilty, and allow your servant to finish his explanation. This would be my good fortune. Your servant has heard that the Song Confucian scholar Cai Chen said: “The government of emperors and kings is rooted in the Way; the Way of emperors and kings is rooted in the heart.” Upon examining the classics and histories, I find that the splendid rule of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu was so outstanding as to be beyond reach, whereas the government of the Han, Tang, and Song fell short of antiquity, because of differences in the purity or admixture of this heart. Thus we know that the human heart, though its volume does not fill a cupped hand and its body does not exceed an inch square, can, if fully developed, provide support to all within the Four Seas; if left undeveloped, it cannot preserve even one's own person. As the saying goes, its beginnings are exceedingly slight, but its effects exceedingly great: a deviation of a hair's breadth leads to an error of a thousand li. The crucial point lies precisely here.
Moreover, the heart of a ruler differs from that of other men. Desires for music, sensual beauty, wealth, and profit readily lead it into excess; the power of lofty station, riches, and honor readily leads it into arrogance; slanderers, flatterers, and those who offer praise to his face readily entice it; and tales of immortals and fantastic marvels readily delude it. The dazzling attractions that unsettle, shake, and batter it are certainly not limited to these, but these four are the most serious. If scrutiny is ever incomplete or steadfastness insufficient, and these influences happen to find a gap and enter [?], the heart becomes diseased through them and utterly beyond rescue. How, then, can one speak of good government? Is it not abundantly clear that the ruler must guard his heart with care? Although what depends upon the heart is supremely weighty, the extension of its practical workings has no more than six principal aspects: cultivating oneself, revering Heaven, emulating one's ancestors, loving the people, showing consideration for one's ministers, and pursuing learning. If the heart is pure, all six attain their utmost perfection; if it is impure, all six lose their proper principles.
Your servant observes that Your Majesty follows prescribed dress even in private repose and observes rules in movement and stillness: your self-cultivation is indeed rigorous.

求才必廣所以體臣者備矣
經筵日御師保時接所以講學者勤矣其於六者
之功用可謂至精至密盡善盡美蔑以加矣然
豈襲取强為之哉又嘗觀其
敬一有箴五箴有註所以敦操存涵養之功懋精
一緝熙之學以正其心者足以為之根本故得
於深造之後流於既溢之餘所行所發無不追

烈祖凡臣之所欲言者皆先得之矣臣復何言臣獨

punctuated: 齋明享祀，自咎有說，所以敬天者至矣；事遵祖訓，動率典章，所以法祖者善矣；恤刑有旨，減租有詔，所以愛民者周矣；守令必重，求才必廣，所以體臣者備矣；經筵日御，師保時接，所以講學者勤矣。其於六者之功用，可謂至精至密，盡善盡美，蔑以加矣。然豈襲取强為之哉？又嘗觀其敬一有箴，五箴有註，所以敦操存涵養之功，懋精一緝熙之學，以正其心者，足以為之根本。故得於深造之後，流於既溢之餘，所行所發，無不追並先王，而昭配烈祖。凡臣之所欲言者，皆先得之矣，臣復何言？臣獨懼夫人之常情，飾外者多遺其内，有初者莫保其終。故汲黯於武帝有内多慾而外施仁義之言，魏徵於太宗亦以十漸不克終者為之諫。臣願陛下矜臣之愚，采臣之言，益加謹勉。凡物之感於前者，必察何者為天理，何者為人慾。如仲尼所謂「非禮勿視，非禮勿聽，非禮勿言，非禮勿動」，不使其淫吾心。凡勢之有於已者，必思若何為德之
translation_en:
…You purify yourself with reverent clarity for sacrificial offerings and have issued statements reproaching yourself: thus your reverence for Heaven is utmost. In affairs you follow the Ancestral Instructions, and in every action observe the established statutes: thus your emulation of the ancestors is excellent. You have issued directives calling for compassion in punishments and edicts reducing taxes: thus your love for the people is comprehensive. You invariably give weight to the appointment of prefects and magistrates and seek talent widely: thus your consideration for your ministers is complete. You attend the Classics Colloquium daily and regularly receive your preceptors and guardians: thus your diligence in learning is unremitting. The practical achievements of these six endeavors may be called supremely refined and thorough, perfect in goodness and beauty, with nothing further to add. Yet could these have been achieved through mere imitation and forced effort?

I have also observed that you have composed an Admonition on Reverent Unity and annotated the Five Admonitions. By these means you strengthen the work of preserving and nurturing the mind and advance the learning of refinement, single-mindedness, and continuing illumination. This rectification of the mind provides a sufficient foundation for all these endeavors. Thus, what you have attained through profound study flows forth from its abundance. Every action and expression matches the former kings and gloriously accords with your illustrious ancestors. Everything your servant wishes to say you have already grasped. What more can your servant say?

My sole fear concerns ordinary human tendencies: those who embellish the exterior often neglect the interior, and those who make a beginning cannot be certain of sustaining it to the end. Thus Ji An told Emperor Wu that inwardly he had many desires while outwardly he practiced benevolence and righteousness. Wei Zheng likewise remonstrated with Emperor Taizong concerning ten gradual failings that prevented him from sustaining his efforts to the end. I ask Your Majesty to have compassion for your servant’s foolishness, accept his words, and exercise still greater care and diligence. Whenever something before you stirs a response, you must examine what accords with Heaven’s principle and what constitutes human desire. As Zhongni said, “Look at nothing contrary to ritual propriety; listen to nothing contrary to ritual propriety; say nothing contrary to ritual propriety; do nothing contrary to ritual propriety.” Do not let such things corrupt your mind. Whenever you consider the power you possess, you must reflect on how it may serve virtue …

其若何為惡之大如仲尼所謂聰明睿智守之
以愚功盖天下守之以謙富有四海守之以讓
不使其驕吾心凡言之陳於下者必審如某言

於前者必辨從之有何益違之有何損如仲尼

translation_en:
…[?], and how it may become a great evil. As Zhongni said: “Though intelligent and wise, preserve these qualities through simplicity; though your achievements surpass all under Heaven, preserve them through humility; though you possess the wealth of the Four Seas, preserve it through deference.” Do not allow these advantages to make your heart arrogant. Whenever statements are presented from below, examine them carefully: which words constitute flattery, and which constitute loyalty? As Zhongni said: “Now, in dealing with people, I listen to their words and observe their conduct.” Do not let their words beguile your heart. Whenever methods are presented before you, distinguish them carefully: what benefit would following them bring, and what harm would rejecting them cause? As Zhongni said: “Applying oneself to heterodox teachings is harmful indeed.” Do not let them confuse your heart.

Be circumspect in outward conduct and also order your inner life; be diligent at the beginning and never slacken at the end. Then perhaps your government will not rest content with small accomplishments, nor your achievements be confined by attachment to immediate gains. The flourishing revival of the Way of Zhou and the blessed peace of the state of Yin may once again be witnessed. How, then, could celestial anomalies remain unabated, the people's hearts remain disunited, and appointments to office remain improper, [to the detriment of the kingly Way?], troubling Your Majesty's profound deliberations? The crucial initiative assuredly begins with rectifying the heart. Zhongni also said: “Occupy your position without weariness, and carry out your duties with devotion.” Without weariness, one remains the same from beginning to end; with devotion, one's inner and outer selves are as one.

What your servant pursues is Zhongni's learning; what Your Majesty employs is Zhongni's Way. Thus, earnestly and repeatedly, I offer Zhongni's words. Should you graciously adopt them, it would be a blessing for all under Heaven through myriad generations, and good fortune for your foolish servant. Your servant is a man from the countryside, ignorant of taboos, who has presumptuously offended Your Majesty's awe-inspiring presence. I am overcome with trembling fear and utter trepidation. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

御批條論精詳殆盡
臣唐順之
臣對臣聞保民所以格天也正百官所以保民
也振紀綱所以正百官也何則君者代天理物
者也百官者行君之令而致之民以共亮天工
者也百官弗正則下有倒懸之危而莫為之恤
上有子惠之仁而莫為之施而欲民之安也不
可得矣紀綱弗振則憸邪者或以矯飾取容循
良者或以朴魯見黜任者不必賢賢者不必任
===
而欲百官之正也不可得矣故曰君得臣而萬
化行言安民在乎能官人也曰正朝廷以正百
官言官人在乎振紀綱也立法以任人任人以
安民則人心和而天地之和亦應矣于此見上
下交修之責焉見天人合一之理焉蓋自古帝
王敬天勤民以致天下之治者其要端在乎此
而不可易也我
皇帝陛下上畏
天變下究民隱
臨軒一詔于知人安民二者拳拳焉臣知

御批：條論精詳殆盡。
臣唐順之。
臣對：臣聞保民所以格天也，正百官所以保民也，振紀綱所以正百官也。何則？君者，代天理物者也；百官者，行君之令而致之民，以共亮天工者也。百官弗正，則下有倒懸之危而莫為之恤，上有子惠之仁而莫為之施，而欲民之安也，不可得矣。紀綱弗振，則憸邪者或以矯飾取容，循良者或以朴魯見黜，任者不必賢，賢者不必任，而欲百官之正也，不可得矣。故曰：「君得臣而萬化行。」言安民在乎能官人也。曰：「正朝廷以正百官。」言官人在乎振紀綱也。立法以任人，任人以安民，則人心和而天地之和亦應矣。于此見上下交修之責焉，見天人合一之理焉。蓋自古帝王敬天勤民，以致天下之治者，其要端在乎此，而不可易也。我皇帝陛下，上畏天變，下究民隱，臨軒一詔，于知人安民二者拳拳焉。臣知
translation_en:
Imperial comment: The discussion is precise and detailed, nearly exhaustive.
Your servant, Tang Shunzhi.
Your servant replies: I have heard that protecting the people is the means of moving Heaven; setting the officials right is the means of protecting the people; and invigorating the governing order is the means of setting the officials right. Why is this so? The ruler orders all things on Heaven’s behalf. The officials carry out the ruler’s commands and convey them to the people, together assisting in Heaven’s work. If the officials are not upright, those below suffer distress as dire as being hung upside down, yet no one relieves them; the ruler above possesses the benevolence of one who cherishes his children, yet no one puts it into effect. Under these circumstances, peace for the people cannot be attained. If the governing order is not invigorated, the crafty and wicked may win favor through dissimulation, while the dutiful and good may be dismissed for their plainness and lack of polish. Those appointed are not necessarily worthy, and the worthy are not necessarily appointed. Under these circumstances, uprightness among the officials cannot be attained.
Thus it is said, “When the ruler obtains the right ministers, all transformations take effect.” This means that bringing peace to the people depends on the ability to appoint men to office. It is also said, “Set the court right in order to set all the officials right.” This means that appointing men to office depends on invigorating the governing order. Establish laws for appointing men, and appoint men to bring peace to the people: then the people’s hearts will be harmonious, and the harmony of Heaven and Earth will respond in turn. Here we see the responsibility of those above and below to cultivate themselves together, and the principle that Heaven and humanity form a unity. From antiquity, emperors and kings who revered Heaven and labored for the people, thereby bringing order to the realm, have found the essential means in this; it cannot be changed.
Your Majesty, our Emperor, stands in awe of Heaven’s portents above and investigates the people’s hidden sufferings below. Presiding at the palace, you have issued an edict expressing earnest concern for these two matters: discerning men’s worth and bringing peace to the people. Your servant knows …

translation_en:
…this concern of Your Majesty’s is the very concern that moved Tang of Yin to reproach himself at Sanglin, and that moved Emperor Gao to sit exposed to the sky upon a mat of straw when no rain fell in midsummer. Though your servant is exceedingly ignorant, even while living in obscurity I have long felt deeply concerned about the worthiness or unworthiness of officials and the sources of benefit and harm to the people’s livelihood. Now that Your Majesty so earnestly seeks advice, how could I dare not reply with all my heart? I have respectfully examined the Great Plan and sought confirmation in the Spring and Autumn Annals. In general, when government is good and the people secure, auspicious signs arise; when government is neglected and the people distressed, disasters and baleful influences appear. Heaven’s sending of calamities or blessings depends upon virtue; the unfailing correspondence of good and ill fortune depends upon human conduct. Your Majesty reverently maintains unity of purpose in serving Heaven with manifest devotion, and establishes the supreme standard through equilibrium and harmony. Auspicious signs should therefore arrive, and the six baleful influences disappear. Yet there are things that cannot be fathomed by ordinary reasoning. Although Heaven’s benevolent intention is to support Your Majesty’s anxious labors from before dawn until late in the day and to bring the governance of the Jiajing reign to greater heights, might there also be peril, suffering, and destitution among the people that disturb and injure the harmonious vital forces?
Your Majesty remits taxes to enrich the people, distributes relief and makes loans to meet their urgent needs, and exercises compassion in punishment to preserve their lives. This is the utmost benevolence under Heaven: your provisions for securing the people’s welfare are consummate. You draw close to the worthy and dismiss the wicked, distinguishing whom to employ and whom to reject, and implement the policy of long tenure in office to obtain effective government. This is the utmost discernment under Heaven: your provisions for appointing officials are consummate. Yet the people may not all be secure, and offices may not all be filled by suitable men. Might there still be instances in which the worthy and unworthy are placed in reversed positions, appointments are inappropriate, and encouragement and punishment have yet to produce evident effects, just as Your Majesty’s policy question apprehends? Revitalizing the governing principles and disciplinary order, so as to set all officials right and bring security to all the people, surely admits of no delay. text:
虞廷發之皐陶之告舜曰在知人在安民禹曰
知人則哲能官人安民則惠黎民懷之分之以
三德六德皆以廣知人之旨也詳之以惇典庸

行而天下蒙其福官匪其人則橫政行而天下
受其害約而言之非二致也哲也者成其惠者
也知人非哲弗能知人而至於能官人則非紀
綱之振亦弗能也紀綱也者濟其哲者也雖哲

虞廷發之。皐陶之告舜曰：「在知人，在安民。」禹曰：「知人則哲，能官人；安民則惠，黎民懷之。」分之以三德六德，皆以廣知人之旨也；詳之以惇典庸禮，皆以廣安民之旨也。要之，官得其人，則善政行而天下蒙其福；官匪其人，則橫政行而天下受其害。約而言之，非二致也。哲也者，成其惠者也。知人非哲弗能；知人而至於能官人，則非紀綱之振亦弗能也。紀綱也者，濟其哲者也。雖哲如堯舜，而三載考績，三考黜陟幽明。內則九官十六相，以為岳牧之倡；外則四岳十二牧，以任總領之責。規為精密，斯哲有所寄，而其為哲也大矣。哲大而惠斯大矣。「仁急親賢，知急先務」，此之謂也。勳格上下，治底平□成，由此其致也。是故陛下欲弭災沴，則莫若安民矣；欲安民，則莫若正百官矣；欲正百官，則莫若振紀綱矣。紀綱之所以振者，臣雖不能悉舉，請得以其槩言之。

In essence, when offices are filled by the right men, good government prevails and all under Heaven enjoy its blessings; when offices are filled by the wrong men, oppressive government prevails and all under Heaven suffer its harm. Put succinctly, these are not two separate ends. Discernment is what brings benevolence to fruition. …officials who have held office for more than half a year: investigate fully the facts of their competence or incompetence, integrity or corruption, and report them to the throne.” Your servant wishes Your Majesty to give luminous expression to this great instruction and carefully select regional inspectors, choosing them either through the collective recommendation of your ministers or through the independent discernment of your sagely judgment. Appoint only those whose commanding bearing is long established and whose integrity is firm and unyielding. Thereafter, those who truly suppress the corrupt and promote the upright, without fearing the powerful and overbearing, should receive appropriate commendations and rewards. Those who favor private interests and harbor wrongdoers, or conceal worthy men and fail to recommend them, should receive appropriate dismissal and censure. Use these investigations not only to establish whether officials are worthy, but also to grade the regional inspectors themselves. With regional inspectors in awe of the severity of the statutes, who would dare fail to devote every effort to carrying out imperial authority throughout their circuits? With officials assured of the impartiality of their regional inspectors, who would dare fail to devote their minds to caring for the people? When regional inspectors are worthy, prefects and magistrates will be worthy as well.
The second proposal is to purify the procedures for selecting officials, so as to make dismissal and promotion manifestly just. Your servant notes that during the Chenghua reign, Grand Secretary Qiu Jun argued: “Under the court’s regulations, every three years officials throughout the realm bring their registers to court. The Six Ministries and the Censorate examine their conduct of affairs and impeach those whose reports of completed business remain outstanding, thereby carrying out dismissals and promotions. Later, because appointments and transfers had accumulated in a backlog, means were devised to expedite them. These relied entirely on the evaluations of the Regional Inspectors, without further investigation of actual performance. Officials’ offenses were recorded and assigned such labels as ‘corrupt and tyrannical’ or ‘improper in conduct,’ in order to dismiss them. …“improper conduct,” one must specify exactly what constituted that improper conduct. Then men will be unable to embellish their reputations to claim merit, or to evade punishment through artful wording.
The third point is to make rewards and punishments dependable so as to stir men’s hearts. Your servant has heard that to have officials without rewards and punishments is to have no officials; to have rewards and punishments insufficient to spur all under Heaven to action is to have no rewards and punishments. Nowadays, men are promoted according to seniority and advanced for accumulated service. They will say, “My seniority and my service naturally entitle me to this.” Wealth, distinction, rank, and emoluments all seem to them things they have attained by their own efforts, and their desire to repay imperial favor grows weak. Corrupt officials drain away wealth and oppress the people harshly, always hoping that their wrongdoing will escape exposure. If, unfortunately, it is exposed, they are merely dismissed, and count themselves fortunate to escape execution and disgrace. Thus their disposition to gamble on escaping punishment grows, and they learn no salutary lesson. Your servant wishes Your Majesty to illuminate all things with the radiance of Li and decide independently with the firmness of Qian. Where administrative achievements are outstanding, even appointment to a position outside the normal sequence should not be regarded as an objectionable leap over grades. Where corruption is substantiated, even imposing a sentence under the Five Punishments should not be regarded as impairing imperial benevolence. Sometimes encouragement might be given through letters bearing the imperial seal, following Han precedents, to bring an official’s achievements to full fruition. Sometimes officials might be required to continue serving while bearing their guilt, as court officials were dealt with in the Great Pronouncements (Da Gao), so as to demand results from their subsequent service. Only by employing punishments and rewards beyond ordinary expectation to spur all under Heaven to action can this be accomplished.
The fourth point is to make commands dependable so as to extend tangible benefits. The Book of Documents says, “Be cautious in issuing commands; once issued, commands must be carried out.” The Book of Changes says, “He disperses his great proclamations as sweat pours forth.” Your servant humbly believes that Your Majesty has the admirable intention of caring for the people, but that the responsible officials have fallen short in carrying it out. Your Majesty has issued edicts calling for the remission of taxes, relief loans, and merciful treatment in penal matters. Yet the people suffer to the utmost from officials’ demands for payment, and those among the people who die of hunger or from penal punishment…

These four measures all serve to revitalize discipline and order and fully realize the proper way of appointing officials, thereby laying the foundation for bringing peace to the people.
As for eliminating bandits and repelling foreign peoples, these are certainly also urgent tasks for anyone seeking to bring peace to the people. Your servant believes that their essential requirement, too, is simply to obtain the right men. When common people become bandits, can this truly be their original intention? They are driven to it because they have no alternative, or fall into it through ignorance. Thus it is said: “That there are no bandits in prosperous times is due to sufficiency; that there are no bandits in well-governed times is due to moral transformation.” If Your Majesty obtains and appoints good officials like Gong Sui and Yu Xu, their authority and trustworthiness will command sufficient confidence to break the bandits’ spirit; their benevolence and kindness will reach far enough to win their hearts; and their well-directed encouragement and assistance will suffice to secure their livelihoods. Banditry will then cease of itself, without its suppression having to be specially sought.
When the Son of Heaven possesses the Way, his defenses lie among the foreign peoples of the four quarters. Today, the various foreign peoples exploit openings to launch sudden attacks, harass our frontiers, and slaughter our people. This is indeed cause for concern. Your servant maintains, however, that the true concern lies not with foreign peoples but with the lack of generals in our own Central Realm. Those now called generals are drawn from hereditary military families and from the military examinations. It is not impossible to find capable men through these channels. Yet those accustomed to silks and luxury may be unfamiliar with military strategy, while men whose talents lie in archery, horsemanship, and rote memorization may be unequal to the changing deployment of unconventional and regular forces. Your servant requests that Your Majesty put Su Xun’s proposal into practice and order each high minister to recommend men he knows who possess both courage and strategic ability and can…

備飭矣至於財充而食足此亦百官有司之事
耳百官得其人則經理有道儲畜有方而邦之
財可充斂散得宜補助以時而民之食可足要
不足以煩
陛下也以此言之紀綱克振百官之所以正者此也
民之所以安者此也

出入險阻者，然後督之以治兵，寄之以邊障，養其望，專其任，而良將可得矣。將良則士練，而邊備飭矣。至於財充而食足，此亦百官有司之事耳。百官得其人，則經理有道，儲畜有方，而邦之財可充；斂散得宜，補助以時，而民之食可足。要不足以煩陛下也。以此言之，紀綱克振，百官之所以正者此也，民之所以安者此也，天心之所助順而反災為祥者亦此也。
抑臣猶有獻焉。《中庸》曰：「為政在人，取人以身。」則人固立政之本，而身尤取人之本也。朱熹曰：「紀綱不能以自立，必人主之心公平正大，無偏黨反側之私，然後紀綱有所係而立。」則心者尤立紀綱之本也。臣伏讀陛下《敬一》之箴，則于堯舜禹湯文武之心法，而為知人安民之要機者，固自有在矣。惟陛下始終此心，弗以隱顯異其功，弗以久暫易其守，弗以宴安荒其志。必講學以涵養此心，必親近君子以維持此心。由是心純而賢才輔，已正而物自正，將不待於慶賞黜陟之及其身，而風聲
translation_en:
…those able to venture into and out of perilous terrain. Then charge them with training the troops, entrust them with frontier defenses, foster their prestige, and give them undivided responsibility: capable generals can thereby be obtained. With capable generals, the soldiers will be well trained and frontier preparations put in order. As for ample revenues and sufficient food, these too are simply the business of the officials and responsible agencies. If the right men fill the offices, administration will follow sound principles and reserves will be properly accumulated, so that the state's resources can be plentiful. Collections and disbursements will be appropriate, and assistance provided at the proper times, so that the people's food can be sufficient. These matters need not, after all, trouble Your Majesty. Viewed in this light, revitalizing the governing framework is what sets the officials right, brings peace to the people, and causes Heaven to favor righteous rule and turn calamity into auspicious fortune.
Yet your servant still has something to offer. The Doctrine of the Mean says: “The conduct of government depends on men; obtaining such men depends on one's own person.” Thus, although men are the foundation of establishing good government, one's own person is still more fundamentally the basis for obtaining them. Zhu Xi said: “The governing framework cannot establish itself. The ruler's mind must be impartial, fair, upright, and magnanimous, without the selfishness of partiality, factionalism, or duplicity; only then does the governing framework have something on which to rest and become established.” The mind, then, is the ultimate foundation for establishing the governing framework. Your servant has reverently read Your Majesty's Admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness. Within it are indeed the essential principles for discerning men and bringing peace to the people, drawn from the teachings concerning the mind transmitted by Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, and Kings Wen and Wu. May Your Majesty preserve this mind from beginning to end: do not vary your efforts according to whether you are unseen or in public; do not alter what you uphold according to whether the duration is long or short; and do not let ease and comfort dissipate your resolve. You must pursue learning to nurture this mind and draw close to gentlemen to sustain it. In this way, when your mind is pure, worthy and talented men will assist you; when your own person is upright [?], others will naturally become upright. There will then be no need to wait for rewards, dismissals, or promotions to reach the individuals themselves before the influence of your example…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
氣習之所加衆正遂彙征之願群邪沮窺覬之
心亦其勢之必至者矣故以之知人則其知如
神者也以之安民則其仁如天者也以之除盗
賊則如舜之玄德在上而寇賊奸宄者自消也
以之禦夷狄則所謂無怠無荒四夷来王明王
慎德四夷咸賓而禦戎之上策在乎此也即董
仲舒所謂正心以正朝廷正朝廷以正百官正
百官以正萬民遠近一于正而罔有邪氣干其
間者也即公孫弘所謂心和則氣和氣和則形
和而天地之和應者也即劉向所謂衆賢和於
===
朝萬物和於野而和氣致祥者也由是而三光
全寒暑時天地位萬物育天不愛其道地不愛
其寶諸福之物畢致而王道終矣則夫知人安
民以臻盛治又在
陛下此心轉移間耳臣不勝拳拳忠愛之至幸
陛下垂聽焉臣謹對

punctuated: 氣習之所加，衆正遂彙征之願，群邪沮窺覬之心，亦其勢之必至者矣。故以之知人，則其知如神者也；以之安民，則其仁如天者也；以之除盗賊，則如舜之玄德在上，而寇賊奸宄者自消也；以之禦夷狄，則所謂「無怠無荒，四夷来王」，「明王慎德，四夷咸賓」，而禦戎之上策在乎此也。即董仲舒所謂「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民，遠近一于正，而罔有邪氣干其間」者也。即公孫弘所謂「心和則氣和，氣和則形和，而天地之和應」者也。即劉向所謂「衆賢和於朝，萬物和於野，而和氣致祥」者也。由是而三光全，寒暑時，天地位，萬物育，天不愛其道，地不愛其寶，諸福之物畢致，而王道終矣。則夫知人安民以臻盛治，又在陛下此心轉移間耳。臣不勝拳拳忠愛之至，幸陛下垂聽焉。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…where the influence of prevailing dispositions and habits reaches, all upright men will fulfill their wish to advance together, while the wicked will be checked in their covetous ambitions. This, too, will necessarily follow. Thus, by this means, in discerning men, your wisdom will be like that of the spirits; in bringing peace to the people, your benevolence will be like Heaven’s. In eliminating robbers and bandits, you will resemble Shun, whose profound virtue prevailed above, so that marauders and wrongdoers within and without disappeared of themselves. In defending against foreign peoples, you will fulfill the sayings, “Be neither idle nor neglectful, and the peoples of the four quarters will come to acknowledge you as king,” and “When the enlightened king attends carefully to his virtue, the peoples of the four quarters all come as guests.” Herein lies the highest strategy for defense against foreign foes.

This is what Dong Zhongshu meant by saying, “Rectify your heart in order to rectify the court; rectify the court in order to rectify the hundred officials; rectify the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people. Near and far alike will be united in rectitude, with no deviant influence intruding among them.” It is what Gongsun Hong meant by saying, “When the heart is harmonious, the vital energy is harmonious; when the vital energy is harmonious, the bodily form is harmonious, and the harmony of Heaven and Earth responds.” It is what Liu Xiang meant by saying, “The assembled worthy men are harmonious at court, and all things are harmonious in the countryside; harmonious vital energy brings auspicious signs.”

Thereby the three luminaries—the sun, moon, and stars—will retain their full splendor; cold and heat will arrive in season; Heaven and Earth will occupy their proper places; and all things will flourish. Heaven will not withhold its Way, nor Earth its treasures. All things that bring blessings will arrive, and the kingly Way will reach fulfillment. Thus, discerning men and bringing peace to the people so as to attain flourishing government rests, once again, simply upon the direction Your Majesty gives to this heart. Your servant cannot contain his utmost earnest loyalty and devotion, and hopes that Your Majesty will graciously hear him. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
御批仁智之用本諸吾心此不易之說
臣陳束
臣對臣聞天下無不可致之治而其本在乎人
主有必欲治之心盖治天下之道不越乎知人
安民二者人主以一身臨于億兆之上弛張舉
措固惟吾意之所欲為以是而用天下之人以
安天下之民其於致治奚難焉而乃有未必然
者則其心之未定而所以為天下之計或過也
夫人不足適政不足間變故不足憂也欲捄天
===
下之弊莫若自力於其治欲求天下之治莫若
先决於其心夫惟有必欲治之心而所以存養
培植之者無時少懈則其本立而施之於治自
將有毅然不可遏之勢以之用人而真才得以
之安民而羣生遂而凡一切災沴凶荒盜賊夷
狄之變舉當今之可憂者可以坐理而無難矣
傳曰心既正然後天下之事可從而理此之謂
也恭惟
皇帝陛下具神聖之德應中興之期典則肇修倫制
兼盡可謂盛矣兹復

punctuated:
御批：「仁智之用，本諸吾心，此不易之說。」

臣陳束。

臣對：臣聞天下無不可致之治，而其本在乎人主有必欲治之心。盖治天下之道，不越乎知人、安民二者。人主以一身臨于億兆之上，弛張舉措，固惟吾意之所欲為。以是而用天下之人，以安天下之民，其於致治奚難焉？而乃有未必然者，則其心之未定，而所以為天下之計或過也。夫人不足適，政不足間，變故不足憂也。欲捄天下之弊，莫若自力於其治；欲求天下之治，莫若先决於其心。夫惟有必欲治之心，而所以存養培植之者無時少懈，則其本立，而施之於治，自將有毅然不可遏之勢。以之用人，而真才得；以之安民，而羣生遂。而凡一切災沴、凶荒、盜賊、夷狄之變，舉當今之可憂者，可以坐理而無難矣。傳曰：「心既正，然後天下之事可從而理。」此之謂也。恭惟皇帝陛下，具神聖之德，應中興之期，典則肇修，倫制兼盡，可謂盛矣。兹復
translation_en:
Imperial comment: “The exercise of benevolence and wisdom is rooted in one’s own heart. This is an unalterable principle.”

Your servant, Chen Shu.

Your servant replies: I have heard that there is no good order in the realm that cannot be achieved; its foundation lies in the ruler’s firm resolve to achieve it. The way to govern the realm encompasses just two things: discerning men’s abilities and bringing peace to the people. The ruler, in his single person, presides over the countless multitudes. Relaxing or tightening his rule, initiating measures or putting them into effect—all depend upon what he wills to do. If he thereby employs the men of the realm to bring peace to its people, what difficulty could there be in achieving good government? Yet when this does not necessarily follow, it is because his resolve is unsettled and his plans for the realm may be mistaken. Men are not worth reproaching [?], policies are not worth criticizing, and untoward events are not worth worrying over. To remedy the realm’s ills, nothing is better than exerting oneself in its governance; to seek good government for the realm, nothing is better than first resolving upon it in one’s heart. Only establish a firm resolve to govern well, and never slacken even slightly in preserving, nourishing, and cultivating it: then the foundation will stand firm. Applied to government, it will naturally acquire a resolute and irresistible momentum. Employ men through it, and true talent will be found; bring peace to the people through it, and all living beings will flourish. As for every calamity, baleful influence, famine, act of brigandage, and disturbance involving the Yi and Di peoples—all that gives cause for concern today—these can then be managed with ease and without difficulty. A transmitted teaching says: “Only after the heart has been rectified can the affairs of the realm accordingly be put in order.” This is what it means.

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor possesses sagely and divine virtue and has answered the destined occasion for a restoration. You have undertaken the renewal of established standards and fully attended to human relationships and institutions. This may indeed be called flourishing government. Now, once again…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
廷集多士
親發德音下明詔以天下治忽大計詢及草茅豈循
襲故事而姑為是舉耶盖
聖不自聖實欲以求天下之言也臣嘗讀史而至於
三代以還見其君有勵精之心而其臣或不能
副其所欲為故其事功卑陋而不足道或其臣
抱經世之畧而所遇者又不足與有為則亦徒
焉已耳而臣之庸愚乃得與
清問之末不可謂無所遇矣復何所諱而不言乎
臣聞天生民而樹之君以為民也君為民而設
===
官以奉天也官不得其人則天工隳是故知人
之為貴也民不得其所則君道缺是故安民之
為急也然欲安民必先知人盖一日萬幾在君
身有不勝其煩者使非得人以分理則雖有為
民之念憂且勞于上而民不被其澤矣是知人
又所以安民也古之稱絶德者曰臯陶以謨而
其陳謨也不過曰知人安民二者而已則夫人
君治天下之道豈復有加於此哉然人未易知
也訐者似直佞者似忠詐者似信厚貌深情自
非至明或莫之辨而民生有欲饑者欲食寒者

punctuated:
廷集多士，親發德音，下明詔，以天下治忽大計詢及草茅，豈循襲故事而姑為是舉耶？盖聖不自聖，實欲以求天下之言也。臣嘗讀史，而至於三代以還，見其君有勵精之心，而其臣或不能副其所欲為，故其事功卑陋而不足道；或其臣抱經世之畧，而所遇者又不足與有為，則亦徒焉已耳。而臣之庸愚，乃得與清問之末，不可謂無所遇矣，復何所諱而不言乎？
臣聞天生民而樹之君，以為民也；君為民而設官，以奉天也。官不得其人，則天工隳，是故知人之為貴也；民不得其所，則君道缺，是故安民之為急也。然欲安民，必先知人。盖一日萬幾，在君身有不勝其煩者，使非得人以分理，則雖有為民之念，憂且勞于上，而民不被其澤矣。是知人又所以安民也。古之稱絶德者，曰臯陶以謨，而其陳謨也，不過曰知人、安民二者而已，則夫人君治天下之道，豈復有加於此哉？然人未易知也，訐者似直，佞者似忠，詐者似信，厚貌深情，自非至明，或莫之辨。而民生有欲，饑者欲食，寒者
translation_en:
…have assembled the many scholars at court, personally proclaimed your gracious words, and issued an illustrious edict consulting even men of humble station about the great questions of order and disorder in the realm. Could this undertaking merely follow established precedent for form’s sake? Surely the sage does not presume upon his own sagacity, but truly wishes to seek the views of all under Heaven. When reading histories of the Three Dynasties and subsequent times, your servant has seen rulers determined to devote themselves to government whose ministers sometimes could not support what they wished to accomplish; consequently, their achievements were meager and unworthy of mention. Sometimes ministers possessed plans for ordering the world, yet the rulers they encountered were inadequate partners for accomplishing anything, and their efforts remained fruitless. Yet I, your mediocre and foolish servant, have been allowed a place among the last to receive your august inquiry. I cannot say that I have failed to encounter an opportunity. What, then, should I be reluctant to speak of?
Your servant has heard that Heaven brought forth the people and established a ruler over them for their sake; the ruler establishes offices for the people’s sake in order to serve Heaven. If offices are not filled by the right men, Heaven’s work falls into ruin: hence the importance of discerning men. If the people do not find their proper place, the ruler’s way is deficient: hence the urgency of bringing peace to the people. Yet to bring peace to the people, one must first discern men. The myriad affairs of a single day impose burdens that the ruler cannot bear alone. Unless he finds suitable men to share their administration, then, though he intends to serve the people and worries and labors above, the people will not receive his beneficence. Thus discerning men is also the means of bringing peace to the people. Among those of antiquity praised for surpassing virtue, Gao Yao was distinguished for his counsels. Yet the counsels he presented amounted to no more than these two things: discerning men and bringing peace to the people. Could there be anything to add to these as the ruler’s way of governing the realm? Men, however, are not easy to discern. Those who expose others’ faults appear upright; flatterers appear loyal; deceivers appear trustworthy. Behind an honest exterior lie deeply concealed intentions. Without the utmost discernment, one may be unable to distinguish them. And the people are born with desires: the hungry desire food, and those who are cold…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
欲衣閭閻之下愁苦萬狀雖廣濟博施亦安能
使人人各得其所哉故曰知人則哲安民則惠
惟帝其難之夫帝堯且以為難况其下者乎臣
甞考之于書其在唐虞有若羲和以明曆象有
若大禹以平水土有若稷契以播百穀以敷五
教有若臯陶以明刑有若夷夔以典禮樂有若
垂益以若虞工其得人之盛如此當是之時百
姓昭明萬邦協和以至光被四表格于上下其
治化之隆又如此然且君臣相戒以為難蓋於
此而後見聖人兢兢業業憂勤惕勵之心也夫
===
知其難則於用人行政之間自有不容不慎者
觀其命官也疇咨于衆必僉曰可而後俞則其
難且慎之心可見而孔子論安百姓亦曰其猶
病諸於戲此堯舜之聖所以不可及也逮至三
代亦莫不然是故有禹之孜孜則任人有如伯
益而聲教四訖有湯之慄慄則任人有如伊尹
而邦家輯寧有文王之不已武王之無貳則任
人有如周召之徒而萬邦作孚四海永清然則
帝王致治之道亦槩可見矣漢唐而下固不足
論其間英君誼辟亦不能外斯二者以為治但
