punctuated:
欲衣，閭閻之下，愁苦萬狀，雖廣濟博施，亦安能使人人各得其所哉？故曰：「知人則哲，安民則惠，惟帝其難之。」夫帝堯且以為難，况其下者乎？臣甞考之于《書》，其在唐虞，有若羲和以明曆象，有若大禹以平水土，有若稷契以播百穀、以敷五教，有若臯陶以明刑，有若夷夔以典禮樂，有若垂益以若虞工，其得人之盛如此。當是之時，百姓昭明，萬邦協和，以至光被四表，格于上下，其治化之隆又如此。然且君臣相戒以為難，蓋於此而後見聖人兢兢業業、憂勤惕勵之心也。夫知其難，則於用人行政之間，自有不容不慎者。觀其命官也，疇咨于衆，必僉曰可而後俞，則其難且慎之心可見。而孔子論安百姓，亦曰：「其猶病諸！」於戲！此堯舜之聖所以不可及也。

逮至三代，亦莫不然。是故有禹之孜孜，則任人有如伯益，而聲教四訖；有湯之慄慄，則任人有如伊尹，而邦家輯寧；有文王之不已、武王之無貳，則任人有如周召之徒，而萬邦作孚，四海永清。然則帝王致治之道，亦槩可見矣。漢唐而下，固不足論，其間英君誼辟，亦不能外斯二者以為治，但
translation_en:
…want clothing. Among the common people, sorrow and hardship take countless forms. Even with widespread relief and generous beneficence, how could one ensure that everyone finds a secure place? Thus it is said: “To know men is wisdom; to bring peace to the people is benevolence. Even the emperor finds these difficult.” If Emperor Yao himself considered them difficult, how much more must those below him!

Your servant has examined the Book of Documents. In the age of Tang and Yu, there were Xi and He to clarify calendrical calculations and celestial phenomena; the Great Yu to bring the waters and lands into order; Ji and Xie to sow the hundred grains and spread the five teachings; Gao Yao to clarify punishments; Yi 夷 and Kui to preside over rites and music; and Chui and Yi 益 to put forestry and craftsmanship in order. Such was their abundance of worthy men. At that time, the people were enlightened and the myriad states lived in harmony; their radiance reached the four quarters and extended to heaven above and earth below. Such, too, was the flourishing of their governance and transforming influence. Yet ruler and ministers still admonished one another that these tasks were difficult. Here, then, we see the sages’ hearts: ever vigilant and conscientious, anxious and diligent, watchful and striving. Recognizing the difficulty, they necessarily exercised care in employing men and administering government. Consider how they appointed officials: they consulted the assembled multitude and approved an appointment only after all had declared the candidate suitable. Their sense of the difficulty and their caution are evident here. Confucius, too, when discussing bringing peace to the people, said: “Even they would have found it difficult!” Alas! This is why the sageliness of Yao and Shun cannot be equaled.

It was likewise throughout the Three Dynasties. With Yu’s unremitting diligence, men such as Bo Yi were employed, and his civilizing teachings reached the four extremities. With Tang’s trembling vigilance, men such as Yi Yin were employed, and the realm enjoyed harmony and peace. With King Wen’s ceaseless effort and King Wu’s undivided resolve, men such as the Dukes of Zhou and Shao were employed, and the myriad states placed their trust in them, while all within the Four Seas enjoyed enduring tranquility. From this, the way by which emperors and kings achieved good government can broadly be discerned. The Han and Tang and the ages thereafter scarcely merit discussion; yet even the outstanding rulers and righteous sovereigns among them could not govern apart from these two principles. Yet …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
其所存者非帝王之心故其所任者非帝王之
佐而其所以御民者率皆苟且疎畧之政無怪
乎治之不古若也仰惟
陛下誕膺曆數紹
一祖
七宗之業講學修政夙夜圖治者八年于茲臣工之
進退斷自
聖聰章奏之可否悉由
御覽邇者特重守令條格激勸之詔方拳拳焉
陛下之於人可謂知而任之矣蠲貸之恩數及起運
===
賑濟之令發及內帑邇者
祈雨一出都城父老孰不為叩首稱謝者
陛下之於民可謂惠而安之矣然而筭計見效猶未
有大慰于
淵衷者乃復舉此為問顧臣愚陋何能為
聖明助然於
聖制所及者敢不一一敬陳之伏讀
聖制有曰災變頻仍旱潦相繼歲復一歲無處無之
生民流亡朕甚恐懼斯言也臣有以見
陛下憂勤惕勵之心矣臣聞之天道遠人道邇又曰

punctuated:
其所存者非帝王之心，故其所任者非帝王之佐，而其所以御民者率皆苟且疎畧之政，無怪乎治之不古若也。
仰惟陛下誕膺曆數，紹一祖七宗之業，講學修政，夙夜圖治者八年于茲。臣工之進退，斷自聖聰；章奏之可否，悉由御覽。邇者特重守令，條格激勸之詔方拳拳焉。陛下之於人，可謂知而任之矣。蠲貸之恩，數及起運；賑濟之令，發及內帑。邇者祈雨一出，都城父老孰不為叩首稱謝者？陛下之於民，可謂惠而安之矣。然而筭計見效，猶未有大慰于淵衷者，乃復舉此為問。顧臣愚陋，何能為聖明助？然於聖制所及者，敢不一一敬陳之？
伏讀聖制有曰：「災變頻仍，旱潦相繼，歲復一歲，無處無之。生民流亡，朕甚恐懼。」斯言也，臣有以見陛下憂勤惕勵之心矣。臣聞之：「天道遠，人道邇。」又曰：
translation_en:
…what they harbored was not the heart of a true emperor or king; hence those whom they employed were not the worthy assistants of true emperors and kings. The policies by which they governed the people were generally expedient and ill-considered. No wonder their government fell short of that of antiquity.
I respectfully consider that Your Majesty has received Heaven’s allotted succession and inherited the enterprise of the founding emperor and the seven ancestral emperors. For eight years now, you have pursued learning and improved government, striving day and night for good rule. The advancement and dismissal of officials are decided by your sagely discernment; approval or rejection of memorials rests entirely upon your imperial review. Recently, you have placed particular emphasis on prefects and district magistrates, showing earnest concern in your edict setting out regulations to spur and encourage them. In your dealings with officials, Your Majesty may indeed be said to recognize their abilities and employ them accordingly. Your gracious remissions and deferments have repeatedly extended to taxes destined for shipment to the capital; your orders for relief have even drawn upon the Inner Treasury. Recently, when you went out to pray for rain, was there any elder of the capital who did not knock his head to the ground in gratitude? In your dealings with the people, Your Majesty may indeed be said to show them kindness and bring them peace. Yet, reckoning the results achieved, you still find nothing that greatly consoles your profound heart, and so you have again raised these matters as questions. But how can your ignorant and unlearned servant assist your sagely wisdom? Nevertheless, dare I fail to set forth respectfully, one by one, my views on the matters addressed in your imperial pronouncement?
I have reverently read these words in your imperial pronouncement: “Calamities and portentous disturbances recur frequently; droughts and floods follow one another, year after year, with no place spared. The people wander, displaced from their homes. I am deeply fearful.” In these words, your servant sees Your Majesty’s anxious diligence and vigilant resolve. Your servant has heard it said: “The Way of Heaven is distant; the way of humankind is near.” It is also said: …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
應天以實不以文蓋變不虛示而人事之應未
可以一二求也春秋書災變而不書事應漢儒
鄙陋不達聖人之微意而區區指事以明變君
子以為附會今日災變之多謂之適然未可也
而因以求之於微末則又未可臣願
陛下存克謹天戒之心盡應天以實之道赫然震惕
于上而因之以號令天下孰敢不貞白其心以
承
休德者則今日之變固扶持而全安之具也桑穀
雉雊之變豈足以害商宗之治哉伏讀
===
聖制有曰官非人以虐民歟或賢不肖進退倒置歟
或勸懲之典而失其宜歟抑為我選任者而失公
平之道歟臣有以見
陛下因天之變而求所以知人之道也夫任官非人
賢不肖倒置亦於勸懲之道選任之法未加之
意焉耳昔者先王之官人也必使賢者居上不
肖者居下而後可以理安今或未必然矣夫賢
者之言必直不肖者之言必佞賢者之為謀必
忠不肖者之為計必譎
陛下曷為不以是察之因事考言而為之決擇則雖

punctuated:
「應天以實，不以文。」蓋變不虛示，而人事之應未可以一二求也。《春秋》書災變而不書事應，漢儒鄙陋，不達聖人之微意，而區區指事以明變，君子以為附會。今日災變之多，謂之適然，未可也；而因以求之於微末，則又未可。臣願陛下存克謹天戒之心，盡應天以實之道，赫然震惕于上，而因之以號令天下，孰敢不貞白其心以承休德者？則今日之變，固扶持而全安之具也。桑穀、雉雊之變，豈足以害商宗之治哉？
伏讀聖制有曰：「官非人以虐民歟？或賢不肖進退倒置歟？或勸懲之典而失其宜歟？抑為我選任者而失公平之道歟？」臣有以見陛下因天之變而求所以知人之道也。夫任官非人，賢不肖倒置，亦於勸懲之道、選任之法未加之意焉耳。昔者先王之官人也，必使賢者居上，不肖者居下，而後可以理安。今或未必然矣。夫賢者之言必直，不肖者之言必佞；賢者之為謀必忠，不肖者之為計必譎。陛下曷為不以是察之？因事考言而為之決擇，則雖
translation_en:
…“Respond to Heaven with substance, not with outward forms.” Anomalies are not manifested without cause, yet their correspondences in human affairs cannot be sought in merely one or two particulars. The Spring and Autumn Annals records calamities and anomalies without recording the human events corresponding to them. The Han scholars, narrow and ill-informed, failed to grasp the Sage’s subtle intent. They insisted on identifying particular events to explain anomalies, which gentlemen regarded as forced connections. To call today’s numerous calamities and anomalies mere coincidence would be wrong; yet to seek their causes in trivial details would likewise be wrong. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty maintain a heart scrupulously attentive to Heaven’s warnings and fully follow the way of responding to Heaven with substance. If, from your exalted position, you show profound alarm and vigilance and accordingly issue commands throughout the realm, who would dare fail to make his heart upright and pure in support of your excellent virtue? Today’s anomalies would then indeed become means of sustaining and preserving the realm in peace. How could such anomalies as the mulberry and paper-mulberry trees, or the crowing pheasant, have impaired the rule of the revered Shang kings?
I have reverently read these words in Your Majesty’s decree: “Are unsuitable men holding office and oppressing the people? Or have the worthy and unworthy been promoted and dismissed in reverse order? Or have the established measures of encouragement and punishment been improperly applied? Or have those who select and appoint officials for me departed from fairness and impartiality?” Here your servant sees that Your Majesty, responding to Heaven’s anomalies, seeks the means of discerning men’s character. Appointing unsuitable officials and reversing the positions of the worthy and unworthy arise simply from insufficient attention to the principles of encouragement and punishment and the methods of selection and appointment. In former times, when the ancient kings appointed men to office, they invariably placed the worthy above and the unworthy below; only then could order and peace be achieved. Today this may not always be so. The worthy invariably speak frankly; the unworthy invariably flatter. The worthy invariably offer loyal counsel; the unworthy invariably devise deceitful schemes. Why does Your Majesty not assess them by these criteria? If you examine their words against their deeds and make your selections accordingly, then even if…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
有不肖亦豈得以遂其情哉先王之馭羣臣也
既有爵以馭其貴有祿以馭其富而又有刑罰
以馭其威是故勸懲之道立而人知所趨避矣
今之肆然于民上者惟無所畏故也彼無所畏
于名義獨無所畏于刑罰乎誠使廉者必進貪
者必黜慈良者必賞殘虐者必罪則孰敢不自
斂戢以干
陛下之法哉今考課之法雖嚴而黜陟之人未必皆
當銓選之法既拘而授任之際又或弗公故賢
者以之自怠而不肖者得以苟容民怨蓄于下
===
而天變動于上者此也伏讀
聖制有曰內有盜賊之擾外有夷狄之變山亦所以
為民之患者民為邦本而使饑寒困苦流離死亡
至於如此邦欲安而得乎朕欲俾災沴潛消民生

translation_en:
…even if there are unworthy men, how could they succeed in indulging their inclinations? In governing their ministers, the former kings used ranks to regulate their standing, stipends to regulate their wealth, and punishments to keep them in awe. Thus the principles of encouragement and punishment were established, and men knew what to pursue and what to avoid. Those who now act without restraint over the people do so only because they have nothing to fear. Though they have no regard for reputation and moral duty, can they also have no fear of punishment? If the incorruptible were invariably promoted, the greedy invariably dismissed, the kind and good invariably rewarded, and the cruel invariably punished, who would dare fail to restrain himself and transgress Your Majesty’s laws? Today, although the rules for evaluating officials are strict, the decisions about whom to dismiss or promote are not necessarily all appropriate. The rules for selecting officials are restrictive, yet appointments are sometimes unfair. Consequently, worthy men grow lax, while unworthy men manage to retain their positions. This is why popular resentment accumulates below and Heaven manifests anomalies above.
I have reverently read these words in the imperial decree: “Within there are disturbances caused by bandits; beyond there are troubles caused by the alien peoples. Mountains, too, are a source of affliction for the people [?]. The people are the foundation of the state; yet they have been allowed to suffer hunger, cold, hardship, displacement, and death to such an extent. Can the state hope to enjoy peace? I wish to cause calamities and baleful influences to dissipate unseen, the people to live securely, banditry to cease, the frontiers to be peaceful, and wealth and food to be abundant. How can this be achieved?” From this, your servant perceives that Your Majesty, prompted by Heaven’s anomalies, seeks the way to bring peace to the people. Yet if one wishes the people to be at peace, why must one seek elsewhere? It depends only on the character of those employed in office. At present, the trouble within the realm lies in banditry, and responsibility for banditry rests with the prefects and district magistrates. Prefects and district magistrates are the fathers and mothers of the people. title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
催科為撫字以趨承為職業以敲朴為教化使
疆域之民死亡流離而莫之救惡在其為民父
母也聞之遠方貪吏有破民之產咨嗟怨泣無
可控訴者夫民無禮義之心而有饑寒之苦其
去為盜固易也而上又驅迫之如此此盜賊之
所由繁而刑罰之所以不勝也今之議者亦既
欲重守令矣然而弗擇其人固無益也使皆得
如龔遂之儔布之郡縣則盜賊可不治而息矣
至於夷狄之警亦盛世之所不能無者而其要
則在於選將帥大抵夷狄之性貪而無親輕而
===
寡信王者以不治治之而已不治也者恃吾有
以備之也今者邊陲之備可謂虚矣以器械則
不良以儲蓄則不豫以士馬則不練旌鼓之節
不相服習而欲以之禦敵不已難乎聞之邊人
虜騎一入我軍無不驚潰散走者此由統制之
失人而翫愒縱弛之所致也昔者李牧在邊虜
不敢犯今誠得若人而任之則小小之警豈至
煩
當宁之憂哉至於財之不充食之不足則臣於
今日有所深惜蓋天下之財不在官則在民耗於

催科為撫字，以趨承為職業，以敲朴為教化，使疆域之民死亡流離而莫之救，惡在其為民父母也？聞之遠方，貪吏有破民之產，咨嗟怨泣，無可控訴者。夫民無禮義之心，而有饑寒之苦，其去為盜固易也，而上又驅迫之如此，此盜賊之所由繁，而刑罰之所以不勝也。今之議者亦既欲重守令矣，然而弗擇其人，固無益也。使皆得如龔遂之儔，布之郡縣，則盜賊可不治而息矣。
至於夷狄之警，亦盛世之所不能無者，而其要則在於選將帥。大抵夷狄之性，貪而無親，輕而寡信，王者以不治治之而已。不治也者，恃吾有以備之也。今者邊陲之備，可謂虚矣。以器械則不良，以儲蓄則不豫，以士馬則不練，旌鼓之節不相服習，而欲以之禦敵，不已難乎？聞之邊人，虜騎一入，我軍無不驚潰散走者。此由統制之失人，而翫愒縱弛之所致也。昔者李牧在邊，虜不敢犯。今誠得若人而任之，則小小之警，豈至煩當宁之憂哉？
至於財之不充、食之不足，則臣於今日有所深惜。蓋天下之財，不在官則在民，耗於
translation_en:
…taking tax collection for nurturing the people, taking deference to superiors for their official duties, and taking beatings with rods for moral instruction. They let the people within their jurisdictions die and scatter, with no one to rescue them. In what sense are they the people's fathers and mothers? I have heard that in distant regions corrupt officials ruin people's livelihoods, leaving them sighing, lamenting, and weeping in resentment, with nowhere to lodge a complaint. When people lack a sense of ritual propriety and righteousness and suffer hunger and cold, they can easily turn to banditry. Yet those above them drive and harry them in this way as well. This is why bandits multiply and punishments cannot keep pace. Those who discuss affairs today already wish to give greater weight to prefects and magistrates. Yet this is certainly useless unless suitable men are chosen. If men like Gong Sui could be found and stationed throughout the prefectures and counties, banditry could subside without punitive action.
As for alarms caused by the foreign peoples, even a flourishing age cannot be entirely free of them. The essential matter is to select generals and commanders. By and large, these peoples are greedy and recognize no bonds of affection, frivolous and seldom trustworthy. A true king governs them simply by leaving them ungoverned. Leaving them ungoverned means relying on our own means of defense against them. Today, our frontier defenses may well be called hollow. Weapons and equipment are poor; stores have not been laid up in advance; soldiers and horses are untrained. The troops are not practiced in responding together to the signals of banners and drums. Is it not exceedingly difficult to expect them to repel an enemy? I have heard from frontier inhabitants that whenever enemy cavalry enters, our troops invariably panic, break ranks, scatter, and flee. This results from appointing unsuitable commanders and from their idle neglect and lax discipline. In former times, when Li Mu was on the frontier, the enemy dared not invade. If such a man could truly be found and entrusted with command today, how could minor alarms trouble Your Majesty with anxiety?
As for inadequate funds and insufficient food, your servant finds much to deplore deeply in present circumstances. The wealth of the realm is held either by the government or by the people; when it is depleted among …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
下必詘於上今之財力可謂大詘矣額外之官
寢以加多而養官之費冗尺伍之籍漫無所稽
而養兵之費冗此猶可言也豪右貴戚之家勾
蓄游惰之徒不為
朝廷分尺寸之憂而坐食於公者莫之勝計此胡
為也夫田不加闢而賦日廣賦入有限而費出
無經則財與食安得而不匱乎欲財之充必自
其耗財者始欲食之足必自冗食者始
陛下既躬節儉以先天下而又汰冗濫之籍嚴侈靡
之禁塞其流以厚其源則國計其有瘳乎然此
===
亦皆隨事補葺之論也昔人有言以朞月之事
問臣臣以朞月之事對以三年之事問臣臣以
三年之事對臣以為此特不遇聖明之君而然
耳使遇聖明之君則必有拔本塞源之論而豈
為是遷就之說哉今臣之所陳不敢為三年朞
月之說而始終以為
聖明獻者惟曰在
陛下之一心而已蓋天下之事苟其志之所必為未
有為而不成者故曰誠心而王則王矣又曰君
志定而天下之治成彼堯舜之治豈誠不可及

punctuated:
下，必詘於上。今之財力，可謂大詘矣。額外之官，寢以加多，而養官之費冗；尺伍之籍，漫無所稽，而養兵之費冗。此猶可言也。豪右貴戚之家，勾蓄游惰之徒，不為朝廷分尺寸之憂，而坐食於公者，莫之勝計。此胡為也？夫田不加闢，而賦日廣；賦入有限，而費出無經，則財與食安得而不匱乎？欲財之充，必自其耗財者始；欲食之足，必自冗食者始。陛下既躬節儉以先天下，而又汰冗濫之籍，嚴侈靡之禁，塞其流以厚其源，則國計其有瘳乎？
然此亦皆隨事補葺之論也。昔人有言：「以朞月之事問臣，臣以朞月之事對；以三年之事問臣，臣以三年之事對。」臣以為，此特不遇聖明之君而然耳。使遇聖明之君，則必有拔本塞源之論，而豈為是遷就之說哉？今臣之所陳，不敢為三年朞月之說，而始終以為聖明獻者，惟曰在陛下之一心而已。蓋天下之事，苟其志之所必為，未有為而不成者。故曰：「誠心而王，則王矣。」又曰：「君志定，而天下之治成。」彼堯舜之治，豈誠不可及
translation_en:
…among those below, it must leave those above short of resources. Today's financial resources may indeed be called severely depleted. Officials appointed beyond the authorized complement gradually increase in number, making expenditure on their maintenance excessive; the registers of the military ranks [?] are left entirely unchecked, making expenditure on maintaining soldiers excessive. These matters can at least be spoken of. Yet powerful families and the households of imperial relatives gather and harbor idle men who do not shoulder the slightest share of the court's cares but live at public expense. Their numbers are beyond counting. Why should this be so? If no additional land is brought under cultivation while taxation grows daily, and revenue is limited while expenditure is unregulated, how can funds and provisions fail to run short? To replenish funds, one must begin with those who squander them; to secure adequate provisions, one must begin with superfluous mouths supported at public expense. Your Majesty already practices frugality in person as an example to the realm. If you also remove superfluous and improperly enrolled personnel from the registers, rigorously enforce prohibitions on extravagance, and stop the outflow to strengthen the source, might the state's finances recover?
Yet all these proposals merely patch things up as circumstances arise. A man of old said: “If you ask your servant about what can be done in a year, your servant answers about what can be done in a year; if you ask your servant about what can be done in three years, your servant answers about what can be done in three years.” Your servant believes that he spoke thus only because he had not encountered a sage and enlightened ruler. Had he encountered such a ruler, he would surely have offered proposals to uproot the causes and stop the sources of trouble. How could he have offered such accommodating advice? In what your servant now presents, I dare not frame my proposals in terms of three years or a single year. From beginning to end, what I offer to Your enlightened Majesty is simply this: everything rests in Your Majesty's own heart. In the affairs of the realm, when one's resolve is firmly set on accomplishing something, nothing undertaken fails to succeed. Thus it is said: “If, with a sincere heart, one practices true kingship, one will become a true king.” It is also said: “When the ruler's resolve is settled, the good government of the realm is achieved.” Could the government of Yao and Shun truly be beyond reach…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
哉無其心焉耳盖知人則哲哲者心之智也安
民則惠惠者心之仁也仁智也者心之全德也
使此心之德有所未純而意欲之私一有所錯
雜於其間則明有所蔽而所知者未必其所當
用恩有所壅而所及者未必其所當施本原之
地已蠹而弛張舉措之間皆將不得其當如此
而望天下之治猶却行而求前也伏願
陛下以憂勤惕勵之心持之于上智必如堯仁必如
堯二者之德既具則如鑑之空如衡之平是非
賢否之形可以坐照而莫吾亂如水之寒如火
===
之熱而不忍之心觸之而無不應矣何患乎人
之難知民之難安而天下之治不可成哉此切
要之說惟
陛下留神臣不勝隕越之至臣謹對

民則惠惠者心之仁也仁智也者心之全德也
使此心之德有所未純而意欲之私一有所錯
雜於其間則明有所蔽而所知者未必其所當
用恩有所壅而所及者未必其所當施本原之
地已蠧而弛張舉措之間皆將不得其當如此
而望天下之治猶却行而求前也伏願
陛下以憂勤惕勵之心持之于上智必如堯仁必如
堯二者之德既具則如鑑之空如衡之平是非
賢否之形可以坐照而莫吾亂如水之寒如火
之熱而不忍之心觸之而無不應矣何患乎人
之難知民之難安而天下之治不可成哉此切
要之說惟
陛下留神臣不勝隕越之至臣謹對
punctuated:
哉？無其心焉耳。盖知人則哲，哲者，心之智也；安民則惠，惠者，心之仁也。仁智也者，心之全德也。使此心之德有所未純，而意欲之私一有所錯雜於其間，則明有所蔽，而所知者未必其所當用；恩有所壅，而所及者未必其所當施。本原之地已蠹，而弛張舉措之間皆將不得其當。如此而望天下之治，猶却行而求前也。
伏願陛下以憂勤惕勵之心持之于上，智必如堯，仁必如堯。二者之德既具，則如鑑之空，如衡之平，是非賢否之形可以坐照而莫吾亂；如水之寒，如火之熱，而不忍之心觸之而無不應矣。何患乎人之難知、民之難安，而天下之治不可成哉？此切要之說，惟陛下留神。臣不勝隕越之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…indeed? It is only that one lacks the heart for it. For knowing men constitutes discernment, and discernment is the wisdom of the heart; bringing peace to the people constitutes beneficence, and beneficence is the benevolence of the heart. Benevolence and wisdom are the heart’s complete virtues. If the virtue of this heart is not wholly pure, and selfish intentions and desires become mingled within it, then understanding becomes obscured, and those whom one recognizes may not be those whom one ought to employ; gracious favor becomes obstructed, and those whom it reaches may not be those to whom it ought to be extended. Once the very foundation has been corrupted, all decisions about relaxing or tightening measures, and all actions, will fail to be appropriate. To hope for good government throughout the realm under such conditions is like walking backward while seeking to advance.
I humbly beseech Your Majesty to sustain this heart in your exalted position through concern, diligence, vigilance, and self-discipline. Your wisdom must equal Yao’s, and your benevolence must equal Yao’s. Once these two virtues are fully possessed, your heart will be like an unclouded mirror or a balanced scale: the distinctions between right and wrong, and between the worthy and unworthy, can be perceived without effort, with nothing to confuse you. Just as water is cold and fire is hot, your heart, unable to bear the suffering of others, will respond to everything that moves it. Why then fear that men are difficult to know, that the people are difficult to bring peace to, or that good government throughout the realm cannot be achieved? I beg Your Majesty to give heed to this most essential counsel. Your servant is overwhelmed with the utmost trepidation. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
御批勉吾求敬一之為主忠哉
臣任瀚
臣對臣聞聖王保天下之道存乎仁而其行仁
之道存乎智其合智與仁而成之之道存乎敬
王道之行也仁智敬其為之端與仁不足則澤
不下究而民之憔悴困踣者無所與蘇而其弊
也苛智不足則無以辨賢不肖于天下賢者不
必進不肖者不必退于是乎有殘人不德以尸
民上視民之休戚利害若無預已事甚者或肆
===

亂夫是以不為戎首亦善矣如天下之治何此
求賢所以安民而智又所以行乎其仁者也然
是二者不先之敬則其智之所及或至於偏聽
獨任既無以盡吾求賢之誠而其智之所不及
且至于縱奸長慝又無以致吾安民之實仁不
可終而智亦為之缺然矣是敬又所以成乎智
與仁而不可一日忘焉者也敬以養心心以體

御批：勉吾求敬一之為主，忠哉！

臣任瀚。
臣對：臣聞聖王保天下之道存乎仁，而其行仁之道存乎智，其合智與仁而成之之道存乎敬。王道之行也，仁智敬其為之端與？仁不足，則澤不下究，而民之憔悴困踣者無所與蘇，而其弊也苛。智不足，則無以辨賢不肖于天下，賢者不必進，不肖者不必退，于是乎有殘人不德以尸民上，視民之休戚利害若無預已事，甚者或肆其侵漁剥削，一任其凋敝，不為之所，而其弊也亂。夫是以不為戎首亦善矣，如天下之治何？此求賢所以安民，而智又所以行乎其仁者也。然是二者不先之敬，則其智之所及或至於偏聽獨任，既無以盡吾求賢之誠，而其智之所不及且至于縱奸長慝，又無以致吾安民之實，仁不可終，而智亦為之缺然矣。是敬又所以成乎智與仁，而不可一日忘焉者也。敬以養心，心以體道，道以張法，法以盡變。斯海內之化清和咸理，兵革不試，暴濫不作，物道素朴，獄訟衰息，紀綱
translation_en:
Imperial comment: “You urge me to seek reverent single-mindedness as the guiding principle. How loyal!”

Your servant, Ren Han.
Your servant replies: I have heard that the means by which a sage king preserves All-under-Heaven lies in benevolence; the means by which he practices benevolence lies in wisdom; and the means by which he unites wisdom and benevolence and brings them to fulfillment lies in reverence. In putting the Kingly Way into practice, are not benevolence, wisdom, and reverence its starting points? If benevolence is insufficient, beneficence does not reach those below, and those among the people who are worn down, impoverished, and brought low have no means of recovery. The resulting evil is harsh government. If wisdom is insufficient, there is no means of distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy throughout the realm. The worthy are not necessarily advanced, nor the unworthy necessarily dismissed. Thus cruel men without virtue occupy positions over the people, regarding their well-being and distress, their advantages and injuries, as though these were no concern of their own. The worst may even indulge in extortion and exploitation, leaving the people entirely to decline and impoverishment without making provision for them. The resulting evil is disorder. Under such circumstances, merely avoiding becoming the instigator of armed conflict would be fortunate enough; what could one do about bringing good order to All-under-Heaven? This is why seeking worthy men is the means of bringing peace to the people, and wisdom is in turn the means of putting benevolence into practice.

Yet unless reverence precedes these two, even where one's wisdom reaches, one may fall into listening to only one side and entrusting responsibility to a single person, thus failing to fulfill one's sincere intention to seek worthy men. Where one's wisdom does not reach, one may even indulge wickedness and foster evil, thus also failing to achieve the actual results of bringing peace to the people. Benevolence cannot be carried through to completion, and wisdom too is thereby left deficient. Reverence is therefore also the means of bringing wisdom and benevolence to fulfillment, and must not be forgotten for even a single day.

Through reverence one nourishes the mind; through the mind one embodies the Way; through the Way one establishes laws; through laws one responds fully to changing circumstances. Thus the transforming influence throughout the realm becomes pure and harmonious, and all is well ordered. Arms and armor are not put to use; violence and excess do not arise; the ways of things remain plain and simple [?]; lawsuits and litigation dwindle and cease; the guiding principles and bonds of government …

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
正於上風俗昭明於下而頌聲作王道成矣奚
用外焉以取治法為欽惟
皇帝陛下智以明王度仁以惠萬物敬以凝天道而
成世務不自賢聖詢于寡昧究觀王道圖惟化
原此千古人臣獻款攄忠之一遇也臣聞之孔
子曰事君先資其言拜自獻其身以成其信臣
誠不佞顧於致身之始曾無一言可得先資以
為
陛下獻哉謹冒死以對臣伏讀
聖制首曰治天下之道其大者在乎知人安民盖知
===
人則哲能官人安民則惠黎民懷之此皐陶陳
謨之深意而
陛下之言及此天下生人之福也使愚臣於此有所
隱伏回護畏罪而不敢言上以負
陛下之盛心而下以昧天下之至計四方後代其謂
臣何臣請披肝瀝膽為
陛下言之願試聽焉臣竊觀
陛下自即位以來災變頻仍近古未有語謂天心仁
愛之符是也往年下罪已之詔以為政化未臻
民心積怨上干天和究其咎本實乎一人所致

愛之符是也往年下罪己之詔以為政化未臻
民心積怨上干天和不究其咎本實予一人所致
punctuated:
正於上，風俗昭明於下，而頌聲作，王道成矣。奚用外焉以取治法為？欽惟皇帝陛下，智以明王度，仁以惠萬物，敬以凝天道而成世務。不自賢聖，詢于寡昧，究觀王道，圖惟化原，此千古人臣獻款攄忠之一遇也。臣聞之，孔子曰：「事君，先資其言，拜自獻其身，以成其信。」臣誠不佞，顧於致身之始，曾無一言可得先資，以為陛下獻哉？謹冒死以對。
臣伏讀聖制，首曰：「治天下之道，其大者在乎知人安民。」盖知人則哲，能官人；安民則惠，黎民懷之。此皐陶陳謨之深意，而陛下之言及此，天下生人之福也。使愚臣於此有所隱伏回護，畏罪而不敢言，上以負陛下之盛心，而下以昧天下之至計，四方後代，其謂臣何？臣請披肝瀝膽，為陛下言之，願試聽焉。
臣竊觀陛下自即位以來，災變頻仍，近古未有。語謂天心仁愛之符，是也。往年下罪已之詔，以為政化未臻，民心積怨，上干天和，究其咎本，實乎一人所致。
translation_en:
…are set right above, and customs become enlightened below; songs of praise arise, and the Way of the true king is accomplished. Why seek elsewhere for methods of government? I reverently reflect that Your Imperial Majesty uses wisdom to illuminate royal standards, benevolence to benefit all things, and reverence to give firm embodiment to Heaven’s Way and accomplish the affairs of the world. Without deeming yourself worthy or sage, you consult the ignorant and unenlightened, thoroughly examine the kingly Way, and consider the sources of moral transformation. This is an opportunity such as a subject encounters but once in a thousand ages to offer his sincerity and express his loyalty. Your servant has heard these words of Confucius: “In serving a ruler, first present your words, then bow and offer your own person, thereby fulfilling your pledge [?].” Your servant is indeed untalented; yet, at the outset of dedicating myself to service, could I have not a single word to present beforehand as an offering to Your Majesty? At the risk of death, I respectfully submit my reply.
Your servant has reverently read the imperial decree, which begins: “Of the ways to govern all under Heaven, the greatest lie in knowing men and bringing peace to the people.” Knowing men is discernment and enables one to appoint them to office; bringing peace to the people is kindness, and the common people cherish it. This is the profound meaning of Gao Yao’s exposition of his counsels. That Your Majesty speaks of this is a blessing for all living people under Heaven. If your foolish servant were to conceal anything or evade the matter, fearing punishment and not daring to speak, I would fail Your Majesty’s lofty intentions above and obscure the most vital plans for the realm below. What would people in all quarters and in later generations say of me? I beg to lay bare my innermost thoughts before Your Majesty and ask that you hear me out.
Your servant humbly observes that, since Your Majesty ascended the throne, calamities and anomalies have occurred repeatedly, to a degree unprecedented in recent ages. The saying that these are tokens of Heaven’s benevolent concern is correct. In a previous year, you issued an edict reproaching yourself, declaring that government and moral transformation had not reached fulfillment, that accumulated resentment in the people’s hearts had disturbed Heaven’s harmony above, and that, on tracing the fault to its source, it was indeed attributable to you alone.

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
臣時竊伏草茅每見道路聞者皆歎息泣下願
少須臾無死以觀化理之成及今三五年来人
心之望已極猶未見內盡消弭之道上獲天和
之應使海內曠然升于大猷臣竊疑之夫春秋
以天反時為災地反物為妖人反德為亂亂則
妖災生
陛下之德如天之無不覆而地之罔不載臣猶以為
未至是妄言也然而天人之交間不容髮此在
陛下燕閒蠖濩之中深宫獨運之地澄神自思而得
之耳
===
聖制深以任官非人為懼且疑賢不肖進退之差以
及於勸懲之失其宜選任之非其道此見
陛下超然遠覽神洞物外直欲秉至公以消弭變異
阜安生民雖成湯桑林之責周宣雲漢之憂高
宗肜日之修省不是過也臣聞後漢鄭興有言
變咎之来不可不慎其要在因人之心擇人處
位而已
陛下平日宫庭之間所震怒而賜譴者何人也合于
聖意誘而進之者何人也其所賜譴者必當其
罪而其所誘而進之者必當其功大臣不得寵

punctuated:
臣時竊伏草茅，每見道路聞者皆歎息泣下，願少須臾無死，以觀化理之成。及今三五年来，人心之望已極，猶未見內盡消弭之道，上獲天和之應，使海內曠然升于大猷，臣竊疑之。夫《春秋》以天反時為災，地反物為妖，人反德為亂，亂則妖災生。陛下之德，如天之無不覆，而地之罔不載，臣猶以為未至，是妄言也。然而天人之交，間不容髮，此在陛下燕閒蠖濩之中、深宫獨運之地，澄神自思而得之耳。

聖制深以任官非人為懼，且疑賢不肖進退之差，以及於勸懲之失其宜、選任之非其道。此見陛下超然遠覽，神洞物外，直欲秉至公以消弭變異，阜安生民。雖成湯桑林之責、周宣雲漢之憂、高宗肜日之修省，不是過也。臣聞後漢鄭興有言：「變咎之来，不可不慎，其要在因人之心，擇人處位而已。」陛下平日宫庭之間，所震怒而賜譴者何人也？合于聖意，誘而進之者何人也？其所賜譴者必當其罪，而其所誘而進之者必當其功。大臣不得寵
translation_en:
At that time, your servant was living in obscurity. Whenever I encountered people along the roads who had heard the proclamation, they all sighed and shed tears, wishing only to remain alive a little longer to witness the fulfillment of your transforming rule. Now, after three to five years, the people’s expectations have reached their utmost pitch. Yet we have still not seen every means of dispelling calamities fully pursued within the realm, nor a corresponding response of heavenly harmony above, whereby all within the seas might emerge into an age of grand and enlightened governance. Your servant privately wonders at this. The Spring and Autumn Annals regards Heaven’s departure from the seasons as calamity, the earth’s departure from the proper nature of things as portent, and humanity’s departure from virtue as disorder. When disorder arises, portents and calamities follow. Your Majesty’s virtue is like Heaven, which covers everything, and earth, which bears everything. For your servant still to consider it imperfect would be presumptuous speech. Yet the connection between Heaven and humanity admits not even a hair’s breadth of separation. This is something Your Majesty can discover only by stilling your spirit and reflecting upon yourself in the secluded repose of your leisure, within the inner palace where you exercise your judgment alone.

The imperial decree expresses profound concern that offices have been entrusted to unsuitable men. It also questions whether errors in advancing or dismissing the worthy and unworthy have led to inappropriate rewards and punishments and improper selection and appointment. This shows that Your Majesty surveys matters from a lofty and far-reaching perspective, with an understanding that penetrates beyond outward appearances, seeking only to uphold perfect impartiality so as to dispel anomalies and calamities and bring prosperity and peace to the people. Even Cheng Tang’s self-reproach at Sanglin, King Xuan of Zhou’s anxiety expressed in “The Milky Way,” and Gaozong’s self-cultivation and reflection on the day of the supplementary sacrifice did not surpass this. Your servant has heard that Zheng Xing of the Later Han said: “When anomalies and calamities arrive, one must respond with care. The essential thing is simply to heed people’s hearts and choose men to fill the offices.” In Your Majesty’s daily life within the palace, who are those upon whom you vent your anger and bestow punishment? Who are those who accord with your imperial wishes and whom you encourage and advance? Those whom you punish must receive what their offenses merit, and those whom you encourage and advance must receive what their achievements merit. High ministers must not favor…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
名譽之人小臣不得進浮薄之士如此則變安
從生此其逺百姓而近
陛下之耳目者臣固不得而深言之矣其有下親於
民而上之所不及知者泯泯棼棼可為流涕太
息者不少臣亦豈得而勿言哉竊惟勸懲之典
莫急於考課而選任之法當責之銓衡今之選
舉考課則臣之所嘗竊歎而深惜之者也何則
士方窮時讀古書見循良傳躍躍動義色出死
生自誓願作一良有司謝天下及反顧見其家
室無長物展轉歔欷不能自禁靡然無復初志
甚者鑽剌徼倖取中原名郡縣自列得則凌暴
誅求罔所不至不則怨且怒終其身置此等於
民上而欲民之得其所辟之愛其羊豚而牧之
豺也世無完畜矣故
祖宗之於士養之以節義而威勸之以賞罰其用之
各盡其才而其課之也幽明殿最各程其實則
善者益勉而不善者化能官者上而不能官者
斯下下矣若夫選舉之失其平資格壞之也
國初用人或舉于畊商或徵于漁釣脫去流品惟
其才賢是猶有古意語曰不習為吏視已成事

punctuated:
名譽之人，小臣不得進浮薄之士。如此，則變安從生？此其逺百姓而近陛下之耳目者，臣固不得而深言之矣。其有下親於民而上之所不及知者，泯泯棼棼，可為流涕太息者不少，臣亦豈得而勿言哉？

竊惟勸懲之典，莫急於考課，而選任之法，當責之銓衡。今之選舉考課，則臣之所嘗竊歎而深惜之者也。何則？士方窮時，讀古書，見循良傳，躍躍動義色，出死生自誓，願作一良有司，謝天下。及反顧見其家室無長物，展轉歔欷，不能自禁，靡然無復初志。甚者鑽剌徼倖，取中原名郡縣自列，得則凌暴誅求，罔所不至；不則怨且怒，終其身。置此等於民上，而欲民之得其所，辟之愛其羊豚而牧之豺也，世無完畜矣。

故祖宗之於士，養之以節義，而威勸之以賞罰。其用之，各盡其才；而其課之也，幽明殿最，各程其實。則善者益勉，而不善者化；能官者上，而不能官者斯下下矣。若夫選舉之失其平，資格壞之也。國初用人，或舉于畊商，或徵于漁釣，脫去流品，惟其才賢，是猶有古意。語曰：「不習為吏，視已成事。」
translation_en:
…men of reputation; lesser officials must not advance frivolous men. If this is so, whence could calamities arise? These are matters remote from the common people but close to Your Majesty’s eyes and ears; your servant cannot presume to discuss them in depth. Yet there are matters directly affecting the people below that those above cannot know: confused and tangled affairs, many of which call for tears and deep sighs. How could your servant refrain from speaking of them?

I humbly consider that, among the institutions for encouragement and chastisement, none is more urgent than the evaluation of officials, while responsibility for selection and appointment should rest with the personnel authorities. Present practices of selection and evaluation are precisely what your servant has privately lamented and deeply regretted. Why? While a scholar is still in straitened circumstances, he reads ancient books and encounters biographies of benevolent officials. Eagerly stirred, his face lights up with righteousness, and, heedless of life and death, he vows to become a good local official and repay the world. But when he looks back and sees that his household has nothing to spare, he tosses and turns, sighing and sobbing uncontrollably, until he gives way and loses his original resolve. Worse still, some scheme for advancement and seek favors, putting themselves forward for posts in renowned prefectures and counties of the Central Plain. If successful, they resort to every kind of oppression and extortion; if unsuccessful, they remain resentful and angry all their lives. To place such men over the people and expect the people to live securely is like loving one’s sheep and pigs while setting a jackal to tend them. No livestock in the world would remain unharmed.

Thus, in dealing with scholars, the dynastic ancestors nurtured integrity and righteousness, and used rewards and punishments to encourage and deter them. In employing men, they made full use of each man’s abilities; in evaluating them, they assessed actual performance, distinguishing the unworthy from the worthy and the worst from the best. The good were thereby encouraged to strive still harder, and the bad were reformed; those capable of holding office advanced, while those incapable were demoted—the text repeats “down” here [?]. As for the loss of fairness in selection, rigid requirements of qualifications and seniority have undermined it. At the beginning of the dynasty, men were sometimes recommended from farming and commerce, sometimes summoned from fishing. Categories of social standing were set aside, and only ability and worth mattered: this still preserved the spirit of antiquity. As the saying goes: “One need not first train to be an official; look to what has already been done.”

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
蓋言古也比者稍有兵荒動聞入粟買官之令
以為常制累世莫能變臣聞人之所好而爭趨
焉者韓非有言非名之即利之也以粟易官之
名豈人所好而人固趨之不得於名彼其不求
得於利哉人人以其利之心上應於國而國且
便之以布于天下夫其一人入粟幾何而其所
取諸民者必十倍而後饜是為天下謀小利而
獲大害也又况高官顯秩自甲科之外雖智且
賢弗及則彼修於冥冥無所慕而為善者世寧
幾人哉臣故曰資格壞之非人才之罪也董仲
===
===
舒曰邪氣積于下怨惡畜于上此災異所緣而
起矣方今天下之衰氣孰有大于冗員貪吏苟
身圖以誤國家者而災異實因之臣願
陛下嚴僥倖覬覦之禁公賞罰黜陟之典杜買官鬻
爵之弊革年地資望之說則賢才閬伏下吏革
心上天之變異可回生民之流亡可復而所以
為智之道莫大於此矣
聖制又謂內有盜賊之擾外有戎狄之患此亦重為
民之害者以
陛下愛民之深憂民之切如此而

蓋言古也。比者稍有兵荒，動聞入粟買官之令，以為常制，累世莫能變。臣聞人之所好而爭趨焉者，韓非有言：「非名之，即利之也。」以粟易官之名，豈人所好？而人固趨之，不得於名，彼其不求得於利哉？人人以其利之心上應於國，而國且便之，以布于天下。夫其一人入粟幾何，而其所取諸民者必十倍而後饜，是為天下謀小利而獲大害也。又况高官顯秩，自甲科之外，雖智且賢弗及，則彼修於冥冥、無所慕而為善者，世寧幾人哉？臣故曰：「資格壞之，非人才之罪也。」董仲舒曰：「邪氣積于下，怨惡畜于上，此災異所緣而起矣。」方今天下之衰氣，孰有大于冗員貪吏、苟身圖以誤國家者？而災異實因之。臣願陛下嚴僥倖覬覦之禁，公賞罰黜陟之典，杜買官鬻爵之弊，革年地資望之說，則賢才閬伏，下吏革心，上天之變異可回，生民之流亡可復，而所以為智之道，莫大於此矣。

translation_en:
…This presumably refers to antiquity. Recently, whenever there is even a little warfare or famine, we hear of orders permitting people to purchase office by contributing grain. This has become an established practice, which successive generations have been unable to change. Your servant has heard that, concerning what people desire and compete to pursue, Han Fei said: “They seek either reputation or profit.” Is the reputation of having exchanged grain for office something people desire? Yet people certainly pursue it. If they gain nothing in reputation, will they not seek to gain in profit? Everyone responds to the state’s call with a heart bent on profit, while the state finds the practice convenient and promulgates it throughout the realm. How much grain does any one person contribute? Yet he will not be satisfied until he has extracted ten times as much from the people. This is to seek a small profit for the realm and incur great harm.
Moreover, high offices and distinguished ranks are beyond the reach of anyone outside the ranks of those successful in the highest examinations, however wise and worthy he may be. How many people in the world will cultivate themselves in obscurity and do good without aspiring to any reward? Thus your servant says: “The rules of eligibility have spoiled the system; the fault does not lie with the available talent.” Dong Zhongshu said: “Pernicious influences accumulate below, and resentment and hatred gather above: these are the sources from which calamities and anomalies arise.” Among the forces weakening the realm today, what could be greater than superfluous officials and corrupt functionaries who scheme for their own advantage to the detriment of the state? Calamities and anomalies indeed arise from these.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would strictly enforce prohibitions against seeking advancement through undeserved favor, administer impartially the rules for rewards, punishments, dismissals, and promotions, eliminate the abuses of purchasing offices and selling ranks, and discard considerations of age, locality, seniority, and reputation [?]. Then worthy talent would remain concealed [?], subordinate officials would reform their hearts, Heaven’s anomalies could be reversed, and displaced people could return to their homes. No way of exercising wisdom is greater than this.
The imperial decree further states: “Within, there are disturbances caused by bandits; without, there is the menace of the Rong and Di.” These too inflict grave harm upon the people. Given that Your Majesty’s love for the people is so deep and your concern for them so earnest, yet…

title: 嘉靖八年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之臣在内者不能消息寇亂在外者不能愼固
邊圉天未厭禍也而又離民以佐災犬戎樹惇
矣而且觀之兵則
陛下亦豈得晏然已乎周官大司徒以荒政聚萬民
其十有二曰除盜賊夫除盜賊而置之末者先
王之所甚不得已也以人情言之盜賊亦人耳
人有不愛其身與其父母妻子居室畜產百物
而喜棄其壤土者乎愛之而或為人所奪其身
有困于刑罰工役不得息其父母妻子有苦於
流離轉死不得會聚其居室畜產百物有耗于
===
征求貢輸不得自奉自娛是數者皆足以傷於
民心彼其時節不忍捨棄而一旦奪于有力之
疆其不去為盜奚待也語曰德則其人也不德
則其鹿也人情撫則后虐則讎豈有常哉今西
南之國一遇歉歲即赭衣載道旌旗翳空臣愚
以為在上者有以奪其所愛而激成之未必吾
民之能自為盜也若夫邊事之興宋人謂出於
徼功幸利之徒黷武玩寇不以朝廷大計為念
前日榆林松茂之役郡縣嗷嗷令小吏督罷民
轉餉數千里外號稱籌邊夫亦既左矣而荏苒

translation_en:
…Yet Your Majesty’s servants within the realm cannot quell bandit disturbances, and those stationed outside cannot securely defend the frontier. Heaven has not yet tired of sending calamities, yet they further alienate the people and thereby compound the disasters. The Quanrong have grown strong [?], and moreover make a display of arms [?]. How, then, could Your Majesty remain at ease?
In the Offices of Zhou, the Minister of Education gathers and sustains the people through measures for famine relief; the twelfth is called “eliminating bandits.” That eliminating bandits was placed last shows that the former kings resorted to it only when they had no other choice. In terms of human feelings, bandits too are simply people. Is there anyone who does not cherish his own person, his parents, wife and children, his dwelling, livestock, and possessions, but instead delights in abandoning his land? Yet what people cherish may be taken from them. They themselves may be worn down by punishments and compulsory labor, without respite; their parents, wives, and children may suffer displacement and death in their wanderings, unable to reunite; their dwellings, livestock, and possessions may be depleted by exactions and tribute deliveries, leaving them unable to provide for themselves or enjoy their lives. Each of these is enough to wound the people’s hearts. What they cannot bear to relinquish in ordinary times [?] is suddenly seized by the powerful. What else would it take to drive them away to become bandits?
A saying runs: “Treat them with virtue, and they are your people; treat them without virtue, and they are your deer.” Such are human feelings: nurture people, and they regard you as their sovereign; abuse them, and they regard you as their enemy. How could their allegiance be unchanging? Today, whenever the southwestern regions encounter a poor harvest, roads fill with men in convicts’ ochre clothing, and banners obscure the sky. In my humble view, those above have taken away what the people cherish and provoked this outcome; it is not necessarily that our people become bandits of their own accord.
As for the outbreak of frontier troubles, men of the Song said that these arose from those who sought military merit and hoped for personal gain, who recklessly resorted to arms and treated the enemy lightly, without thought for the court’s larger plans. During the recent campaigns at Yulin and Songmao, the prefectures and counties cried out in distress. Petty officials were ordered to compel exhausted people to transport military provisions several thousand li away. This was called planning for frontier defense, but it was already gravely misguided. And as time drifts on…

text:
衰羸之卒不經一戰者又引領待哺謂足以羽
儀塞垣此何理也人有病枵腹者斷肢體脯筋
骸以充之然而無益於死者天下之大舛也先
王備邊以衛中國今邊有莫敵之勢而中國無
聊生之民可矣乎此臣謂王者不治夷狄趙充
國所為善之善者令邊人自給毋以勤國家也
臣願
陛下內擇賢守令以宰治郡邑外擇良將帥以控制
邊鄙誅有位之盜去黷武之戎汰冗兵抑浮費
則寇亂可弭戎狄可清民力可蘇而所以為仁
===
之道莫大於此矣然此但就
陛下所以策臣者而論之耳若以臣愚言上天之變
未息是生民未安也生民之未安是賢才未盡
用也賢才之未盡用或者

punctuated:
衰羸之卒，不經一戰者，又引領待哺，謂足以羽儀塞垣，此何理也？人有病枵腹者，斷肢體，脯筋骸以充之，然而無益於死者，天下之大舛也。先王備邊以衛中國，今邊有莫敵之勢，而中國無聊生之民，可矣乎？此臣謂王者不治夷狄，趙充國所為善之善者，令邊人自給，毋以勤國家也。臣願陛下內擇賢守令以宰治郡邑，外擇良將帥以控制邊鄙，誅有位之盜，去黷武之戎，汰冗兵，抑浮費，則寇亂可弭，戎狄可清，民力可蘇，而所以為仁之道，莫大於此矣。
然此但就陛下所以策臣者而論之耳。若以臣愚言，上天之變未息，是生民未安也；生民之未安，是賢才未盡用也；賢才之未盡用，或者聖心其猶未純乎？然觀陛下覽四方災異奏牘，則惕然懼；見古聖賢箴規，則泠然省，此其心亦未為不純矣。而聖制猶謂保邦安民之念雖存，求其所以，實無一得者，豈非深憂過計，道愈至而心愈不足，必欲臣愚罄竭私悃，而無少隱伏之意哉？臣不敢槩舉
translation_en:
…The weak and emaciated soldiers, who have not fought a single battle, also crane their necks awaiting food. To say that they suffice to lend dignity to the frontier defenses—what reasoning is this? If someone suffering from an empty stomach cuts off his own limbs and makes dried meat of his sinews and bones to fill it, yet gains nothing toward averting death, this is a tremendous perversity. The former kings defended the frontiers to protect the central realm. Can it be acceptable now for the frontier to possess an invincible military force while the people of the central realm have no means of subsistence? This is what your servant means in saying that a true king does not undertake to govern the Yi and Di peoples. The very best feature of what Zhao Chongguo did was to make the frontier population self-supporting, without burdening the state. Your servant wishes Your Majesty to select worthy prefects and magistrates to govern the prefectures and counties within, and capable generals and commanders to control the frontier regions without; execute the robbers who hold office, end campaigns of reckless warfare, discharge superfluous soldiers, and curb wasteful expenditure. Then bandit disturbances can be quelled, threats from the Rong and Di peoples cleared away, and the people's strength restored. There is no greater way to practice benevolence than this.
Yet this discusses only the matters on which Your Majesty has questioned your servant. In my humble view, the fact that Heaven's anomalies have not ceased means that the people are not yet at peace. That the people are not yet at peace means that worthy talent has not been fully employed. That worthy talent has not been fully employed—might this mean that the sagely imperial heart is still not wholly pure? Yet when I observe Your Majesty reading memorials reporting disasters and anomalies from all quarters, you become apprehensive and fearful; when you encounter the admonitions of ancient sages and worthies, you reflect with clear awareness. Your heart therefore cannot be called impure. Yet the imperial decree still says that, although the desire to preserve the state and bring peace to the people remains, you have in fact gained no understanding of how to accomplish it. Surely this expresses your profound concern and painstaking deliberation: the more perfected your Way becomes, the less satisfied your heart is. Is it not your intention that your humble servant should pour out all his sincere thoughts, concealing nothing whatever? Your servant dares not speak merely in generalities…

punctuated:
請得以敬終之。堯之言曰：「允執厥中。」謂執云者，戰兢持守而不敢縱之辭也。其意曰：天無定命，理忽無定形，人心無定幾，執以定其所無定焉云爾。是故「安汝止，惟幾惟康」，「勅天之命，惟時惟幾」者，三聖相授受，守一道也。是故堯舜之世，民罔不安，臣無不可知，而猶曰「帝其難之」者，不敢以易心乘之，敬之道也。
陛下如以前所陳數者為憂，則孰若取聖制所謂堯舜者以為法乎？孔子之後子順曰：「昔者吾先君子欲作文武而至焉，文武欲作堯舜而至焉。」是故大聖人之道存乎有作，不可退然而止也。臣願陛下勿以臣言為迂，留神省覽，益求所謂敬一者而精之。今天下復見唐虞之治，則愚臣幸甚。臣干冒天威，無任隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…Permit me to conclude with reverent attentiveness. Yao said: “Sincerely hold fast to the mean.” The expression “hold fast” conveys maintaining one's grasp with trembling vigilance, not daring to let go. Its meaning is simply this: Heaven's mandate is not fixed; principle has no fixed form [?]; and the incipient impulses of the human heart are not fixed. By holding fast, one gives stability to what is unstable. Thus, “Rest securely in your proper place; attend to incipient developments and to well-being,” and “Attend diligently to Heaven's mandate; attend to the times and to incipient developments” express the single Way that the three sages transmitted to and received from one another and preserved. Thus, in the age of Yao and Shun, none of the people lacked peace, and no minister's character was beyond knowing. Yet they still said, “Let the emperor regard this as difficult.” They dared not approach it with a complacent heart: this is the way of reverent attentiveness.
If Your Majesty is troubled by the several matters set forth above, what could be better than taking as models Yao and Shun, whom Your Majesty's decree mentions? Zishun, a descendant of Confucius, said: “Formerly, my late revered ancestor sought to become like Kings Wen and Wu, and attained that goal; Wen and Wu sought to become like Yao and Shun, and attained that goal.” Thus, the Way of the great sages depends upon active striving; one must not withdraw and stop. Your servant hopes that Your Majesty will not dismiss my words as impractical, but will give them thoughtful scrutiny, pursue still further what is called ‘reverent concentration on the One,’ and refine it. If all under Heaven may now once again witness the governance of Tang and Yu—that is, Yao and Shun—this foolish servant will be most fortunate. Your servant has presumed to offend Your Majesty's heavenly authority and is overcome with dread. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.
